events.enhanced_description: In 179 AD, Abgar IX the Great ascended to the throne as King of Edessa, a significant city in the region that played a crucial role in the cultural and political landscape of the Near East.
events.name: Abgar IX the Great becomes King of Edessa

events.enhanced_description: In 179 AD, Gogukcheon succeeded his father Shindae as King of Goguryeo, continuing the lineage of one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His reign would influence the region's political dynamics.
events.name: Gogukcheon succeeds his father as King of Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: In 179 AD, the full title of the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art was inscribed on two bronze standard measures, marking a significant development in Chinese mathematics. This work would later influence mathematical thought in China.
events.name: Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art appears

events.enhanced_description: In 179 BC, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus was appointed as the Roman governor of Hispania, where he faced uprisings and unrest. His leadership during this tumultuous period was crucial for maintaining Roman authority in the province.
events.name: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus in Hispania

events.enhanced_description: The Pons Aemilius, regarded as the world's first stone bridge, was completed across the Tiber River in Rome in 179 BC. This engineering feat represented a significant advancement in Roman architecture and infrastructure.
events.name: Completion of the Pons Aemilius

events.enhanced_description: In 179 BC, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus was appointed as both censor and princeps senatus in Rome. His dual role highlighted the importance of political leadership and governance in the Roman Republic during this period.
events.name: Appointment of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus

events.enhanced_description: Philip V of Macedon died in 179 BC at Amphipolis, reportedly remorseful for having executed his younger son Demetrius at the urging of his elder son Perseus. His death marked a significant turning point in Macedonian history as Perseus ascended to the throne.
events.name: Death of Philip V of Macedon

events.enhanced_description: In 179 BC, Eumenes II of Pergamum achieved a decisive victory over Pharnaces I of Pontus in a major battle. This conflict resulted in Pharnaces ceding significant territories, reflecting the shifting power dynamics in the region during the Hellenistic period.
events.name: Eumenes II Defeats Pharnaces I

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, the Quadi were chased westwards deeper into Germania by Roman forces, achieving a decisive victory under the command of Praetorian prefect Tarutenius Paternus. This action was part of the ongoing conflicts along the Roman Empire's borders.
events.name: Quadi chased westwards

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, Emperor Marcus Aurelius died after a week's illness at his camp in Vindobona (modern-day Vienna). His death marked the end of the Pax Romana and the beginning of a turbulent period for the Roman Empire.
events.name: Death of Emperor Marcus Aurelius

events.enhanced_description: The year 180 AD marked the end of the Era of the Five Good Emperors, a period characterized by relative peace and prosperity in the Roman Empire. This transition signaled the onset of instability and challenges for the empire.

image.caption: Map of the Roman Empire during Hadrian’s reign.
image.credit: User:Andrein — Own work

events.name: End of the Era of the Five Good Emperors

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, the Roman Empire established a 4-mile wide buffer zone along the Danube River to enhance its defenses against barbarian invasions. This strategic move was part of broader military reforms during a time of increasing external threats.

locations.historical_name: Bavaria (historically relevant region during the 8th century)
locations.name: Salzburg

events.name: Creation of a buffer zone by the Danube

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, work began on the Column of Marcus Aurelius in Rome, intended to commemorate the emperor's victories in the Marcomannic Wars. The column remains a significant historical monument and an example of Roman art.
events.name: Construction of the Column of Marcus Aurelius begins

events.enhanced_description: The period from 180 to 395 AD is recognized as the Late Empire in Rome, characterized by political instability, economic decline, and increasing pressures from external forces. This era set the stage for the eventual fall of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Late Empire in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, Northern tribes from beyond Hadrian's Wall invaded the northern territories of Roman Britain, prompting Emperor Commodus to permit the construction of defensive city walls in several northern cities to protect against these incursions.
events.name: Northern British invasion beyond Hadrian's Wall

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, Cassius Dio, a prominent Roman historian and politician, arrived in Rome and was appointed as a Senator, where he would later contribute significantly to the historical record of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Cassius Dio becomes a Senator

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, the Goths, a group of East Germanic tribes, reached the shores of the Black Sea, marking a significant expansion of their territory and influence in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Goths reach the Black Sea

events.enhanced_description: In 181 AD, the volcano associated with Lake Taupō erupted, one of the largest eruptions in the last 5,000 years, with effects felt as far away as Rome and China, showcasing the far-reaching impact of natural disasters.
events.name: Eruption of Lake Taupō

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, the Greek physician Galen published his influential work 'Methodus Medendo', in which he detailed the connection between paralysis and spinal cord injuries, significantly advancing the understanding of human anatomy and medicine.
events.name: Galen's Methodus Medendo

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, Galen published a popular work on hygiene, which provided insights into health practices and the importance of cleanliness, influencing medical practices for centuries.
events.name: Galen's work on hygiene published

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, twelve Christian inhabitants of Scillium in Numidia were executed in Carthage for refusing to swear an oath to Emperor Commodus, an event that highlighted the growing tensions between the Roman state and early Christians.
events.name: Execution of the Scillitan Martyrs

events.enhanced_description: In 180 AD, Emperor Commodus established an official cult dedicated to the Zoroastrian god Mithra, reflecting the syncretism of religious practices in the Roman Empire and his personal interests.
events.name: Cult of Mithra established

events.enhanced_description: In 180 BC, Perseus of Macedonia orchestrated the execution of his younger brother Demetrius, accusing him of plotting against their father, King Philip V. This act of fratricide was a critical moment in the power struggle within the Macedonian royal family.
events.name: Perseus Persuades Execution of Demetrius

events.enhanced_description: In a decisive battle near modern Genoa, Rome defeated the Ligurians, solidifying its control over the Italian peninsula. This victory led to the deportation of 40,000 Ligurians, marking a significant step in Rome's expansion and consolidation of power in Italy.
events.name: Rome completes its subjugation of all of Italy

events.enhanced_description: The city of Lucca was established as a Roman colony, which played a crucial role in the expansion of Roman influence in the region. This move was part of Rome's broader strategy to secure its territories and integrate various cultures into the Roman Republic.
events.name: Lucca becomes a Roman colony

events.enhanced_description: At just six years old, Ptolemy VI Philometor ascended to the throne as co-regent alongside his mother, Cleopatra I. Despite her Seleucid lineage, Cleopatra maintained amicable relations with Rome, influencing the political landscape of the Hellenistic world.
events.name: Ptolemy VI Philometor begins co-regency

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Aristophanes of Byzantium, Aristarchus of Samothrace was appointed as the chief librarian at the Library of Alexandria. His tenure marked a significant period in the preservation and advancement of knowledge in the ancient world.
events.name: Aristarchus of Samothrace becomes librarian at Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: Demetrius I initiated his invasion of territories that are now part of Pakistan, following the collapse of the Mauryan dynasty. This military campaign aimed to expand his influence and control over the region, which was pivotal for the Indo-Greek Kingdom.
events.name: Demetrius I invades present-day Pakistan

events.enhanced_description: Apollodotus I, a general under Demetrius I, ascended to kingship over the western and southern parts of the Indo-Greek kingdom, including Taxila and regions in Sindh and Gujarat. His reign marked a continuation of Indo-Greek rule in the area, maintaining loyalty to Demetrius I.
events.name: Apollodotus I becomes king of the Indo-Greek kingdom

events.enhanced_description: The Lü Clan Disturbance marked a significant power struggle within the Han dynasty following the death of Empress Lü. Key imperial princes and military leaders orchestrated a coup against the Lü Clan, leading to their overthrow and massacre, which reshaped the political landscape of the dynasty.
events.name: Lü Clan Disturbance

events.enhanced_description: In a desperate bid to secure power, conspirators denied that Emperor Hui was the father of the young Emperor Houshao, leading to a coup that resulted in Houshao's execution. This political upheaval ultimately placed Emperor Wen on the throne, altering the course of the Han dynasty.
events.name: Conspirators deny Emperor Hui's paternity

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty honored the relatives of Zhao Tuo, the ruler of Nanyue, reaffirming the vassal relationship between the two states. This act helped stabilize the region and maintain a semblance of peace between the Han dynasty and the Nanyue kingdom.
events.name: Emperor Wen honors Zhao Tuo's family

events.enhanced_description: In 181 AD, Emperor Commodus and Lucius Antistius Burrus were appointed as Roman Consuls, a position of significant political power in the Roman Republic and Empire.
events.name: Commodus and Burrus become Consuls

events.enhanced_description: Around 181 AD, the Picts successfully overran the Antonine Wall in Britannia, demonstrating the increasing pressure on Roman defenses in the region and leading to a strategic retreat to Hadrian's Wall.
events.name: Picts overrun the Antonine Wall

events.enhanced_description: After 24 years of reign marked by decline, Ptolemy V was poisoned, leading to a power vacuum in Egypt. His young son, Ptolemy VI Philometor, succeeded him under the regency of Cleopatra the Syrian, setting the stage for further political intrigue in the region.
events.name: Ptolemy V is poisoned

events.enhanced_description: Rome established a colony at Aquileia, strategically located to serve as a frontier fortress against Illyrian advances. This foundation was part of Rome's broader military and political strategy to secure its northern borders.
events.name: Rome founds a colony at Aquileia

events.enhanced_description: Pharnaces I of Pontus launched an invasion into Galatia, targeting Eumenes II of Pergamum and Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia. Although initial hostilities were suspended due to Roman intervention, the conflict eventually reignited, demonstrating the volatile political landscape of the region.
events.name: Pharnaces I invades Galatia

events.enhanced_description: Empress Lü of the Han dynasty dispatched an army to reclaim Nanyue, but the campaign faltered due to adverse conditions. This failed military expedition highlighted the challenges faced by the Han dynasty in maintaining control over its vassal states.
events.name: Empress Lü attacks Nanyue

events.enhanced_description: Zhao Tuo, the emperor of Nanyue, successfully launched military campaigns against neighboring vassal kingdoms, securing their submission. His actions solidified his power and influence in the region, establishing Nanyue as a formidable entity in southern China.
events.name: Zhao Tuo secures submission of vassal kingdoms

events.enhanced_description: In 182 AD, Emperor Commodus narrowly escaped an assassination attempt orchestrated by his sister Lucilla and a faction of senators, leading to a brutal crackdown on perceived conspirators and the exile of Lucilla.
events.name: Assassination attempt on Emperor Commodus

events.enhanced_description: The death of Prusias I Chlorus marked a significant transition in Bithynian leadership as his son ascended to the throne as Prusias II. This change in rulership would influence the political dynamics of the region during a period of increasing Roman influence.
events.name: Prusias I Chlorus dies

events.enhanced_description: In 183 BC, the Roman Republic established colonies at Mutina (modern Modena), Pisa, and Parma, as part of its expansion into northern and central Italy. These settlements were crucial for consolidating Roman control over the region and facilitating trade and military logistics.
events.name: Roman colonies established at Mutina, Pisa, and Parma

events.enhanced_description: The renowned Roman general Scipio Africanus, famed for his victory over Hannibal in the Second Punic War, died in 183 BC at Liternum. His death marked the end of an era for Roman military leadership and left a significant impact on Roman politics and military strategy.
events.name: Death of Scipio Africanus

events.enhanced_description: In 183 BC, Roman statesman Titus Quinctius Flamininus was sent to the court of Prusias I of Bithynia to demand the surrender of Hannibal, the former Carthaginian general. Faced with imminent betrayal, Hannibal chose to end his life by poisoning himself in the village of Libyssa.
events.name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus demands Hannibal's surrender

events.enhanced_description: In 183 BC, the town of Messene rebelled against the Achaean League, leading to the capture of its general Philopoemen during a skirmish. Philopoemen was ultimately forced to take poison to die honorably rather than face execution.
events.name: Rebellion of Messene against the Achaean League

events.enhanced_description: In 184 AD, the Yellow Turban Rebellion erupted in China, led by Zhang Jue, as peasants revolted against the Eastern Han dynasty, marking a significant uprising that challenged imperial authority.
events.name: Yellow Turban Rebellion in China

events.enhanced_description: In 184 AD, the Disasters of the Partisan Prohibitions, a series of political purges and conflicts within the Eastern Han dynasty, came to an end, leading to a period of relative stability.
events.name: End of the Disasters of the Partisan Prohibitions

events.enhanced_description: In 184 AD, Zhang Jue led a massive peasant revolt against Emperor Ling of Han, marching towards Luoyang with an army of 360,000 men, which resulted in widespread destruction of government facilities.
events.name: Zhang Jue leads peasant revolt

events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 184 AD, Zhang Jue died of illness while his brothers were killed in battles against Han forces, leading to the scattering of the Yellow Turban rebels and a decline in their organized resistance.
events.name: Zhang Jue's death and scattering of rebels

events.enhanced_description: In 184 AD, the Guanghe era of the Eastern Han dynasty came to an end, transitioning into the Zhongping era, marking a new phase in the imperial timeline.
events.name: Transition from Guanghe to Zhongping era

events.enhanced_description: In 184 AD, King Gogukcheon of Goguryeo successfully repelled Chinese armies back to Liaodong, asserting the strength and independence of his kingdom against external threats.
events.name: King Gogukcheon pushes back Chinese armies

events.enhanced_description: In 184 AD, Beolhyu ascended to the throne as king of Silla, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, during a period marked by cultural and political development.
events.name: Beolhyu becomes king of Silla

events.enhanced_description: In 184 BC, Cato the Elder and Lucius Valerius Flaccus were elected as censors in Rome, where Cato initiated a campaign to restore traditional Roman values and morality. His efforts included taxing luxury and revising the Senate's membership criteria, reflecting a conservative push against Hellenistic influences.
events.name: Cato the Elder and Lucius Valerius Flaccus elected censors

events.enhanced_description: In 184 BC, amid rising tensions regarding Philip V of Macedon, the Roman Senate dispatched Appius Claudius Pulcher to Macedonia to assess the king's military preparations. This diplomatic mission was critical in shaping Rome's strategic response to potential threats.
events.name: Appius Claudius Pulcher sent to Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: In 184 BC, the Romans established the colony of Pisaurum in the territory of the Piceni tribe, located in modern-day Pesaro, Italy. This colony served as a strategic point for Roman expansion and integration of local populations into the Roman political and economic system.
events.name: Establishment of Pisaurum

events.enhanced_description: The Basilica Porcia, the oldest known basilica in Rome, was completed in 184 BC under the supervision of Cato the Elder. This structure played a significant role in Roman public life, serving as a venue for legal proceedings and commercial transactions.
events.name: Completion of the Basilica Porcia

events.enhanced_description: In 184 BC, Empress Lü orchestrated the deposition and execution of her stepson, Emperor Qianshao of Han, following a power struggle within the Han dynasty. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of early imperial China, leading to the ascension of his half-brother, Houshao.
events.name: Empress Lü's coup against Emperor Qianshao

events.enhanced_description: Around 184 BC, Empress Lü banned the trade of iron and horses with the vassal state of Nanyue due to concerns over its growing military strength. This action prompted Nanyue's king Zhao Tuo to declare independence and launch military actions against neighboring states.

image.caption: Map of the ancient kingdom of Nanyue.

events.name: Empress Lü outlaws trade with Nanyue

events.enhanced_description: In June 184 AD, Emperor Ling of Han appointed his brother-in-law He Jin to lead the imperial army against the Yellow Turban rebels, marking a significant military response to the uprising.
events.name: Han imperial army attacks Yellow Turban rebels

events.enhanced_description: In 185 AD, Roman nobles in Britain demanded that Emperor Commodus rescind the powers granted to Tigidius Perennis, leading to his eventual execution amid political turmoil.
events.name: Nobles demand power rescind from Tigidius Perennis

events.enhanced_description: In 185 AD, Publius Helvius Pertinax was appointed governor of Britain, where he faced a mutiny from Roman legions who sought to elevate him to the position of emperor.
events.name: Publius Helvius Pertinax becomes governor of Britain

events.enhanced_description: In 185 AD, Tigidius Perennis, along with his family and many conspirators, were executed for plotting against Emperor Commodus, reflecting the volatile political climate of the time.
events.name: Execution of Tigidius Perennis

events.enhanced_description: In 185 AD, Emperor Commodus drained Rome's treasury to fund extravagant gladiatorial spectacles, participating as a gladiator himself and claiming victories in numerous matches, which further alienated him from the Roman elite.
events.name: Commodus drains treasury for spectacles

events.enhanced_description: In 185 AD, Zhi Yao, a Kushan Buddhist monk, translated significant Buddhist texts into the Chinese language, facilitating the spread of Buddhism in China during the Han dynasty.
events.name: Zhi Yao translates Buddhist texts

events.enhanced_description: Cleomedes, an ancient Greek philosopher, made significant contributions to the understanding of optics, particularly the phenomenon of light refraction through the Earth's atmosphere. His work laid foundational concepts that would influence later scientific thought on light and vision.
events.name: Cleomedes discovers the refraction of light

events.enhanced_description: In 185, Chinese astronomers documented a supernova, now designated SN 185, in the Astrological Annals of the Houhanshu. This event is recognized as the earliest recorded supernova, showcasing the advanced astronomical observations of ancient Chinese scholars.
events.name: Earliest recorded supernova (SN 185)

events.enhanced_description: Around 185, Irenaeus, an early Christian theologian, articulated the belief that there are only four canonical Gospels. His writings were pivotal in shaping the Christian canon and addressing heretical views that proliferated during the early years of the Church.
events.name: Irenaeus writes about the four Gospels

events.enhanced_description: In 185 BC, Scipio Africanus faced accusations from Cato the Elder and his allies regarding alleged bribery from the late Seleucid king Antiochus III. The scandal significantly impacted Scipio's political career, leading him to retreat to his estate at Liternum.
events.name: Accusations against Scipio Africanus

events.enhanced_description: The civil war between northern and southern Egypt concluded in 185 BC with the arrest of Ankmachis by the Ptolemaic general Conanus. This event marked a pivotal moment in Ptolemaic history, stabilizing the region under Ptolemaic control.
events.name: End of the civil war in Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 185 BC, Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated Emperor Brhadrata, marking the end of the Mauryan dynasty and the beginning of the Shunga dynasty. This coup was significant in reshaping the political landscape of ancient India.
events.name: Assassination of Emperor Brhadrata

events.enhanced_description: In February 185, the Yellow Turban Rebellion, a major peasant uprising against the Han dynasty, faced a significant defeat at the hands of the imperial army. However, the rebellion reignited just two months later, spreading to the Taihang Mountains, indicating the resilience of the insurgents and the challenges faced by the Han authorities.
events.name: Defeat of the Yellow Turban Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 186, peasants in Gaul, led by Maternus, staged a significant anti-tax uprising against Roman authorities. This revolt highlighted the growing discontent among the rural population in the Roman Empire, exacerbated by heavy taxation and economic hardship.
events.name: Anti-tax uprising in Gaul

events.enhanced_description: In 186, Roman governor Pertinax narrowly escaped an assassination attempt orchestrated by British usurpers. This incident underscored the political instability and power struggles prevalent in the Roman Empire during this period.
events.name: Assassination attempt on Pertinax

events.enhanced_description: The Hatepe volcanic eruption, occurring around 186, significantly altered the landscape of Lake Taupō and resulted in atmospheric changes that caused red skies worldwide. Recent studies suggest this eruption may have occurred around 233 AD, indicating its far-reaching impact on both the environment and human societies.
events.name: Hatepe volcanic eruption

events.enhanced_description: In 186 BC, the Roman Senate issued the Senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus, which prohibited the Bacchanalia cult throughout Italy due to concerns over its alleged criminal activities and political conspiracies. This decree reflected the Senate's efforts to maintain public order and traditional Roman values.
events.name: Senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus

events.enhanced_description: In 186 BC, Eumenes II of Pergamum achieved a significant victory over Prusias I of Bithynia, consolidating his power in the region. This battle was part of the broader conflicts involving Hellenistic kingdoms and their interactions with Rome.
events.name: Eumenes II defeats Prusias I

events.enhanced_description: The first burial at Mawangdui marks a significant moment in the history of the Western Han dynasty, showcasing the burial practices and beliefs of the time. The site is renowned for its well-preserved tombs and artifacts, providing invaluable insights into Han dynasty culture and society.
events.name: First Burial at Mawangdui

events.enhanced_description: In 187, Septimius Severus married Julia Domna, a Syrian princess, in Lugdunum (modern-day Lyon). This union was politically significant as it strengthened ties between the Roman Empire and the Eastern provinces, and Julia would later play a crucial role in Severus's reign.
events.name: Marriage of Septimius Severus and Julia Domna

events.enhanced_description: In 187, Roman general Clodius Albinus achieved a significant victory against the Chatti, a formidable Germanic tribe inhabiting the area that includes the Black Forest. This battle exemplified the ongoing conflicts between the Roman Empire and the Germanic tribes during this period.
events.name: Clodius Albinus defeats the Chatti

events.enhanced_description: In 187, Olympianus succeeded Pertinax as the bishop of Byzantium, a position he would hold until 198. His leadership during this period was significant in the early Christian community of the city, which would later become a major center of Christianity.
events.name: Olympianus becomes bishop of Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: Antiochus III, the Seleucid king, attempts to collect tribute from a temple near Susa, where he ultimately meets his demise. His death marks a significant turning point for the Seleucid Empire, leading to a power vacuum and succession challenges that would affect the region's political landscape.
events.name: Death of Antiochus III

events.enhanced_description: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus is elected tribune of the plebs, where he famously intervenes to protect Scipio Africanus from prosecution. This act not only highlights the political tensions of the time but also sets the stage for Gracchus's later reforms and conflicts within the Roman Republic.
events.name: Tiberius Gracchus Elected Tribune

events.enhanced_description: The Via Aemilia, a crucial trunk road in northern Italy, is completed, facilitating trade and military movement across the region. This infrastructure project reflects the Roman commitment to connectivity and control over their territories, significantly impacting the economy and culture of ancient Italy.
events.name: Completion of Via Aemilia

events.enhanced_description: Cleopatra I is appointed Vizier to King Ptolemy V Epiphanes, solidifying her influence in the Ptolemaic dynasty. This appointment is significant as it marks the increasing power of women in the political sphere of Hellenistic Egypt during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Cleopatra I Appointed Vizier

events.enhanced_description: In 188, Pertinax was appointed pro-consul of Africa, a position that would enhance his political influence within the Roman Empire. His governance in this region was marked by efforts to stabilize local administration and address the challenges posed by external threats.
events.name: Pertinax becomes pro-consul of Africa

events.enhanced_description: In 188, Queen Himiko, also known as Shingi Waō, ascended to the throne in Japan, ruling until 248. Her reign is noted for its influence on the early formation of Japanese statehood and the establishment of diplomatic relations with neighboring states.
events.name: Queen Himiko begins her reign

events.enhanced_description: Philopoemen, leader of the Achaean League, enters Laconia with his army, dismantling the defenses built by the tyrant Nabis. This event signifies the decline of Spartan power and the rise of the Achaean League as a dominant force in the region, reshaping the political landscape of Greece.
events.name: Philopoemen Enters Laconia

events.enhanced_description: The ongoing conflicts among Greek city-states lead to a growing conviction in Rome that it must take full control of Greece to ensure peace. This sentiment reflects Rome's imperial ambitions and foreshadows its eventual domination of the Greek territories.
events.name: Roman Control Over Greece

events.enhanced_description: The peace treaty of Apamea forces Antiochus III to cede significant territories and pay reparations, marking a pivotal moment in Roman expansion. This treaty not only diminishes the Seleucid Empire but also establishes Rome as the preeminent power in the eastern Mediterranean.
events.name: Peace Treaty of Apamea

events.enhanced_description: Hannibal flees to the court of King Prusias I of Bithynia, seeking refuge after his defeat. This flight underscores the shifting allegiances and the precarious position of former military leaders in the face of Roman power.
events.name: Hannibal Flees to Bithynia

events.enhanced_description: Following the peace of Apamea, Eumenes II is granted several provinces by the Romans, establishing a buffer state against Seleucid expansion. This maneuver illustrates Rome's strategic approach to maintaining influence in Hellenistic Anatolia without direct governance.
events.name: Eumenes II Receives Provinces

events.enhanced_description: After the death of Emperor Hui, Empress Lü effectively consolidates power by installing her grandson as Emperor Qianshao and placing her clan members in key positions. This act marks a significant moment in the political dynamics of the Han dynasty, highlighting the role of women in governance.

events.name: Empress Lü's Control Over Han

events.enhanced_description: In 189, Liu Bian ascended to the throne as the emperor of the Han dynasty, succeeding Emperor Ling. His reign marked a period of political turmoil and the eventual decline of the Han dynasty, setting the stage for the Three Kingdoms period.
events.name: Liu Bian succeeds Emperor Ling

events.enhanced_description: In 189, Dong Zhuo orchestrated the deposition of Liu Bian, replacing him with Emperor Xian as the puppet ruler of the Han dynasty. This power grab marked a significant turning point in Chinese history, leading to widespread chaos and the eventual fragmentation of the empire.
events.name: Dong Zhuo deposes Liu Bian

events.enhanced_description: In 189, a violent purge in Luoyang led to the slaughter of approximately two thousand eunuchs within the Han palace. This brutal event was part of the larger power struggles that characterized the late Han dynasty, reflecting the intense factionalism and political intrigue of the time.
events.name: Purge of eunuchs in Luoyang

events.enhanced_description: In 189, the prominent physician Galen published his influential work, "Treatise on the Various Temperaments," which explored the relationship between bodily humors and health. This treatise contributed significantly to the field of medicine and remained a reference for centuries.
events.name: Galen publishes his treatise

events.enhanced_description: In 189, Pope Victor I became the fourteenth pope of the Christian Church, succeeding Pope Eleuterus. Notably, he was the first pope from Africa, and his leadership played a crucial role in the early development of the Church's structure and doctrine.
events.name: Pope Victor I succeeds Pope Eleuterus

events.enhanced_description: In 189, Demetrius of Alexandria was appointed as the Patriarch of Alexandria, a significant position in the early Christian Church. His tenure was marked by theological developments and the establishment of Alexandria as a major center of Christian thought.
events.name: Demetrius of Alexandria becomes Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: In 189, Pantaenus, sent by the bishop of Alexandria, embarked on a mission to India to spread Christianity. Despite his efforts, he met with limited success, reflecting the challenges of early Christian evangelism in foreign lands.
events.name: Pantaenus's mission to India

events.enhanced_description: Cato the Elder publicly criticizes consul Marcus Fulvius Nobilior for awarding Roman soldiers for mundane tasks, reflecting the growing tension between traditional Roman values and the changing nature of military rewards. This incident underscores Cato's staunch conservatism and his influence in Roman politics.
events.name: Cato the Elder's Criticism

events.enhanced_description: The Romans defeat Antiochus III at the Battle of Magnesia, a crucial victory that cripples the Aetolian League's foreign support. This battle not only solidifies Roman dominance in the region but also leads to significant political changes in Greece and Asia Minor.
events.name: Battle of Magnesia

events.enhanced_description: The Romans, alongside Eumenes II's forces, achieve victory over the Galatians in Anatolia, establishing Roman influence in the region. This military success further cements the alliance between Rome and Pergamum, showcasing the strategic importance of military coalitions in Hellenistic politics.
events.name: Roman Victory Over Galatians

events.enhanced_description: King Eumenes II founds the city of Philadelphia, naming it in honor of his brother Attalus. This city becomes a significant cultural and economic center in the region, reflecting the Hellenistic tradition of city-building and dynastic loyalty.
events.name: Foundation of Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: In 190, a significant fire ravaged parts of Rome, prompting Emperor Commodus to order the city's reconstruction. The rebuilt area was named Colonia Commodiana, reflecting the emperor's desire to leave a lasting legacy amidst the chaos of urban disasters.
events.name: Fire in Rome and rebuilding

events.enhanced_description: In 190, Lucius Septimius Severus was appointed as a Roman Council, marking a significant step in his political career that would eventually lead to his rise as emperor during the tumultuous Year of the Five Emperors.
events.name: Lucius Septimius Severus appointed as Roman Council

events.enhanced_description: In 190, the construction of a Roman road across the Alps via the Simplon Pass was completed, facilitating trade and military movement between the Italian Peninsula and the northern provinces. This engineering feat exemplified Roman ingenuity and their commitment to connectivity across challenging terrains.
events.name: Roman road crosses the Alps

events.enhanced_description: The year 190 marked the beginning of the Chuping era in the Chinese Han Dynasty, a period characterized by significant political and social changes as the dynasty faced internal strife and external pressures.
events.name: First year of the Chuping era

events.enhanced_description: In 190, the Campaign against Dong Zhuo commenced, with the Battle of Xingyang marking a significant confrontation between Cao Cao's forces and Dong Zhuo's troops. This conflict was pivotal in the power struggles that characterized the late Eastern Han dynasty.
events.name: Campaign against Dong Zhuo begins

events.enhanced_description: In 190 AD, the warlord Dong Zhuo ordered the burning and plundering of Luoyang, the Han Dynasty's capital, as he faced increasing opposition from a coalition of warlords. Following this devastation, the imperial court was relocated to Chang'an, marking a significant shift in power dynamics during the late Han period.
events.name: Luoyang is burned and plundered by the forces of Dong Zhuo

events.enhanced_description: In 190 AD, Osroes II, who controlled Media, declared himself king of the Parthian Empire amidst political turmoil. His claim was contested by King Vologases IV, who ultimately suppressed the rebellion and restored order in the region.
events.name: Osroes II claims the throne of the Parthian Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 190 AD, the philosopher Cleomedes articulated the understanding that the moon does not emit its own light but instead reflects sunlight, contributing to the early scientific discourse on celestial bodies. This teaching laid groundwork for future astronomical studies.
events.name: Cleomedes teaches about the moon's reflection of sunlight

events.enhanced_description: By 190 AD, Egypt, under Roman rule, faced severe economic challenges, including an inflation rate that had soared to 100% over the previous decade. This economic instability significantly impacted the livelihoods of the Egyptian populace.
events.name: Egypt suffers from inflation under Roman rule

events.enhanced_description: In 190 AD, the Roman authorities reduced the silver content in the Egyptian denarius from 90% to 70%, a move that reflected the economic pressures of the time and contributed to the ongoing inflation crisis in the province.
events.name: Reduction of silver content in the Egyptian denarius

events.enhanced_description: In 191 AD, King Vologases IV of Parthia passed away after a 44-year reign, marking the end of an era for the Parthian Empire. He was succeeded by his son, Vologases V, who faced immediate challenges to his rule.
events.name: Death of King Vologases IV of Parthia

events.enhanced_description: In 191 AD, a coalition of Chinese warlords launched a punitive campaign against Dong Zhuo, who had seized control of the Han government and held Emperor Xian hostage. After initial defeats, Dong Zhuo ordered the destruction of Luoyang before relocating the capital to Chang'an.
events.name: Coalition of Chinese warlords against Dong Zhuo

events.enhanced_description: In 191 AD, the Battle of Jieqiao saw Yuan Shao narrowly defeat Gongsun Zan in northern China, a significant conflict during the power struggles of the late Eastern Han Dynasty. This battle was part of the broader conflict against Dong Zhuo's regime.
events.name: Battle of Jieqiao

events.enhanced_description: Around 191-192 AD, the sculpture of Emperor Commodus as Hercules was created on Esquiline Hill in Rome. This artwork, now housed at the Palazzo dei Conservatori, reflects the emperor's self-aggrandizing portrayal and his fascination with gladiatorial combat.
events.name: Sculpture of Commodus as Hercules

events.enhanced_description: In 191 AD, Serapion was appointed as the Patriarch of Antioch, a significant position within early Christianity. His leadership would influence the development of the Christian community in this pivotal region.
events.name: Serapion becomes Patriarch of Antioch

events.enhanced_description: The Carthaginians managed to collect the indemnity owed to Rome as per the peace treaty signed a decade earlier, but the payment was not completed in full for 50 years. The Romans, seeking to maintain their influence over Carthage, refused to accept early payment, leading to ongoing tensions between the two powers.
events.name: Carthaginian Indemnity Collection

events.enhanced_description: Arsaces II, the king of Parthia, was reportedly murdered on the orders of Antiochus III, marking a significant power shift in the region. Following his death, Arsaces was succeeded by his cousin, Phriapatius, as the Parthian leadership faced instability.
events.name: Murder of Arsaces II

events.enhanced_description: In a significant cultural shift, Emperor Hui of Han lifted the ban on Confucian writings that had been imposed in 213 BC. This action allowed for the revival of Confucian thought and its teachings, which would greatly influence Chinese society and governance.
events.name: Lifting of the Ban on Confucian Writings

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 192 AD, Emperor Commodus shocked the Roman Senate by appearing in gladiatorial attire during his consulship. This act, along with the subsequent assassination plot orchestrated by his mistress Marcia, marked a turning point in the political landscape of Rome.
events.name: Commodus appears as a gladiator

events.enhanced_description: Between 192 and 193 AD, Ancient Rome was engulfed in civil war, a period characterized by political instability and power struggles following the assassination of Commodus. This turmoil set the stage for the Year of the Five Emperors.
events.name: Civil war strikes Ancient Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 192 AD, Lü Bu assassinated the warlord Dong Zhuo, who had dominated the Han Dynasty's central government since 189. This assassination was a pivotal moment in the power struggles of the late Han period, leading to further conflicts among warlords.
events.name: Lü Bu assassinates Dong Zhuo

events.enhanced_description: Around 192 AD, the kingdom of Champa began to establish control over south and central Vietnam, marking the rise of this significant cultural and political entity in Southeast Asia. This expansion would influence the region's history for centuries.
events.name: Kingdom of Champa begins control over Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: In 192 AD, a fire destroyed the library of Galen, a prominent physician and philosopher in Ancient Rome. This loss represented a significant setback for the preservation of medical knowledge and literature of the time.
events.name: Fire destroys Galen's library

events.enhanced_description: In 192 AD, Syriac Christians established one of the earliest Christian communities in Kerala, India. This community played a crucial role in the spread of Christianity in the region and contributed to the rich tapestry of Indian religious history.
events.name: Syriac Christians establish community in Kerala

events.enhanced_description: In response to Sparta's renewed ambitions to reclaim lost territories, the Achaeans sent an envoy to Rome seeking assistance. The Roman Senate responded by dispatching the praetor Atilius along with a naval force and an embassy led by Titus Quinctius Flamininus.
events.name: Achaeans Seek Roman Assistance

events.enhanced_description: The Achaean army and navy, under the command of Philopoemen, advanced towards Gythium without waiting for the Roman fleet. However, they faced defeat at the hands of the Spartan fleet, and on land, they were unable to overcome Spartan forces, leading to a retreat to Tegea.
events.name: Achaean Naval Campaign Against Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Philopoemen made a second attempt to re-enter Laconia, where his forces were ambushed by the Spartan tyrant Nabis. Despite the surprise attack, Philopoemen managed to achieve a significant victory over the Spartan forces, showcasing his military prowess.
events.name: Philopoemen's Victory Over Spartans

events.enhanced_description: Philopoemen's plans to capture Sparta were postponed at the request of the Roman envoy Flaminius, who arrived in Greece to mediate. Consequently, Nabis, the Spartan tyrant, chose to maintain the status quo for the time being.
events.name: Philopoemen's Plans Halted

events.enhanced_description: Nabis appealed to the Aetolians for military assistance, leading to the dispatch of 1,000 cavalry under Alexamenus to Sparta. However, the Aetolians betrayed Nabis, murdering him and briefly occupying Sparta before being driven out by the city's inhabitants.
events.name: Nabis Appeals to Aetolians

events.enhanced_description: Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire invaded Greece at the request of the Aetolian League, who were revolting against Roman influence. He landed in Demetrias with a small force, but found limited support among the Greek states, complicating his campaign.
events.name: Antiochus III Invades Greece

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, the Roman Senate chose Publius Helvius Pertinax as Emperor, marking the beginning of the Year of the Five Emperors. Pertinax's reign was characterized by attempts to restore order and financial stability in the empire after the chaos of Commodus's rule.
events.name: Year of the Five Emperors begins

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, Emperor Pertinax was assassinated by members of the Praetorian Guard, who stormed the imperial palace. His death led to a power vacuum, resulting in the auctioning of the Roman Empire to the highest bidder.
events.name: Assassination of Pertinax

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, Lucius Septimius Severus was proclaimed Emperor by his troops at Carnuntum in Pannonia Superior. His ascension marked the beginning of a new dynasty and a significant shift in the Roman political landscape.

locations.name: Carnuntum Archaeological Park, Lower Austria, Austria

events.name: Lucius Septimius Severus proclaimed Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, Septimius Severus entered Rome and ordered the execution of Marcus Didius Julianus, the highest bidder for the imperial throne. This decisive action solidified his control over the Roman Empire and initiated the Severan dynasty.
events.name: Septimius Severus enters Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, the battles of Cyzicus and Nicaea saw Septimius Severus defeat the forces of Pescennius Niger, consolidating his power during the tumultuous Year of the Five Emperors. These victories were crucial in establishing Severus's authority in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Battle of Cyzicus and Nicaea

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, Clodius Albinus allied with Septimius Severus in Britain, accepting the title of Caesar. This alliance was significant as it united forces against rival claimants to the imperial throne during a period of civil unrest.
events.name: Clodius Albinus allies with Septimius Severus

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, counterfeiting workshops began to proliferate throughout the Roman Empire, reflecting the economic instability and devaluation of currency during this tumultuous period. This rise in counterfeiting posed significant challenges for the Roman economy.
events.name: Counterfeiting workshops emerge in the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, the Council of Rome convened, marking a significant moment in early Christian history as it addressed various theological and organizational issues within the burgeoning Christian community. This council laid the groundwork for future ecumenical gatherings.
events.name: The Council of Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, the last year of the Chuping era of the Han dynasty marked a period of significant political upheaval and fragmentation within China. This era's conclusion was emblematic of the broader decline of the Han Dynasty.
events.name: Last year of Chuping era of the Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 193 AD, Cao Cao launched an invasion of Xu Province, blaming Tao Qian for the death of his father, Cao Song. This military campaign marked a significant power struggle during the late Eastern Han dynasty, contributing to the fragmentation of the empire.
events.name: Cao Cao's invasion of Xu Province

events.enhanced_description: Under Emperor Septimius Severus in 193 AD, the silver content of the Roman denarius was reduced to 50%, down from 68% during the reign of Marcus Aurelius. This devaluation reflected the economic challenges faced by the Roman Empire during this period.
events.name: Devaluation of the Roman denarius

events.enhanced_description: Eumenes II of Pergamum sought assistance from Rome against the encroaching threat of Antiochus III, who aimed to conquer Greece. The Roman proconsul, Titus Quinctius Flamininus, supported the Greek autonomy in the region, reinforcing Roman influence.
events.name: Eumenes II Appeals to Rome

events.enhanced_description: Titus Quinctius Flamininus was sent to negotiate with Antiochus III, warning him against interfering with Greek states. Antiochus, however, rejected Flamininus's authority and insisted that both Romans and Seleucids should refrain from meddling in Greek affairs.
events.name: Flamininus Negotiates with Antiochus III

events.enhanced_description: Flamininus worked to rally Greek states against Antiochus III, countering the pro-Seleucid stance of the Aetolians. His diplomatic efforts led to the Achaean League declaring war on both the Aetolians and Antiochus, while preventing Philopoemen from advancing on Sparta.
events.name: Flamininus Rallies Greeks Against Antiochus III

events.enhanced_description: The Spartan ruler Nabis initiated efforts to recover lost territories, including Gythium, reflecting the ongoing regional tensions. His ambitions set the stage for further conflicts with both the Achaeans and the Romans.
events.name: Nabis's Territorial Ambitions

events.enhanced_description: Carneades of Cyrene moved to Athens to establish the Third Academy, contributing to the philosophical landscape of the city. His work would influence future generations of philosophers and scholars in the Hellenistic period.
events.name: Carneades Founding the New Academy

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the first porticos in Rome marked a significant architectural development in the city, enhancing public spaces and influencing urban design. This innovation contributed to the cultural and social life of ancient Rome.
events.name: Construction of the First Porticos in Rome

events.enhanced_description: Cleopatra I Syra, the daughter of Antiochus III, marries Ptolemy V Epiphanes, strengthening the political alliance between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic dynasties. This union is significant in the context of the ongoing power struggles in the Hellenistic world and the influence of these two powerful families.
events.name: Marriage of Cleopatra I Syra and Ptolemy V Epiphanes

events.enhanced_description: In 194 AD, Decimus Clodius Septimius Albinus was appointed as a Roman Consul, a significant political position in the Roman Republic and Empire. His rise to power was part of the broader political turmoil during the Severan dynasty.
events.name: Decimus Clodius Septimius Albinus becomes Roman Consul

events.enhanced_description: In 333 BC, Alexander the Great achieved a decisive victory over the Persian forces at the Battle of Issus, located near the Issus River in Cilicia. Despite his success, Persian Emperor Darius III managed to escape, leaving behind his family, which included his wife and daughters.
events.name: Battle of Issus

events.enhanced_description: Between 194 and 196 AD, Emperor Septimius Severus besieged Byzantium, causing extensive damage to the city's walls. This siege was part of Severus's campaign to consolidate power and eliminate rivals.

image.caption: Locator map of Byzantion (Byzantium).
image.credit: Evil berry — Own work

events.name: Siege of Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: In 194 AD, the Battle of Yan Province erupted between warlords Cao Cao and Lü Bu, lasting over 100 days. This conflict was pivotal in the struggle for control over northern China during the late Han dynasty.
events.name: Battle of Yan Province

events.enhanced_description: The year 194 AD marked the first year of the Xingping era during the Han Dynasty in China. This era was characterized by significant political and military events that shaped the future of the dynasty.
events.name: First year of the Xingping era

events.enhanced_description: Around 194 AD, the physician Galen authored his influential manual on pathology, titled The Art of Curing. This work contributed significantly to the field of medicine and influenced medical practices for centuries.
events.name: Galen writes The Art of Curing

events.enhanced_description: In 194 AD, Irenaeus, a prominent early Christian theologian, declared Gnostic doctrines to be heretical. This declaration was part of the early church's efforts to define orthodoxy and combat heretical beliefs.
events.name: Irenaeus declares Gnostic doctrines heretical

events.enhanced_description: After successfully curbing the ambitions of Nabis, the tyrant of Sparta, Roman proconsul Titus Quinctius Flamininus orders the withdrawal of Roman forces from Greece. This marks a significant moment in the Roman influence over Greek affairs and the shifting power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Withdrawal of Roman Forces from Greece

events.enhanced_description: With the Roman legions under the command of Titus Quinctius Flamininus returning to Italy, the Greek states find themselves once again without Roman support. This shift allows local powers such as Macedonia and the Aetolian League to vie for control, leading to renewed tensions in the region.
events.name: Return of Roman Legions to Italy

events.enhanced_description: Following a peace agreement with Egypt, Antiochus III focuses on expanding his influence in the West, encouraged by his advisor Hannibal. This strategic shift sets the stage for future conflicts with Rome as Antiochus seeks to challenge Roman dominance in the region.
events.name: Antiochus III Turns Attention to the West

events.enhanced_description: Philip V of Macedon allies with Rome, along with other regional powers like Rhodes and Pergamum, to oppose Antiochus III. This coalition marks a significant alignment in the power dynamics of the Hellenistic world, as the Romans and their allies prepare for conflict with the Seleucid king.
events.name: Philip V Joins Rome Against Antiochus III

events.enhanced_description: The towns of Liternum and Puteoli are established as Roman colonies, reflecting the expansion of Roman influence in Italy and the integration of these areas into the Roman administrative framework.
events.name: Roman Colonization of Liternum and Puteoli

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the first city wall of Chang'an begins, marking an important development in the urban planning and defense of one of ancient China's most significant capitals. This wall would later play a crucial role in the city's protection and administration.
events.name: Construction of the First City Wall of Chang'an

events.enhanced_description: Empress Lü secures the accession of her son, Emperor Hui, by executing Consort Qi and her son, Liu Ruyi. This brutal act underscores the intense power struggles within the Han dynasty and the lengths to which Empress Lü would go to maintain her family's hold on power.
events.name: Empress Lü Protects Her Son's Accession

events.enhanced_description: The Wiman Joseon kingdom is founded by the Han dynasty general Wiman in northern Korea. This establishment marks a significant moment in Korean history as it represents the beginning of a new political entity that would influence the region for centuries.
events.name: Foundation of Wiman Joseon

events.enhanced_description: In 195 AD, Emperor Septimius Severus had the Roman Senate deify the previous emperor Commodus, aiming to gain favor with the family of Marcus Aurelius. This act was part of Severus's broader political strategy during his reign.
events.name: Deification of Commodus

events.enhanced_description: In 195 AD, King Vologases V and other eastern princes supported Pescennius Niger's claims, leading to a revolt in the Roman province of Mesopotamia. This conflict prompted Emperor Severus to march into Mesopotamia to confront the Parthians.
events.name: Support for Pescennius Niger

events.enhanced_description: In 195 AD, the Roman province of Syria was divided, diminishing the role of Antioch. The annexation of Edessa and Nisibis marked a significant administrative change under Emperor Septimius Severus.

image.caption: Locator map of the Roman province of Syria within the Roman Empire.
image.credit: Milenioscuro — Own work
image.date_qualification: Map depicts 125 AD; created 2015-11-17. It predates the event and is contextual rather than an event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Division of the Roman province of Syria

events.enhanced_description: In 195 AD, Lucius Septimius Bassianus, also known as Caracalla, changed his name to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus at the age of 7. This name change was intended to solidify connections with the family of Marcus Aurelius and enhance his political stature.
events.name: Lucius Septimius Bassianus changes name

events.enhanced_description: In 195 AD, Clodius Albinus, proclaimed emperor in Britain, crossed into Gaul with his legions while recruiting new soldiers. This maneuver positioned him as a formidable rival to Emperor Septimius Severus.
events.name: Clodius Albinus crosses into Gaul

events.enhanced_description: In 195 AD, Emperor Septimius Severus further devalued the denarius, reducing its precious metal content to 50%. This decision reflected ongoing economic pressures within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Devaluation of the denarius

events.enhanced_description: In 195 AD, the Xiongnu federation crossed the Great Wall and established itself in Shanxi Province, posing a significant threat to the Han Dynasty. This incursion marked a critical moment in the ongoing conflicts between the Han and the nomadic tribes.
events.name: Xiongnu federation crosses the Great Wall

events.enhanced_description: The year 195 AD marked the last year of the Xingping era during the Han Dynasty. This period was characterized by significant political upheaval and military conflicts that would shape the future of China.
events.name: Last year of the Xingping era

events.enhanced_description: Hannibal, following his unpopular reforms in Carthage, is denounced to the Romans and chooses voluntary exile to avoid capture. His departure marks a significant turning point for Carthage as it loses one of its most formidable military leaders.
events.name: Hannibal's Exile from Carthage

events.enhanced_description: Hannibal is granted refuge by Antiochus III in Ephesus, where he becomes an adviser. This alliance heightens tensions between Antiochus and Rome, as Hannibal's military expertise poses a potential threat to Roman interests in the region.
events.name: Hannibal Advises Antiochus III

events.enhanced_description: Following Roman diplomatic intervention, Antiochus III halts his war with Egypt and formalizes the Peace of Lysimachia. This agreement allows Antiochus to solidify his control over southern Syria, marking a significant shift in the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Peace of Lysimachia

events.enhanced_description: Marcus Porcius Cato effectively suppresses a revolt in Spain against Roman consolidation of former Carthaginian colonies. His controversial tactics, including bribing the Celtiberians, highlight the complexities of Roman governance in newly acquired territories.
events.name: Cato's Suppression of Spanish Revolt

events.enhanced_description: The Roman sumptuary law, Lex Oppia, is repealed despite strong opposition from consul Marcus Porcius Cato. This repeal reflects changing social attitudes towards wealth and gender roles in Roman society during this period.
events.name: Repeal of the Lex Oppia

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Gythium was a significant conflict between Sparta and a coalition of Rome, Rhodes, the Achaean League, and Pergamum. The allies aimed to capture the strategically important port of Gythium, leading to a Spartan surrender after the arrival of Roman reinforcements under Flamininus, ultimately resulting in Spartan territorial losses.
events.name: The Battle of Gythium

events.enhanced_description: Aristophanes of Byzantium, a prominent Greek scholar and grammarian, was appointed as the chief librarian at the famed Library of Alexandria. His tenure marked a significant period in the preservation and organization of ancient texts, contributing greatly to the intellectual heritage of the Hellenistic world.
events.name: Aristophanes of Byzantium becomes chief librarian at Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: In a politically charged atmosphere, Lu Wan, the king of Yan, fled north of the Great Wall of China to escape the suspicions of Emperor Gaozu of Han. This flight marked a significant moment in the power dynamics of the Han dynasty, reflecting the tensions between regional rulers and the central authority.
events.name: Lu Wan flees north of the Great Wall of China

events.enhanced_description: General Fan Kuai was sent by Emperor Gaozu to locate the fleeing Lu Wan but was arrested on suspicion of plotting against the emperor's family. This incident underscores the volatile political climate of the early Han dynasty, where trust was scarce and suspicion could lead to severe consequences.
events.name: General Fan Kuai is arrested

events.enhanced_description: During this period, Chang'an, the capital of the Han dynasty, is believed to have surpassed Pataliputra as the largest city in the world. This transformation reflects the economic and cultural prosperity of the Han dynasty, making it a central hub for trade and governance.
events.name: Chang'an becomes the largest city in the world

events.enhanced_description: The death of Haemosu Dangun, the first ruler of Buyeo, marked a significant transition in the region's leadership as his son, Mosuri Dangun, succeeded him. This event is pivotal in the history of Buyeo, contributing to the lineage of its rulers and the development of early Korean states.
events.name: Haemosu Dangun dies

events.enhanced_description: In 196 AD, Emperor Septimius Severus attempted to assassinate Clodius Albinus, but the plot failed, leading Albinus to retaliate militarily. This event escalated the power struggle between the two leaders.
events.name: Assassination attempt on Clodius Albinus

events.enhanced_description: In 196 AD, Emperor Septimius Severus captured and sacked Byzantium. Following the conquest, the city was rebuilt and regained its previous prosperity, showcasing Severus's military might and administrative capabilities.
events.name: Capture and sack of Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: In 196 AD, Clodius Albinus was declared Augustus by his army while crossing Gaul, a strategic move to secure the loyalty of the Roman legion in Germany. This declaration marked a significant escalation in the power struggle against Emperor Septimius Severus.
events.name: Clodius Albinus declared Augustus

events.enhanced_description: In 196 AD, Hadrian's Wall in Britain was partially destroyed, reflecting the ongoing conflicts and pressures faced by the Roman Empire in its northern territories. This event highlighted the challenges of maintaining control over distant provinces.
events.name: Destruction of Hadrian's Wall

events.enhanced_description: The year 196 AD marked the first year of the Jian'an Era during the reign of the Xian Emperor of the Han Dynasty. This era was characterized by significant political turmoil and military conflicts.
events.name: First year of the Jian'an Era

events.enhanced_description: In 196 AD, the Xian Emperor returned to the war-ravaged city of Luoyang and sought protection from warlord Cao Cao. Under Cao's influence, the emperor was advised to move the capital to Xuchang, becoming a pawn in the power struggles of the time.
events.name: Xian Emperor seeks protection from Cao Cao

events.enhanced_description: In 196 AD, Naehae ascended to the throne as king of Silla, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His reign marked a significant period in the history of Silla, contributing to its cultural and political development.
events.name: Naehae becomes king of Silla

events.enhanced_description: In 196 AD, a church council was convened in Caesarea to discuss the date of Easter, reflecting the early Christian church's efforts to establish unified practices and doctrines. This council was part of the broader development of Christian theology.
events.name: Church council in Caesarea

events.enhanced_description: The defeat of the Insubres, a Gallic tribe in the Po Valley, marked the end of a significant conflict believed to have been incited by Carthage. This victory for the Romans solidified their control over northern Italy and demonstrated their military prowess against the Gallic tribes.
events.name: The Insubres are defeated

events.enhanced_description: The establishment of the tresviri epulones, a new category of Roman priests, marked an important development in the religious practices of ancient Rome. The first priests, including notable figures like Gaius Licinius Lucullus, were tasked with overseeing the feasts of the gods, enhancing the public religious life.
events.name: Tresviri epulones are elected

events.enhanced_description: At the Isthmian Games in Corinth, Roman proconsul Titus Quinctius Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of all Greeks, allowing them to govern themselves. This declaration was met with widespread acclaim and solidified Flamininus's reputation as a liberator among the Greek city-states.
events.name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus proclaims Greek freedom

events.enhanced_description: Titus Quinctius Flamininus accused the Spartan ruler Nabis of tyranny and successfully captured Gythium, forcing Nabis to surrender Argos. This military action was part of the broader conflict between Rome and Sparta, illustrating the shifting power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Flamininus accuses Nabis of tyranny

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the first triumphal arch in Rome represented a significant architectural achievement and a symbol of military victory. This arch would set a precedent for future triumphal arches, becoming a hallmark of Roman commemorative architecture.
events.name: The first triumphal arch built in Rome

events.enhanced_description: The foundation of a library at Pergamum by Eumenes II is believed to have led to the invention of parchment, as an alternative to papyrus due to an embargo by Ptolemy V. This innovation had lasting impacts on the preservation of texts and the development of writing materials.
events.name: Foundation of a library at Pergamum

events.enhanced_description: The Rosetta Stone, inscribed with the same text in three scripts, was created during the Ptolemaic period and became crucial for the understanding of Egyptian hieroglyphs. Its discovery in the early 19th century provided key insights into ancient Egyptian civilization and language.
events.name: The Rosetta Stone is created

events.enhanced_description: Antiochus III's army crossed the Hellespont into Thrace, asserting control over territories previously won by Seleucus I. This aggressive expansion led to diplomatic tensions with Rome, highlighting the geopolitical struggles of the Hellenistic period.
events.name: Antiochus III claims sovereignty over Thrace

events.enhanced_description: The execution of Han Xin, a former General-in-Chief of the Han dynasty, by Empress Lü and Prime Minister Xiao He, reflects the intense political rivalries and suspicions within the early Han court. His death marked a significant loss for the Han military leadership during a turbulent period.
events.name: Han Xin is executed

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Lugdunum in 197 CE marked a decisive conflict during the Year of the Five Emperors, where Emperor Septimius Severus defeated the self-proclaimed emperor Clodius Albinus. Following his defeat, Albinus committed suicide, leading to the sacking of Lyon by Severus's legionaries.
events.name: Battle of Lugdunum

events.enhanced_description: After his victory at Lugdunum, Septimius Severus returned to Rome and executed approximately 30 senators who had supported Clodius Albinus. This act solidified his power and marked a shift in the political landscape of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Septimius Severus returns to Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 197 CE, Emperor Septimius Severus established new naval units, equipping all triremes in Italy with heavily armed troops in preparation for military campaigns in the East. This strategic move aimed to bolster Roman naval power against potential threats.
events.name: Formation of new naval units

events.enhanced_description: Septimius Severus levied the Legio I, II, and III Parthica in 197 CE to support his military campaign against the Parthians. This move was part of his broader strategy to expand Roman influence in the East.
events.name: Levies for Parthian campaign

events.enhanced_description: In 197 CE, the Roman army, under the command of Septimius Severus, marched eastward to repel a Parthian invasion of Mesopotamia. They successfully looted the royal palace at Ctesiphon, capturing many inhabitants as slaves.
events.name: Roman army's campaign in Mesopotamia

events.enhanced_description: Septimius Severus reconstituted the Province of Mesopotamia in 197 CE, appointing an equestrian governor to command two legions. This administrative change aimed to strengthen Roman control over the region.
events.name: Reconstitution of the Province of Mesopotamia

events.enhanced_description: In 197 CE, Septimius Severus declared a military dictatorship, effectively excluding the Senate from power and consolidating his authority over the Roman Empire. This marked a significant shift in the governance of Rome.
events.name: Military dictatorship declared

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Wancheng in 197 CE saw Zhang Xiu launch a surprise attack against the forces of Cao Cao. This engagement was part of the larger power struggles during the late Eastern Han dynasty in China.
events.name: Battle of Wancheng

events.enhanced_description: In 197 CE, Yuan Shu declared himself emperor of the short-lived Zhong dynasty, a move that reflected the fragmentation of power during the late Eastern Han dynasty in China. His claim was part of the broader chaos of the period.
events.name: Yuan Shu declares himself emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 197 CE, Sansang ascended to the throne as the ruler of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo. His reign marked a continuation of the kingdom's influence in the region during a time of significant political change.
events.name: Sansang becomes ruler of Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: In 197 CE, Galen published his major work on medicines, titled Pharmacologia. This text contributed significantly to the field of medicine and pharmacology in the ancient world.
events.name: Publication of Pharmacologia

events.enhanced_description: In 197 CE, a Christian council was convened in Edessa, a significant event for the early Christian community in the region. This council played a role in shaping early Christian doctrine and governance.
events.name: Christian council in Edessa

events.enhanced_description: In 198 CE, Publius Septimius Geta, the son of Emperor Septimius Severus, was granted the title of Caesar. This title signified his position as a potential heir and marked his increasing prominence in Roman politics.
events.name: Publius Septimius Geta receives title of Caesar

events.enhanced_description: In 198 CE, Caracalla, the son of Septimius Severus, was bestowed the title of Augustus. This title elevated his status within the Roman hierarchy and indicated his role in the imperial succession.
events.name: Caracalla receives title of Augustus

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 198 CE, the allied forces of Cao Cao and Liu Bei achieved a significant victory against Lü Bu at the Battle of Xiapi. Following the defeat, Cao Cao executed Lü Bu, marking a pivotal moment in the power struggles of the late Eastern Han dynasty.
events.name: Battle of Xiapi

events.enhanced_description: In 198 CE, Marcus I succeeded Olympianus as the Patriarch of Constantinople, a position he would hold until 211 CE. His leadership contributed to the early Christian church's development in the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Marcus I becomes Patriarch of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: After being elected consul, Titus Quinctius Flamininus takes command in Macedonia, aiming to secure peace by undermining King Philip V of Macedon. He seeks alliances and initiates peace talks at Nicaea, but negotiations ultimately collapse, leading to renewed conflict.
events.name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus replaces Publius Sulpicius Galba Maximus in Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: In a decisive campaign, Titus Quinctius Flamininus successfully drives Philip V of Macedon from most of Greece, securing significant territories except for a few strongholds. His forces achieve a crucial victory at the Battle of the Aous, near modern-day Tepelenë, Albania.
events.name: Flamininus pushes Philip V out of Greece

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Panium sees the Seleucid forces under Antiochus III defeat the Ptolemaic army led by Scopas of Aetolia. This victory allows Antiochus to gain control over Palestine and Coele-Syria, significantly shifting the balance of power in the region.

image.caption: Photograph of the Temple of Pan at Banias (Paneas).

events.name: Battle of Panium

events.enhanced_description: Following the conflict, Antiochus III solidifies his power through a marriage alliance, offering his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemy V. This union aims to strengthen ties between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms amidst ongoing regional tensions.
events.name: Marriage alliance between Antiochus III and Ptolemy V

events.enhanced_description: In 199 CE, Mesopotamia was partitioned into two Roman provinces, Mesopotamia and Osroene, divided by the Euphrates River. This administrative change aimed to enhance Roman governance and control over the region.
events.name: Partition of Mesopotamia

events.enhanced_description: In 199 CE, Emperor Septimius Severus laid siege to the city-state of Hatra in Central Mesopotamia. Despite breaching its walls, he ultimately failed to capture the city, highlighting the challenges of Roman expansion in the region.
events.name: Siege of Hatra

events.enhanced_description: In 199 CE, two new legions, I Parthica and III Parthica, were formed as a permanent garrison to bolster Roman military presence in the East. This strategic decision was part of the ongoing conflicts with the Parthian Empire.
events.name: Formation of new legions

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Yijing in 199 CE saw the Chinese warlord Yuan Shao defeat Gongsun Zan, a significant event in the power struggles of the late Eastern Han dynasty. This victory helped solidify Yuan Shao's influence in northern China.
events.name: Battle of Yijing

events.enhanced_description: In 199 CE, Geodeung succeeded Suro as the king of the Korean kingdom of Gaya. His ascension marked a continuation of the royal lineage and the kingdom's influence in the region.
events.name: Geodeung succeeds Suro

events.enhanced_description: In 199 CE, Pope Zephyrinus succeeded Pope Victor I as the 15th pope of the Roman Catholic Church. His papacy contributed to the early development of church leadership and doctrine.
events.name: Pope Zephyrinus succeeds Pope Victor I

events.enhanced_description: Roman general Gnaeus Baebius Tamphilus leads an attack against the Insubres in Gaul, suffering heavy losses with over 6,700 soldiers killed. This defeat highlights the challenges faced by Rome in its expansion efforts during this period.
events.name: Gnaeus Baebius Tamphilus attacks the Insubres

events.enhanced_description: Scipio Africanus, renowned for his military leadership during the Second Punic War, is appointed censor and becomes princeps Senatus, the leading figure in the Roman Senate. His influence shapes Roman politics in the years to come.
events.name: Scipio Africanus becomes censor and princeps Senatus

events.enhanced_description: Tribune P. Porcius Laeca proposes Lex Porcia, a significant Roman law aimed at granting citizens the right of appeal in capital cases. This legislation reflects the evolving legal landscape of the Roman Republic.
events.name: Proposal of Lex Porcia by P. Porcius Laeca

events.enhanced_description: Around the year 200, the estimated global human population reaches approximately 257 million, marking a significant milestone in human demographic history. This population growth reflects various factors including agricultural advancements and the stability of empires.
events.name: Human population reaches about 257 million

events.enhanced_description: In the year 200, Emperor Septimius Severus undertakes a significant tour of the provinces of Syria, Palestine, and Arabia, reinforcing Roman authority and governance in these regions. His visits are marked by efforts to consolidate power and promote Roman culture.
events.name: Emperor Septimius Severus visits the provinces of Syria, Palestine, and Arabia

events.enhanced_description: Around the year 200, the Roman Empire reorganizes its provinces, taking Numidia from the African proconsul and establishing it as an Imperial province. This change reflects the centralization of power and the administrative reforms of the Severan dynasty.
events.name: The province of Numidia is taken from the African proconsul, and made an Imperial province

events.enhanced_description: In the early 200s, Rudrasena I ascends to the throne as the Saka ruler of the Western Satrap dynasty, establishing his reign over Malwa in Classical India. His rule is characterized by efforts to strengthen the Satrap's influence and trade in the region.
events.name: Rudrasena I, Saka ruler of the Western Satrap dynasty, becomes king of Malwa in Classical India

events.enhanced_description: In the year 200, Himiko, the shaman queen of Yamatai, extends her authority over several clans in Japan, consolidating power and establishing a centralized rule. Her reign is noted for its cultural and political significance in early Japanese history.
events.name: Himiko extends her authority over clans in Japan

events.enhanced_description: Around the year 200, the Classic Age of Maya civilization begins, marking a period of significant cultural, architectural, and scientific advancements. This era sees the rise of powerful city-states and the development of complex societal structures.
events.name: The Classic Age of Maya civilization begins

events.enhanced_description: Around the year 200, the Paracas culture, known for its advanced textile work and burial practices, comes to an end. This transition marks a significant shift in the cultural landscape of the Andes region.
events.name: The Paracas culture in the Andes ends

events.enhanced_description: In the year 200, the Severan Tondo is created, depicting Emperor Septimius Severus, his wife Julia Domna, and their children Geta and Caracalla. This artwork is significant for its representation of the imperial family and is now housed in Berlin.
events.name: The Severan Tondo is made

events.enhanced_description: In the year 200, Judah ha-Nasi, a prominent Jewish scholar, compiles the Mishnah, laying the foundation for Talmudic law. This work is crucial for the preservation and interpretation of Jewish oral traditions.
events.name: Judah ha-Nasi compiles the Mishnah

events.enhanced_description: In the year 200, Clement of Alexandria publicly denounces the use of musical instruments in Christian worship, advocating for the purity of human voices in music. His views reflect early Christian attitudes towards music and worship practices.
events.name: Clement of Alexandria denounces musical instruments in Christian music

events.enhanced_description: Around the year 200, Brahmanism begins to evolve into what we now recognize as Hinduism, marking a significant transformation in religious practices and beliefs in the Indian subcontinent. This evolution reflects the integration of various cultural and spiritual influences.
events.name: Brahmanism evolves into Hinduism
