events.name: Lady Triệu's resistance against Chinese invasion

events.enhanced_description: In 245 BC, the Ptolemaic armies under Ptolemy III captured the ancient cities of Babylon and Susa, marking a significant expansion of Ptolemaic influence in the region. This military success was part of Ptolemy III's campaigns during the ongoing conflicts with the Seleucid Empire.
events.name: Babylon and Susa fall to the Ptolemaic armies of Ptolemy III

events.enhanced_description: In 245 BC, Ptolemy III Euergetes married Berenice II, the daughter of Magas, king of Cyrene, thereby solidifying political ties between Egypt and Cyrenaica. This marriage was a strategic move to strengthen Ptolemaic control over the region and enhance its influence in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Ptolemy III marries Berenice II, reuniting Egypt and Cyrenaica

events.enhanced_description: In 245 BC, following the death of his nephew Alexander of Corinth, Antigonus II Gonatas arranged the marriage of Nicaea, Alexander's widow, to his son Demetrius. This political maneuver was aimed at re-establishing control over Corinth, which had gained independence under Alexander's rule.
events.name: Antigonus II marries Nicaea to his son Demetrius

events.enhanced_description: In 245 BC, Aratus of Sicyon was elected as the general (strategos) of the Achaean League, a significant political body in ancient Greece. His leadership marked a pivotal moment in the league's efforts to unify and strengthen the region against external threats.
events.name: Aratus of Sicyon is elected general of the Achaean League

events.enhanced_description: In 245 BC, the Qin general Pao Gong successfully captured the Wei city of Juan, contributing to the Qin state's military campaigns during the Warring States period. This victory was part of the larger strategy to consolidate power and territory in northern China.
events.name: The Qin general Pao Gong captures the Wei city of Juan

events.enhanced_description: In 245 BC, Lian Po, a prominent general of the State of Zhao, captured the Wei city of Fanyang. This military action was part of the ongoing conflicts during the Warring States period, showcasing Zhao's military strength and territorial ambitions.
events.name: The Zhao general Lian Po captures the Wei city of Fanyang

events.enhanced_description: In 246, Emperor Philip the Arab engaged in military campaigns against Germanic tribes along the Danube River, reflecting the ongoing conflicts faced by the Roman Empire during his reign.
events.name: Philip the Arab fights Germans along the Danube

events.enhanced_description: The first of two Councils of Arabia was held in Bostra in 246, addressing issues within the Roman Christian Church and reflecting the growing importance of Christianity in the Roman Empire.
events.name: First Council of Arabia

events.enhanced_description: In 246, the Baekje Kingdom, under King Goi, launched an attack against the Chinese commandery of Daifang, illustrating the military ambitions of Baekje during this period.
events.name: Baekje attacks Daifang

events.enhanced_description: In 246 BC, the death of Ptolemy II Philadelphus marked a significant transition in the Ptolemaic dynasty as his son, Ptolemy III Euergetes, ascended to the throne. This change in leadership would lead to various military campaigns and political maneuvers that shaped the future of the Ptolemaic Kingdom.
events.name: Death of Ptolemy II and succession of Ptolemy III

events.enhanced_description: In 246 BC, the Ashokan pillar was erected in Lauriya, Nandangarh, as part of Emperor Ashoka's efforts to promote Buddhism and his edicts throughout his empire. This pillar is a significant cultural artifact, symbolizing the spread of Buddhist teachings in ancient India.
events.name: The Ashokan pillar in Lauriya, Nandangarh is made

events.enhanced_description: In 246 BC, Antiochus II Theos abandoned his wife Berenice to return to his former wife Laodice, leading to a political crisis. This decision resulted in Laodice's subsequent actions to eliminate Berenice and her children, which escalated tensions within the Seleucid dynasty.
events.name: Antiochus II leaves Berenice for Laodice

events.enhanced_description: In 246 BC, Ptolemy III Euergetes launched an invasion of Syria to avenge the murder of his sister Berenice, marking the beginning of the Third Syrian War. This conflict involved significant military engagements and territorial disputes between the Ptolemaic and Seleucid empires.
events.name: Ptolemy III invades Syria, beginning the Third Syrian War

events.enhanced_description: In 246 BC, Ptolemy III Euergetes achieved significant victories over Seleucus II Callinicus in Syria and Anatolia, briefly occupying Antioch. These victories were pivotal in the ongoing conflict between the Ptolemaic and Seleucid empires, though they were marred by losses elsewhere.
events.name: Ptolemy III wins victories over Seleucus II

events.enhanced_description: In 246 BC, Laodice, mother of Seleucus II Callinicus, sought to exert control over the Seleucid Empire by demanding her son appoint his brother Antiochus Hierax as co-regent. This power struggle led to a civil conflict that further destabilized the Seleucid realm.
events.name: Laodice attempts to control the Seleucid Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 246 BC, Seleucus II Callinicus arranged a marriage between one of his sisters and King Diodotus of Bactria to secure an alliance. This diplomatic move was aimed at strengthening ties with the Bactrian kingdom amidst the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Marriage alliance with Bactrian King Diodotus

events.enhanced_description: In 246 BC, facing challenges from Hamilcar Barca in Sicily, the Romans initiated a private subscription to build a new fleet aimed at regaining control of the Mediterranean Sea. This effort was crucial for the Romans as they sought to reassert their naval dominance during the First Punic War.
events.name: Romans build a fleet to regain command of the sea

events.enhanced_description: In a significant change to the Roman judicial system, the number of praetors was increased from one to two. This allowed for more efficient handling of legal matters and ensured that the Republic had a magistrate with imperium capable of leading an army in emergencies when both consuls were unavailable.
events.name: Increase in Number of Praetors in Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Zhengguo Canal, a monumental engineering project, was constructed in the Qin dynasty, enhancing agricultural productivity and military logistics. This canal played a crucial role in the consolidation of power by the Qin state and set the foundation for future infrastructural developments in China.
events.name: Construction of the Zhengguo Canal

events.enhanced_description: General Meng Ao of the Qin state successfully suppressed a revolt in Jinyang, showcasing the military prowess of the Qin forces. This victory was significant in maintaining the stability and control of the Qin dynasty during a period of internal strife.
events.name: Meng Ao Crushes Revolt in Jinyang

events.enhanced_description: In 247, Rome celebrated its 1,000th anniversary with the Ludi Saeculares festivals, a grand event that showcased the city's rich history and cultural heritage, celebrated throughout the Roman Empire.
events.name: Rome's 1,000th anniversary

events.enhanced_description: In 247, Emperor Philip the Arab and his 10-year-old son were appointed as Roman Consuls, a significant political move that underscored the dynastic ambitions of Philip's reign.
events.name: Philip the Arab and his son become Roman Consuls

events.enhanced_description: In 247, the Goths emerged on the lower Danube frontier, launching invasions into present-day Ukraine and Romania, marking a significant threat to the stability of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Goths invade lower Danube

events.enhanced_description: In 247, Emperor Philip the Arab commemorated the millennium of Rome by organizing the Ludi Saeculares, a series of public games and festivals that celebrated the city's history and cultural achievements.
events.name: Ludi Saeculares held by Philip the Arab

events.enhanced_description: The last of the two Councils of Arabia was held in Bostra in 247, further addressing ecclesiastical matters within the Roman Christian Church and reflecting the growing influence of Christianity.
events.name: Last Council of Arabia

events.enhanced_description: In 247, Himiko of Yamataikoku initiated a war against King Himikoku of Kunukoku, reflecting the political and military struggles of early Japanese states during this period.
events.name: Himiko's war against Himikoku

events.enhanced_description: Cheomhae ascended to the throne of Silla, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, marking a significant moment in the kingdom's history. His reign contributed to the consolidation of power and cultural development in Silla.
events.name: Cheomhae becomes king of the Korean kingdom of Silla

events.enhanced_description: Carthaginian general Hanno achieved a notable victory by conquering the city of Theveste, also known as Hekatompylos. Following this conquest, he successfully negotiated a peace settlement with the Numidians, ending the ongoing conflict and earning praise for his fairness.
events.name: Hanno Conquers Theveste in Numidia

events.enhanced_description: General Wang He of the Qin state captured the city of Shangdang from the Zhao state, marking a significant territorial gain for Qin. This victory contributed to the expansion of Qin influence in the region and the establishment of the Taiyuan Commandery.
events.name: Wang He Takes Shangdang

events.enhanced_description: After an initial defeat at the Battle of Hewai, the Qin armies, led by Generals Meng Ao and Wang He, successfully repelled a coalition of rival states attempting to invade through the strategic Hangu Pass. This victory was crucial for the defense of the Qin heartland.
events.name: Qin Defeats Combined Forces at Hangu Pass

events.enhanced_description: At a young age, Ying Zheng ascended to the throne of the Qin state, later known as Qin Shi Huang. His reign marked the beginning of significant political and military reforms, with Lü Buwei serving as regent during his early years.
events.name: Ying Zheng Becomes King of Qin

events.enhanced_description: Senator Trajan Decius was tasked with quelling revolts led by Pacatianus in Moesia and Iotapianus in Syria, demonstrating the political instability of the Roman Empire during this period. Decius's actions were crucial in maintaining imperial authority.
events.name: The revolts of Pacatianus in Moesia and Iotapianus in Syria are put down by Senator Trajan Decius, by order of Emperor Philip the Arab

events.enhanced_description: The Roman Empire celebrated its millennium with the ludi saeculares, a series of games and festivities organized by Emperor Philip the Arab. This event highlighted the empire's rich cultural heritage and its enduring legacy.
events.name: The Roman Empire continues the celebration of the 1,000th anniversary of Rome, with the ludi saeculares, organized by Philip the Arab

events.enhanced_description: Jungcheon ascended to the throne of Goguryeo, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, where he ruled until 270. His leadership played a significant role in the kingdom's expansion and cultural development.
events.name: Jungcheon becomes ruler of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo (until 270)

events.enhanced_description: Cyprian, a prominent Christian writer and theologian of Berber descent, became the bishop of Carthage, where he significantly influenced early Christian thought and practice. His leadership was marked by theological writings and the defense of the faith during persecutions.
events.name: Cyprian, Christian writer of Berber descent, becomes bishop of Carthage

events.enhanced_description: Origen, an early Christian scholar, composed an extensive eight-volume critique of the pagan philosopher Celsus, defending Christian doctrine and addressing philosophical challenges. His work laid the groundwork for future theological discourse.
events.name: Origen writes an eight-volume work, criticizing the pagan writer Celsus

events.enhanced_description: By this point in the First Punic War, Carthage had lost nearly all of its Sicilian territories to Rome, retaining only Lilybaeum and Drepanum. Hamilcar Barca took command of the Carthaginian forces in Sicily, launching a series of defensive raids against Roman positions.
events.name: Carthage Loses Sicilian Possessions

events.enhanced_description: General Meng Ao of the Qin state achieved a significant military victory by capturing the Wei cities of Gaodu and Ji. This conquest further solidified Qin's territorial expansion and military dominance in the region.
events.name: Meng Ao Captures Wei Cities

events.enhanced_description: Following his earlier victories, General Meng Ao annexed 37 towns and cities from the State of Zhao, including Yuci, Xincheng, and Langmeng. This expansion was part of Qin's broader strategy to consolidate power and territory.
events.name: Meng Ao Annexes Zhao Towns

events.enhanced_description: King Ashoka of the Mauryan Empire dedicated himself to the propagation of Buddhism, establishing monuments at significant sites associated with the life of Gautama Buddha. His reign marked a pivotal moment in the spread of Buddhist teachings across India and beyond.
events.name: Ashoka Promotes Buddhism

events.enhanced_description: Trajan Decius successfully quelled a revolt in the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia, showcasing his military leadership and political acumen. His actions helped stabilize the region during a time of unrest in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Trajan Decius puts down a revolt in Moesia and Pannonia

events.enhanced_description: In a decisive battle at Verona, Trajan Decius defeated and killed Emperor Philip the Arab, marking a significant shift in power within the Roman Empire. This battle underscored the intense political rivalries of the time.
events.name: Battle of Verona: Decius defeats and kills Emperor Philip the Arab

events.enhanced_description: The Decian persecution marked a systematic effort by Emperor Trajan Decius to enforce traditional Roman religious practices by compelling Christians to sacrifice to the Roman gods. This period was characterized by significant suffering for Christians and resistance to imperial authority.
events.name: Decian persecution: Decius begins persecuting Christians, and others refusing to sacrifice publicly to the Roman gods for the well-being of the emperor

events.enhanced_description: In a dramatic coup at the Gaoping Tombs, Sima Yi seized control from his co-regent Cao Shuang, solidifying his power in the state of Cao Wei. This event was pivotal in the power struggles of the Three Kingdoms period in China.
events.name: Incident at Gaoping Tombs: In the Chinese state of Cao Wei, regent Sima Yi, in a coup d'état, forces his co-regent Cao Shuang to relinquish his power, after taking control of the capital city of Luoyang

events.enhanced_description: In a wave of anti-Christian sentiment, the populace of Alexandria attacked and pillaged the homes of Christians, reflecting the growing tensions between different religious groups during the Decian persecution. This incident highlighted the societal divisions of the time.
events.name: In Alexandria, the populace pillages the homes of Christians

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Drepana saw Roman forces, commanded by Consul Publius Claudius Pulcher, engage the Carthaginian fleet led by Adherbal in the harbor of Drepanum. The Romans suffered a devastating defeat, losing a significant portion of their naval fleet.
events.name: Battle of Drepana

events.enhanced_description: Following the catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Drepana, Consul Publius Claudius Pulcher faced severe repercussions, including a hefty fine, while his colleague Lucius Junius Pullus took his own life. Aulus Atilius Calatinus was subsequently appointed dictator, leading a successful campaign in Sicily.
events.name: Consequences of the Battle of Drepana

events.enhanced_description: Prime Minister Lü Buwei led the Qin forces to victory against the last remnants of the Zhou dynasty, effectively quelling their rebellion. This victory marked a significant step in the consolidation of Qin power in the region.
events.name: Defeat of the Last Zhou Remnants

events.enhanced_description: General Meng Ao of the Qin state successfully captured the Taiyuan region from the State of Zhao, further expanding Qin's territory. This conquest was part of the broader military campaigns that established Qin dominance in northern China.
events.name: Meng Ao Seizes Taiyuan Region

events.enhanced_description: In 249 BCE, King Kaolie of the Chu state successfully annexed the State of Lu, a significant event in the history of the Warring States period in China. This annexation contributed to the expansion of Chu's territory and influence in the region, further escalating the conflicts among the various states vying for dominance.
events.name: King Kaolie of Chu annexes the State of Lu

events.enhanced_description: A group of Franks made significant incursions into the Iberian Peninsula, reaching Tarragona, which was then a Roman city known as Tarraco. This event marked the beginning of increased barbarian incursions into Roman territories.
events.name: A group of Franks penetrate as far as Tarragona in Spain (approximate date)

events.enhanced_description: The Goths, led by King Cniva, invaded Moesia, crossing the Danube River and laying siege to Roman cities such as Novae and Marcianopolis. This invasion was part of a larger pattern of barbarian incursions that threatened the stability of the Roman Empire.
events.name: The Goths under King Cniva invade Moesia

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Augusta Traiana, Roman forces faced a significant defeat against the invading Goths. This loss underscored the vulnerabilities of the Roman military during a period of increasing external threats.
events.name: Battle of Augusta Traiana: The Romans lose the battle against the Goths

events.enhanced_description: King Cniva of the Goths laid siege to Philippopolis, modern-day Plovdiv, after a prolonged resistance, ultimately conquering the city and causing significant casualties among its inhabitants. This event marked a critical moment in the Gothic invasions of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Cniva lays siege to Philippopolis (modern Plovdiv)

events.enhanced_description: The Alamanni successfully drove Roman forces from the region of Donau-Ries, highlighting the increasing pressure on the Roman Empire's borders from various barbarian tribes. This event was part of a broader pattern of military challenges faced by Rome.
events.name: The Alamanni drive the Romans from the modern area of Donau-Ries

events.enhanced_description: The Plague of Cyprian began in Ethiopia and spread throughout the Roman Empire, causing widespread devastation and societal upheaval. Named after St. Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, this epidemic had profound effects on the population and the church.
events.name: An epidemic begins in Ethiopia, moves into Egypt and the Roman colonies in North Africa, and spreads through the Roman Empire (named the Plague of Cyprian, after St. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage)

events.enhanced_description: The Kingdom of Aksum emerged as a dominant power in the Red Sea trade, controlling commerce and establishing itself as a significant player in regional politics. This period marked the rise of Aksum as a major trading empire.
events.name: The Kingdom of Aksum (Axum) takes control of commerce on the Red Sea

events.enhanced_description: During this period, the earliest references to the 'emperor's south-pointing carriage' emerged in China, showcasing early advancements in navigational technology. This invention highlighted the ingenuity of Chinese engineering.
events.name: The earliest Chinese references to a device known as "emperor's south-pointing carriage" date to this period

events.enhanced_description: Teotihuacán underwent significant reconstruction, transforming into a four-quartered cosmogram under the guidance of Zapotec architects from Monte Albán. This architectural shift reflected the cultural and religious significance of the city.
events.name: Teotihuacán is rebuilt as a four-quartered cosmogram by Zapotec architects brought from Monte Albán in Oaxaca

events.enhanced_description: The Classic period of Mesoamerican civilization commenced, characterized by the rise of complex societies, monumental architecture, and advanced cultural practices. This era laid the foundation for the development of later Mesoamerican cultures.
events.name: Classic period of Mesoamerican civilization begins

events.enhanced_description: Diophantus authored 'Arithmetica', a groundbreaking work that laid the foundations for algebra as a systematic discipline. His contributions significantly influenced mathematical thought in both the ancient and modern worlds.
events.name: Diophantus writes Arithmetica, the first systematic treatise on algebra

events.enhanced_description: The Family of Vunnerius Keramus medallion was crafted, later incorporated into the Brescia Cross, showcasing the artistic skills of the time. This piece reflects the cultural and artistic developments of the Roman Empire.
events.name: The family portrait medallion, traditionally called the Family of Vunnerius Keramus, is made

events.enhanced_description: The Ludovisi Battle sarcophagus was created, illustrating the conflict between Romans and Barbarians, and later became part of the collection at the National Roman Museum. This artwork exemplifies the artistic and cultural themes of the period.
events.name: The Ludovisi Battle sarcophagus, depicting battle between the Romans and the Barbarians, is made for use in Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Igel Column, a Roman funerary monument, was erected in Trier, Germany, during the mid-3rd century AD. It is notable for its intricate reliefs that depict scenes from Roman life and mythology, reflecting the cultural and artistic influences of the Roman Empire.
events.name: The Igel Column is erected at Trier in Germany

events.enhanced_description: The Decian persecution began in 250 AD when Emperor Decius mandated that all citizens of the Roman Empire, except for Jews, perform sacrifices to the Roman gods. This decree led to widespread persecution of Christians, with Pope Fabian becoming one of the first martyrs during this period.
events.name: Decian persecution of Christians initiated

events.enhanced_description: Saint Denis, the bishop of Paris, is believed to have been martyred by beheading around 250 AD. He is venerated as the patron saint of France, and his martyrdom is a significant event in the history of early Christianity in Gaul.
events.name: Possible date – Denis, a bishop of Paris, is martyred by beheading

events.enhanced_description: Around 250 BCE, Ptolemy II Philadelphus compelled the Jewish community in Alexandria to translate their sacred texts, the Torah, into Greek. This monumental task, carried out by approximately seventy translators, resulted in the Septuagint, which became a cornerstone of Jewish and Christian scripture in the Hellenistic world.
events.name: Ptolemy II forces the translation of the Torah into Greek

events.enhanced_description: In 250 BCE, following the death of Magas, the King of Cyrene, a political marriage was arranged between Demetrius the Fair and Berenice, the daughter of Magas. However, the ensuing romantic entanglement between Demetrius and Apama II led to a violent uprising, culminating in Demetrius's assassination.
events.name: Marriage arrangement between Demetrius the Fair and Berenice of Cyrene

events.enhanced_description: In 250 BCE, during the First Punic War, the Romans redirected their military efforts towards the southwest coast of Sicily, launching a naval expedition against the Carthaginian stronghold of Lilybaeum. They successfully seized and burned the cities of Selinous and Heraclea Minoa before commencing the siege of Lilybaeum, marking a pivotal moment in the conflict.
events.name: Roman naval expedition during the Punic War

events.enhanced_description: According to tradition, after the Romans defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of Panormus in 250 BCE, Marcus Atilius Regulus was released from captivity to negotiate peace. However, upon returning to Rome, he urged the Senate to continue the war, ultimately returning to Carthage where he faced execution.
events.name: Marcus Atilius Regulus negotiates with Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 250 BCE, Andragoras, a satrap of the Seleucid province of Partahia, sought to assert independence from the Seleucid Empire under Antiochus II. His actions reflected the growing discontent and fragmentation within the Seleucid territories during this period.
events.name: Andragoras attempts to gain independence

events.enhanced_description: Around 250 BCE, the Third Buddhist Council was convened in Pataliputra under the Mauryan Emperor Ashoka and the monk Moggaliputta Tissa. This council aimed to purify the Buddhist community and address the growing factions that were emerging due to royal patronage.
events.name: Third Buddhist Council convened by Ashoka

events.enhanced_description: The Didarganj Yakshi, a significant sculpture from the Mauryan period, was created around 250 BCE in Patna, Bihar. This exquisite piece of art, which depicts a female figure holding a fly whisk, is now housed in the Patna Museum and is celebrated for its intricate craftsmanship and historical importance.
events.name: Didarganj Yakshi sculpture created

events.enhanced_description: Around 250 BCE, the Lion Capital of Ashoka was erected as part of a pillar at Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh. This iconic sculpture, which symbolizes the teachings of Buddha, is now preserved at the Sarnath Museum and is recognized as a national emblem of India.
events.name: Lion Capital of Ashoka erected at Sarnath

events.enhanced_description: In 250 BCE, Zichu ascended to the throne as the king of the Qin state, with Lü Buwei serving as his Prime Minister. This period marked significant political developments in the Qin state, which would later play a crucial role in the unification of China.
events.name: Zichu becomes king of Qin

events.enhanced_description: In 250 BCE, the Qin general Meng Ao successfully captured the Han cities of Chenggao and Xingyang, leading to the establishment of the Sanchuan Commandery. This military success was part of the broader expansionist strategy of the Qin state during the Warring States period.
events.name: Qin general Meng Ao captures Han cities

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Abritus took place in 251 AD, where the Goths decisively defeated Roman Emperor Decius and his son Herennius Etruscus. This battle marked a significant loss for Rome and highlighted the growing threat of the Gothic tribes.
events.name: Battle of Abritus

events.enhanced_description: In 251 AD, Hostilian, the son of Emperor Decius, succeeded his father after Decius's death in battle. Trebonianus Gallus was proclaimed emperor by the troops, leading to a brief co-emperorship amidst a backdrop of plague and political instability.
events.name: Hostilian succeeds Decius

events.enhanced_description: During the mid-3rd century, Roman Britain experienced a decline in prosperity as Germanic tribes, including the Franks and Saxons, began raiding the southeastern coast. This marked a significant shift in the stability of Roman control over the region.
events.name: Decline of Roman Britain's prosperity

events.enhanced_description: In 251 AD, Emperor Trebonianus Gallus negotiated a peace with the Goths, allowing them to keep their plunder in exchange for a bribe to prevent further invasions. This decision reflected the Roman Empire's struggle to manage external threats during a time of crisis.
events.name: Gallus makes peace with the Goths

events.enhanced_description: The year 251 AD marked the beginning of a devastating plague that swept through the Roman Empire, contributing to the empire's decline and exacerbating the challenges faced by its leaders during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Plague begins in the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 251 AD, Sassanid King Shapur I ordered an invasion of Syria, aiming to capture the city of Antioch. This campaign was part of a broader conflict between the Sassanid Empire and the Roman Empire during the 3rd century.
events.name: Shapur I orders invasion of Syria

events.enhanced_description: In 251 AD, Wang Ling's rebellion against the Wei regent Sima Yi was successfully quelled, reinforcing Sima Yi's power during a period of instability in the Three Kingdoms period of China.
events.name: Wang Ling's rebellion quelled

events.enhanced_description: Sima Yi, a prominent general and regent during the Three Kingdoms period, passed away in Luoyang in 251 AD. His death marked a significant turning point in the power dynamics of the Wei state.
events.name: Sima Yi passes away

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Sima Yi in 251 AD, his eldest son, Sima Shi, inherited his father's authority, continuing the legacy of power within the Wei state during the turbulent Three Kingdoms period.

image.caption: Qing dynasty illustration of Sima Shi.
image.credit: Unknown author — Taken from Gongjin's Campaign Memorials: a Three Kingdoms Wiki Zengxiang quantu Sanguoyanyi
image.date_qualification: The image is dated in the source to the Qing Dynasty (1906), centuries after the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Sima Shi inherits authority

events.enhanced_description: In 251 BCE, Paseas, the tyrant of Sicyon, was assassinated by Nicocles with the support of King Antigonus II of Macedonia. Following this power shift, Nicocles ruled briefly before being overthrown by exiled citizens led by Aratus, leading to a turbulent period in Sicyon's political landscape.
events.name: Assassination of Paseas in Sicyon

events.enhanced_description: In 251 BCE, Aratus, a prominent leader in Sicyon, initiated the recall of citizens exiled by the tyrant Nicocles. This move led to internal strife and prompted Aratus to seek alliance with the Achaean League, aiming to strengthen the city's defenses against potential Macedonian aggression.
events.name: Aratus recalls exiles to Sicyon

events.enhanced_description: In 251 BCE, the Romans, under the command of Lucius Caecilius Metellus, launched an assault on the Carthaginian-held port city of Panormus after capturing Kephalodon. The ensuing Battle of Panormus resulted in a decisive Roman victory, marking a significant turning point in the First Punic War.
events.name: Roman attack on Panormus

events.enhanced_description: Following the Roman capture of Panormus in 251 BCE, much of western Sicily fell under Roman control. Cities such as Ieta, Solous, Petra, and Tyndaris sought peace with the Romans, effectively ending significant Carthaginian military presence on the island.
events.name: Western Sicily falls to Romans after Panormus

events.enhanced_description: In a significant battle, Zhao general Lian Po achieved a decisive victory over the State of Yan at Hao, solidifying Zhao's military power. Following this victory, Lian Po was promoted to Prime Minister after the death of Lord Pingyuan, marking a pivotal moment in Zhao's political landscape.
events.name: Victory of Lian Po at Hao

events.enhanced_description: In March 251 AD, Pope Cornelius succeeded Pope Fabian as the 21st pope of the Catholic Church. His papacy occurred during a time of significant persecution of Christians, and he played a crucial role in addressing the challenges faced by the church.
events.name: Pope Cornelius succeeds Pope Fabian

events.enhanced_description: The First Synod of Carthage was convened in May 251 AD under the presidency of Saint Cyprian. This early church council addressed issues of church governance and the treatment of lapsed Christians during the Decian persecution.
events.name: First Synod of Carthage

events.enhanced_description: In 252 AD, Shapur I successfully quelled a revolt in Khorasan, a region that spans modern-day Iran and Turkmenistan. This victory allowed him to rejoin his main army and continue his campaigns against the Roman Empire.
events.name: Shapur I puts down revolt in Khorasan

events.enhanced_description: In 252 AD, Shapur I invaded Armenia and appointed Artavazd VI as the new king. This invasion was part of Shapur's broader strategy to expand the Sassanid Empire's influence in the region.
events.name: Shapur I invades Armenia

events.enhanced_description: In 252 AD, the region of Georgia submitted peacefully to Shapur I, becoming a vassal of the Sassanid Empire. This submission marked a significant expansion of Sassanid influence in the Caucasus region.
events.name: Georgia submits to Shapur I

events.enhanced_description: In 252 AD, Sun Liang succeeded his father, Sun Quan, as emperor of the Eastern Wu state during the Three Kingdoms period in China. His ascension marked a continuation of the Sun family's rule amidst ongoing conflicts with rival states.

image.caption: Family tree of Sun Quan and his family.
image.credit: zh-classical:User:曹孟德 . — Own work
image.date_qualification: A family-tree diagram providing genealogical context for Sun Liang’s succession; the recorded image date is 2007-04-25, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Sun Liang succeeds Sun Quan

events.enhanced_description: In 252 AD, Pope Cornelius was exiled to Centumcellae by Emperor Trebonianus Gallus. This exile was part of the broader context of the Decian persecution, which targeted Christian leaders and communities.
events.name: Pope Cornelius exiled

events.enhanced_description: Abantidas, the tyrant of Sicyon, was assassinated by his enemies, leading to the ascension of his father, Paseas, as the new ruler. This event marked a significant shift in the political dynamics of Sicyon, reflecting the volatile nature of tyrannical rule in ancient Greece.
events.name: Murder of Abantidas of Sicyon

events.enhanced_description: In 253, King Shapur I of the Sasanian Empire achieved a significant victory over a Roman field army at the Battle of Barbalissos, marking a pivotal moment in the ongoing conflict between the two empires. This battle showcased the military prowess of the Sasanian forces and contributed to the instability of Roman control in the region.
events.name: Battle of Barbalissos

events.enhanced_description: In 253 AD, the legions campaigning against the Goths elected Marcus Aemilius Aemilianus as their new emperor. His election reflected the military's influence in Roman politics during a time of crisis and external threats.

image.caption: Antoninianus of Aemilian, an ancient Roman coin depicting the emperor.
image.credit: CNG — https://auctions.cngcoins.com/lots/view/4-71VKC3/aemilian-ad-253-ar-antoninianus-21mm-462-g-12h-rome-mint-near-ef
image.date_qualification: AD 253; the coin’s stated date, not a date for the election scene.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Aemilianus elected emperor

events.enhanced_description: Aemilianus was declared an 'enemy of the State' by the Roman Senate in 253 AD. Following his defeat at Interamna Nahars, he fled with his son Volusianus but was ultimately killed by his own troops, illustrating the volatile nature of Roman political life.
events.name: Aemilianus proclaimed enemy of the State

events.enhanced_description: Aemilianus ruled the Roman Empire for a brief three-month period in 253 AD, during which he promised to lead military campaigns against the Goths and Persia. His short reign was marked by significant challenges and instability.
events.name: Aemilianus rules for three months

events.enhanced_description: In 253 AD, Aemilianus was murdered at Spoletium, leading to Publius Valerianus being recognized as the new emperor by the Rhine legions. This event marked another shift in the leadership of the Roman Empire amidst ongoing military conflicts.
events.name: Aemilianus murdered at Spoletium

events.enhanced_description: In 253 AD, Valerianus I divided the Roman Empire into two halves, with Gallienus governing the West and Valerianus ruling the East. This division was a strategic response to the increasing pressures from external threats, particularly from Persia.
events.name: Valerianus I splits the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 253, Emperor Valerian undertook significant reforms of the Legio III Augusta to strengthen the Roman military's capacity against the 'five peoples,' a coalition of Berber tribes threatening Roman territories in North Africa. This strategic move aimed to bolster defenses and maintain Roman authority in the region.
events.name: Valerian reforms Legio III Augusta

events.enhanced_description: In 253, Pope Cornelius was exiled during a period of persecution against Christians under Emperor Decius. His exile marked a significant moment in the early Christian church, highlighting the struggles faced by church leaders during times of political turmoil.
events.name: Pope Cornelius is sent into exile

events.enhanced_description: Following the exile of Pope Cornelius in 253, Pope Lucius I was elected as the 22nd pope. His election occurred during a tumultuous period for the Christian church, characterized by persecution and internal strife.
events.name: Pope Lucius I succeeds Pope Cornelius

events.enhanced_description: Shortly after his election in 253, Pope Lucius I was arrested and exiled, reflecting the precarious position of church leaders during the Roman persecutions of Christians. His arrest underscored the challenges faced by the early church in maintaining leadership and unity.
events.name: Lucius is arrested and exiled

events.enhanced_description: The Second Syrian War concluded with Antiochus II regaining significant territories in Anatolia from Ptolemy II, including the cities of Miletus and Ephesus. This conflict reshaped the power dynamics between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms, influencing the course of Hellenistic history.
events.name: End of the Second Syrian War

events.enhanced_description: The conclusion of the Second Syrian War was marked by the marriage of Antiochus II to Berenice Syra, the daughter of Ptolemy II. This political alliance was significant as it aimed to secure peace between the two powerful dynasties, though it also led to complications in Antiochus's previous marriage.
events.name: Marriage of Antiochus II and Berenice Syra

events.enhanced_description: Antiochus II successfully recaptured the city of Miletus, overthrowing its tyrant and earning the adoration of the citizens who worshipped him as a god. This event not only solidified his power but also marked a significant moment in the cultural landscape of the region.
events.name: Recapture of Miletus by Antiochus II

events.enhanced_description: A Roman war fleet consisting of 150 ships was wrecked while en route from Lilybaeum to Rome, demonstrating the perils faced by naval forces during this period. This loss significantly impacted Roman military operations in the ongoing conflicts with Carthage.
events.name: Wreck of Roman War Fleet

events.enhanced_description: Tiberius Coruncanius made history by becoming the first plebeian elected as pontifex maximus of Rome, breaking the patrician monopoly on this powerful religious office. His election marked a significant step towards greater political representation for the plebeians in Roman society.
events.name: Election of Tiberius Coruncanius as Pontifex Maximus

events.enhanced_description: Alexander, the nephew of Antigonus II, instigated a revolt in Corinth with the support of Ptolemy II, declaring himself an independent monarch. This revolt significantly weakened Antigonus's control over southern Greece and altered the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Revolt of Alexander in Corinth

events.enhanced_description: Macedonia's involvement in the Second Syrian War came to an end as Antigonus II became preoccupied with the revolt in Corinth and increased enemy activity along Macedonia's northern frontier. This shift allowed other powers to gain ground in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Macedonia's Withdrawal from the Second Syrian War

events.enhanced_description: In 254, Publius Licinius Valerianus Augustus and his son Publius Licinius Egnatius Gallienus were appointed as Roman Consuls. This joint consulship marked a significant moment in the governance of the Roman Empire during a time of crisis and instability.
events.name: Valerianus and Gallienus become Roman Consuls

events.enhanced_description: In 254, the Roman Empire faced multiple threats from various peoples on its borders, including Germanic tribes and the Sassanid Persians. This period, known as the Crisis of the Third Century, highlighted the vulnerabilities of the empire and the challenges of maintaining control over its vast territories.
events.name: Threats to the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 254, Pope Stephen I was elected to succeed Pope Lucius I, continuing the leadership of the Christian church during a time of persecution. His papacy would be marked by significant theological debates and challenges within the early church.
events.name: Pope Stephen I succeeds Pope Lucius I

events.enhanced_description: A Roman army, led by consuls Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina and Aulus Atilius Calatinus, successfully captured the city of Panormus in Sicily. This victory was part of the larger conflict between Rome and Carthage, further establishing Roman influence in the region.
events.name: Capture of Panormus by Roman Consuls

events.enhanced_description: The Romans suffered a setback as they lost control of the Sicilian city of Agrigentum to the Carthaginians. This defeat highlighted the challenges faced by Rome in maintaining its territorial gains during the ongoing conflict with Carthage.
events.name: Loss of Agrigentum to Carthaginians

events.enhanced_description: In 255, Sima Shi, a prominent general and politician during the Three Kingdoms period, successfully quelled a rebellion led by Guanqiu Jian and Wen Qin. This event solidified his power and influence within the state of Cao Wei.
events.name: Sima Shi quells rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 255, Sima Shi, a key figure in the politics of the Three Kingdoms period, passed away. His death marked a significant turning point in the power dynamics of the state of Cao Wei.

image.caption: Qing dynasty illustration of Sima Shi.
image.credit: Unknown author — Taken from Gongjin's Campaign Memorials: a Three Kingdoms Wiki Zengxiang quantu Sanguoyanyi
image.date_qualification: Described as Qing dynasty (1906); this is the illustration’s date, not the date of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Sima Shi passes away

events.enhanced_description: In 255, Sima Zhao, the younger brother of Sima Shi, inherited his brother's authority following Sima Shi's death. This transition of power was crucial for the continuation of the Sima family's influence in the state of Cao Wei.
events.name: Sima Zhao inherits authority

events.enhanced_description: In 255, Ma Jun, a notable mechanical engineer from the state of Cao Wei, invented the south-pointing chariot, a remarkable vehicle that utilized a differential gear system for navigation. This invention represented a significant advancement in engineering and technology during the period.
events.name: Ma Jun invents the south-pointing chariot

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Adis was fought near the city of Adis, where Roman forces led by Marcus Atilius Regulus inflicted a crushing defeat on the Carthaginians. The harsh terms demanded by Regulus after the battle led to further conflict, as the Carthaginians resolved to continue fighting despite their losses.
events.name: Battle of Adis

events.enhanced_description: In response to the demands of Regulus, the Carthaginians hired Xanthippus, a Spartan mercenary, to reorganize their army. Under his leadership, the revitalized Carthaginian forces decisively defeated the Romans at the Battle of Tunis, capturing Regulus and shifting the momentum of the war.
events.name: Carthaginian Army Reorganization by Xanthippus

events.enhanced_description: During the Second Syrian War, Ptolemy II suffered significant territorial losses in Cilicia, Pamphylia, and Ionia, while Antiochus II regained control of Miletus and Ephesus. This conflict underscored the shifting power dynamics in the Hellenistic world, leading to a peace agreement that included a marriage alliance.
events.name: Ptolemy II's Losses in the Second Syrian War

events.enhanced_description: Diodotus I, the Seleucid satrap of Bactria, rebelled against Antiochus II and established the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, marking a significant shift in power in the region. His rebellion laid the foundation for a new political entity that would influence the cultural and political landscape of Central Asia.
events.name: Diodotus I's Rebellion in Bactria

events.enhanced_description: In 256, the Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 3035 was written, containing a warrant for the arrest of a Christian. This document provides insight into the legal and social challenges faced by early Christians in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 3035 written

events.enhanced_description: In 256, the Goths launched an invasion into Asia Minor, leading to the loss of Dacia for the Roman Empire and threatening the city of Thessalonica. This invasion was part of the broader conflicts that characterized the Crisis of the Third Century.
events.name: Goths invade Asia Minor

events.enhanced_description: In 256, the Franks crossed the Rhine River, marking a significant incursion into Roman territory. This event, along with the Alemanni reaching Mediolanum, exemplified the increasing pressures faced by the Roman Empire from various barbarian groups.
events.name: Franks cross the Rhine

events.enhanced_description: In 256, Berber tribes in North Africa launched a massacre against Roman colonists, reflecting the growing tensions and conflicts between indigenous populations and Roman settlers. This event was part of the broader unrest affecting the Roman Empire during this period.
events.name: Berbers massacre Roman colonists

events.enhanced_description: In 256, King Shapur I of the Sasanian Empire invaded Mesopotamia and Syria, successfully conquering and plundering key cities such as Antioch and Dura-Europos. His campaigns significantly weakened Roman control in the region and were followed by natural disasters that further devastated the area.
events.name: Shapur I invades Mesopotamia and Syria

events.enhanced_description: In 256, cities across the Roman Empire began constructing defensive walls as the stability of the empire's frontiers deteriorated. This initiative was indicative of the growing threats from external forces and the need for enhanced security measures.
events.name: Cities in the Roman Empire build walls

events.enhanced_description: In 256, peace and unity were restored in China as the Wei Kingdom achieved significant victories in the north. This restoration of order marked a critical moment in the Three Kingdoms period, allowing for a temporary reprieve from the ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Peace restored in China

events.enhanced_description: In 256, a devastating pandemic swept through the Roman world, particularly affecting regions such as Pontus and Alexandria. The widespread loss of life led to a significant increase in the number of individuals embracing Christianity, as many sought solace in faith during the crisis.
events.name: Pandemic strikes the Roman world

events.enhanced_description: In 256, Emperor Valerian intensified the persecution of Christians within the Roman Empire, reflecting the ongoing tensions between the state and the growing Christian community. This persecution was part of a broader campaign against religious dissenters during his reign.
events.name: Emperor Valerian persecutes Christians

events.enhanced_description: In 256, Pope Stephen I issued a threat of excommunication against Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, and other bishops in Africa and Asia Minor, due to their practice of rebaptizing heretics. This conflict highlighted the theological divisions within early Christianity and the potential for schism between different regions of the church.
events.name: Pope Stephen I threatens excommunication

events.enhanced_description: In 256, a significant Synod of Carthage was convened, addressing critical issues within the Christian community, particularly regarding the rebaptism of heretics. This synod was pivotal in shaping the theological landscape of early Christianity and the authority of church leaders.
events.name: A Synod of Carthage is held

events.enhanced_description: In 257, Gallienus entered into a joint consulship with his father Valerian I, having successfully restored some order in the Danube region. This partnership was significant for the governance of the Roman Empire during a time of crisis.
events.name: Gallienus enters joint consulship

events.enhanced_description: In 257, Aurelian, a future emperor of Rome, achieved a decisive victory against the Goths, capturing many prisoners and bringing them back to Rome. This victory was crucial in restoring Roman authority and stability in the face of external threats.
events.name: Aurelian defeats the Goths

events.enhanced_description: The Limes Germanicus, a fortified boundary marking the northern frontier of the Roman Empire, was abandoned by Roman forces along the Iller River in Bavaria, signaling a significant retreat from the region during a period of increasing pressure from Germanic tribes.
events.name: Abandonment of the Limes Germanicus

events.enhanced_description: Valerian, under the guardianship of Ingenuus, was appointed to represent the Roman government in Sirmium, a key city in the troubled Illyrian provinces, amidst growing unrest and challenges to Roman authority.
events.name: Valerian established at Sirmium

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Valerian successfully recaptured Antioch from the forces of King Shapur I of Persia, reaffirming Roman control over this vital city in the eastern provinces during a time of conflict with the Persian Empire.
events.name: Valerian recovers Antioch

events.enhanced_description: The Goths constructed a fleet on the Black Sea, marking a significant development in their military capabilities and signaling their intent to expand their influence across the region.
events.name: Goths build a fleet

events.enhanced_description: During this period, the Goths began to separate into two distinct groups: the Ostrogoths and the Visigoths, a division that would have lasting implications for the history of Europe and the Roman Empire.
events.name: Separation of the Goths

events.enhanced_description: Pope Sixtus II ascended to the papacy, succeeding Pope Stephen I as the 24th pope of the Roman Catholic Church, during a time of significant challenges for Christians in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Pope Sixtus II succeeds Pope Stephen I

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Valerian initiated a severe persecution of Christians, issuing an edict that mandated pagan sacrifices by bishops and priests, while prohibiting Christians from gathering at the tombs of the deceased under threat of death.
events.name: Valerian's persecution of Christians begins

events.enhanced_description: This year is noted for the absence of significant recorded events in historical records.
events.name: No major events

events.enhanced_description: The Goths launched raids across Asia Minor, causing widespread destruction and instability in the region, particularly targeting the city of Trapezus.
events.name: Goths ravage Asia Minor

events.enhanced_description: The silver content in the Roman denarius fell below 10%, leading to a severe economic crisis that devastated craftsmen, tradesmen, and small farmers, while enriching landowners who capitalized on the situation.
events.name: Decline of silver content in denarius

events.enhanced_description: Valerian II, the eldest son of Emperor Gallienus, died under suspicious circumstances, possibly murdered by Ingenuus, the governor of Pannonia. Following his death, Gallienus appointed his other son, Saloninus, as Caesar.
events.name: Death of Valerian II

events.enhanced_description: A second edict issued by Emperor Valerian intensified the persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire, categorizing them into four groups for punishment, including death for priests and exile for nuns.
events.name: Second Imperial edict against Christianity

events.enhanced_description: Sima Zhao successfully suppressed Zhuge Dan's rebellion in Shouchun, effectively concluding a series of uprisings known as the Three Rebellions, which had threatened the stability of the state.
events.name: Sima Zhao quells Zhuge Dan's rebellion

events.enhanced_description: Sun Xiu ascended to the throne as emperor of the Eastern Wu state, succeeding his brother Sun Liang, during a period of significant political maneuvering and conflict in the Three Kingdoms era.
events.name: Sun Xiu succeeds Sun Liang

events.enhanced_description: Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, was martyred by decapitation, becoming a significant figure in early Christian history and a symbol of the struggle against Roman persecution.
events.name: Martyrdom of Cyprian

events.enhanced_description: Pope Sixtus II was martyred during the reign of Emperor Valerian, becoming a significant figure in the history of the papacy and early Christian martyrdom.
events.name: Martyrdom of Pope Sixtus II

events.enhanced_description: Gaius Duilius Nepos, a Roman commander celebrated for his naval victory over the Carthaginians, is appointed censor alongside Lucius Cornelius Scipio. This appointment is significant as it marks a rare honor for a novus homo, indicating Duilius's rise in the political hierarchy of Rome.
events.name: Gaius Duilius Nepos becomes Censor

events.enhanced_description: Ptolemy II Philadelphus, the ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, experiences a significant territorial loss as he loses control over Cyrenaica. This event reflects the shifting power dynamics in the region during the Hellenistic period.
events.name: Ptolemy II loses control of Cyrenaica

events.enhanced_description: Erasistratus of Ceos establishes a medical school in Alexandria, which becomes a prominent center for medical knowledge and practice in the ancient world. His contributions to medicine and anatomy significantly influence future generations of physicians.
events.name: Erasistratus founds a medical school at Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: The combined forces of Macedonian King Antigonus II and Seleucid King Antiochus II achieve a decisive naval victory at Cos against Ptolemy II. This victory not only secures Antigonus's control over the Aegean Sea but also weakens Ptolemaic naval power in the region.
events.name: Naval victory at Cos

events.enhanced_description: The State of Qin lays siege to Handan, the capital of the State of Zhou, but suffers heavy casualties under the command of Wang Ling. Following the losses, Wang Ling is replaced by Wang He, indicating the fierce competition and military struggles among the states during this period.
events.name: Siege of Handan by the State of Qin

events.enhanced_description: Merchant Lu Buwei successfully rescues the Qin prince Ying Yiren, who was held hostage at the Zhao court in Handan. This act is pivotal as Ying Yiren later becomes King Zhuangxiang of Qin, a significant figure in the unification of China.
events.name: Lu Buwei rescues Qin prince

events.enhanced_description: According to legend, the Hồng Bàng dynasty, the first ruling dynasty of Vietnam, comes to an end. This event marks a significant transition in Vietnamese history, leading to the rise of new dynasties and influences.
events.name: End of the Hồng Bàng dynasty

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Valerian led a massive army of 70,000 men to relieve the besieged city of Edessa from the forces of Persian King Shapur I. However, an outbreak of plague severely weakened the Roman forces, complicating their military efforts.
events.name: Valerian leads army to Edessa

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Mediolanum, Roman legions under Emperor Gallienus defeated a massive Germanic confederation of Alamanni warriors, successfully defending the city and the empire's northern frontier.
events.name: Battle of Mediolanum

events.enhanced_description: Postumus, the governor of Gaul, revolted against Emperor Gallienus, successfully establishing an independent realm known as the Gallic Empire, which included the western provinces of Britain and Spain.
events.name: Postumus revolts in Gaul

events.enhanced_description: Postumus declared himself Emperor of the Gallic Empire, ruling over the breakaway provinces until his death in 269, marking a significant moment in the fragmentation of Roman authority.
events.name: Postumus declares himself Emperor

events.enhanced_description: The Roman fort at Wiesbaden was captured by the Alamanni, demonstrating the increasing pressure on Roman defenses in the region during the 3rd century crisis.
events.name: Capture of Wiesbaden by Alamanni

events.enhanced_description: After invading the Roman Empire near Cologne in 257, the Franks advanced southward, reaching the city of Tarraco in Hispania, further threatening Roman control in the region.
events.name: Franks reach Tarraco

events.enhanced_description: Odaenathus, the ruler of Palmyra, led a campaign that resulted in the sacking of Nehardea, destroying its prominent yeshiva and significantly impacting the Jewish community in the region.
events.name: Odaenathus sacks Nehardea

events.enhanced_description: Pope Dionysius was elected as the pope, succeeding Pope Sixtus II during a tumultuous period for the early Christian church, marked by persecution and internal strife.
events.name: Election of Pope Dionysius

events.enhanced_description: Antiochus II Philadelphus initiates the Second Syrian War against Ptolemy II Philadelphus to avenge the losses suffered by his father. This conflict marks a significant escalation in hostilities between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms.
events.name: Antiochus II starts the Second Syrian War

events.enhanced_description: Following their victory at Thermae, the Carthaginians, under the command of Hamilcar Barca, counterattack the Romans and successfully seize Enna. This maneuver is part of the broader conflict in Sicily during the First Punic War.
events.name: Carthaginian counterattack at Enna

events.enhanced_description: The State of Zhou cedes the Han region of Yuanyong and six cities of Zhao to the State of Qin in exchange for peace. This territorial concession reflects the ongoing power struggles and shifting alliances among the states during the Warring States period.
events.name: Zhou cedes territory to Qin

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Edessa, Emperor Valerian led a large Roman army in an attempt to reclaim the city from Persian forces. The battle ended disastrously for the Romans, with Valerian captured and the majority of his troops killed or taken prisoner.
events.name: Battle of Edessa

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, King Shapur I of the Sassanian Empire captured the Roman Emperor Valerian during a campaign in the East. This event marked a significant humiliation for Rome and showcased the military prowess of the Sassanian forces.
events.name: King Shapur I captures Valerian

events.enhanced_description: After capturing Valerian, King Shapur I sent him to Bishapur, where he utilized the captured Roman soldiers to construct significant engineering projects, including the Band-e Kaisar, also known as the Bridge of Valerian. This bridge symbolized the power of the Sassanian Empire and its ability to mobilize resources.
events.name: King Shapur I sends Valerian to Bishapur and uses the captured Roman army for engineering plans

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Gallienus became the sole emperor of Rome following the death of his father, Valerian. His reign was marked by internal strife, including a revolt led by Ingenuus, the governor of Pannonia, which threatened the stability of the empire.
events.name: Gallienus becomes the sole emperor of Rome; during his reign the Pannonian governor Ingenuus revolts on the Danube

events.enhanced_description: In response to the threat posed by the invading Alamanni, Emperor Gallienus ordered the evacuation of the fortifications known as the limes in the Agri Decumates region in 260 AD. This strategic retreat reflected the challenges faced by the Roman Empire during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Gallienus evacuates the fortifications (limes) in the Agri Decumates (Germania Superior), covering the Black Forest area in the face of invading Alamanni

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Emperor Gallienus established his base in Mediolanum (modern-day Milan) where he reorganized the Roman army, enhancing its cavalry units. This move was crucial for reinforcing the Rhine frontier against external threats.
events.name: Gallienus establishes himself at Mediolanum (modern Milan); he reorganizes the army, supported by elite cavalry, and dispatches troops to the Rhine frontier

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Postumus declared himself emperor and established the Gallic Empire, a breakaway state from the Roman Empire. He focused on defending the Rhine frontier against invasions from Germanic tribes, solidifying his power in the region.
events.name: Postumus, Roman usurper, forms the Gallic Empire and protects the Rhine against an invasion of Germanic tribes

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Saloninus, the son of Emperor Gallienus, was proclaimed Augustus by his troops in Cologne. This act was part of the power struggles during a time of civil unrest and competing claims to the imperial throne.
events.name: Saloninus, son of Gallienus, is proclaimed Augustus by his troops

events.enhanced_description: After breaching the walls of Cologne in 260 AD, Postumus executed Saloninus and his adviser Silvanus, solidifying his claim to power as emperor of the Gallic Empire. This brutal act underscored the violent nature of the political landscape during this period.
events.name: Postumus executes Saloninus and his adviser Silvanus after breaching the walls of Cologne

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Postumus successfully asserted control over all Roman provinces west of the Alps, including Gaul, Britain, and Hispania, effectively establishing the Gallic Empire as a significant power within the fragmented Roman world.
events.name: Postumus wins over all the Roman provinces west of the Alps, including Gaul, Britain and Hispania

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, the Alamanni successfully captured the Roman fort at Wiesbaden, marking a significant victory against Roman forces. This event highlighted the increasing pressure on Roman frontiers during a time of internal strife.
events.name: The Roman fort of Wiesbaden (Germany) is captured by the Alamanni

events.enhanced_description: Around 260 AD, the Franks gained control over the Scheldt estuary, a strategic location that allowed them to enhance their power and influence in the region. This event marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Northern Europe.
events.name: The Franks take control over the Scheldt estuary (approximate date)

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, King Shapur I of Persia ordered the destruction of Caesarea Mazaca, a significant city in Asia Minor. This act was part of the broader conflict between the Sassanian Empire and Rome, showcasing the aggressive expansionist policies of Shapur.
events.name: Persian king Shapur I destroys Caesarea Mazaca in Asia Minor

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Emperor Cao Mao of the Former Wei state attempted to lead a coup against the regent Sima Zhao, who held significant power. However, Cao Mao was killed before the coup could be executed, further entrenching Sima Zhao's control over the state.
events.name: Emperor Cao Mao of Former Wei state attempts to lead a coup against the powerful regent Sima Zhao, but he himself is killed before it comes to a confrontation

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Cao Mao was assassinated during a coup d'état aimed at overthrowing Sima Zhao. His death marked a pivotal moment in the power struggle within the Former Wei state, leading to the ascension of the Sima clan.
events.name: Cao Mao is killed in a coup d'état against Sima Zhao

events.enhanced_description: Around 260 AD, the earliest known forms of chess began to emerge in India, evolving from earlier games. This strategic board game would later spread across cultures and become a significant part of global history.
events.name: Earliest known date of chess (approximate date)

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Pope Dionysius convened a synod in Rome to address concerns regarding the teachings of Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria, who was accused of misrepresenting the nature of the Trinity. This synod was significant in the early Christian church's efforts to define orthodox beliefs.
events.name: Pope Dionysius convenes a synod at Rome to demand an explanation from bishop Dionysius of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: In 260 AD, Paul of Samosata was appointed as the Patriarch of Antioch, a position that would place him at the center of theological debates within early Christianity. His tenure was marked by controversy over his views on the nature of Christ.
events.name: Paul of Samosata becomes Patriarch of Antioch

events.enhanced_description: The Romans continue their military campaign from Agrigentum, successfully relieving the besieged cities of Segesta and Macella, which had allied with them against Carthaginian forces. This advance demonstrates the Romans' strategic efforts to secure their position in Sicily during the First Punic War.
events.name: Roman advance from Agrigentum

events.enhanced_description: Hannibal Gisco returns to Sicily as the admiral of the Carthaginian fleet in the Strait of Messina, determined to counter the Roman naval threat. He achieves a temporary victory by defeating part of the Roman fleet and capturing the consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina.
events.name: Hannibal Gisco returns to Sicily

events.enhanced_description: In a display of naval innovation, the Romans, led by Gaius Duilius Nepos, achieve a significant victory over the Carthaginian fleet at the Battle of Mylae. Utilizing land tactics in naval warfare, the Romans defeat the Carthaginians, marking a turning point in the First Punic War.

image.caption: Diagram showing how the Roman corvus boarding device works.
image.credit: Chewie — based on Model of the "corvus" by Martin Lokaj
image.date_qualification: The supplied date is an upload date, not the date the illustration depicts.

events.name: Battle of Mylae

events.enhanced_description: Following his defeat at the Battle of Mylae, Hannibal Gisco loses the confidence of his peers and is executed for incompetence, along with other defeated generals. This reflects the harsh realities of military leadership in Carthage during the First Punic War.
events.name: Execution of Hannibal Gisco

events.enhanced_description: With their naval flank secured by the victory at the Battle of Mylae, Roman forces advance toward Thermae in northern Sicily. However, they face defeat against the Carthaginian forces led by Hamilcar, highlighting the ongoing conflict in the region.
events.name: Roman advance toward Thermae

events.enhanced_description: Callimachus of Cyrene, a prominent poet and scholar of the Hellenistic period, was appointed as the chief librarian at the Library of Alexandria, one of the most significant cultural and intellectual centers of the ancient world. His work in cataloging and preserving texts contributed to the library's reputation as a hub of knowledge and learning.
events.name: Callimachus of Cyrene becomes chief librarian at the Library of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Changping was a decisive conflict during the Warring States period in which the Qin state, led by General Bai Qi, defeated the Zhao state, commanded by General Lian Po. This battle marked a significant turning point, establishing Qin's military dominance over its rivals and leading to the eventual unification of China.
events.name: Battle of Changping

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move during the prolonged stalemate at Changping, King Xiaocheng of Zhao replaced the cautious General Lian Po with the more aggressive Zhao Kuo, influenced by Qin spies. This decision ultimately led to disastrous consequences for Zhao as the Qin army, under the command of Bai Qi, capitalized on this change in leadership.

image.caption: Map of the Battle of Changping between the Qin and Zhao states.
image.credit: SY — Own work
