events.name: Battle of Gaugamela

events.enhanced_description: Following his victory at Gaugamela, Alexander the Great encounters war elephants for the first time in Darius' camp. In Susa, he gains access to immense treasures, significantly enhancing his resources for future campaigns.
events.name: Encounter with War Elephants

events.enhanced_description: While Alexander the Great is engaged in campaigns in Asia, Agis III of Sparta capitalizes on his absence by leading a revolt among several Greek cities. With support from Persian finances and mercenaries, Agis III challenges Macedonian authority in the Peloponnese, demonstrating the ongoing tensions in Greek politics.
events.name: Agis III's Revolt During Alexander's Campaign

events.enhanced_description: In a critical engagement, Antipater leads the Macedonian forces to victory over Agis III of Sparta in the Battle of Megalopolis. This battle effectively quells the Spartan revolt and reasserts Macedonian dominance in Greece during Alexander's absence.
events.name: Battle of Megalopolis

events.enhanced_description: Alexander of Epirus successfully captures the cities of Heraclea from the Lucanians and both Terina and Sipontum from the Bruttii. His military campaigns expand his influence in southern Italy, showcasing the ongoing conflicts between various Italic tribes and external powers.
events.name: Alexander of Epirus' Conquests

events.enhanced_description: In 331 BC, the city of Tarentum in southern Italy revolted against Alexander of Epirus upon realizing his intentions to establish a personal kingdom. This conflict culminated in the Battle of Pandosia, where Alexander was defeated and killed, marking a significant shift in power in the region.
events.name: Tarentum turns against Alexander of Epirus

events.enhanced_description: In 331 BC, a peace treaty was established between the Gallic tribe of the Senones and the Romans, leading to a prolonged period of amicable relations that lasted throughout the century. This agreement marked a significant moment in the interactions between the Romans and the Gallic tribes.
events.name: Peace between the Senones and Romans

events.enhanced_description: From Thapsacus on the Euphrates River, Alexander leads his army towards the Tigris River, culminating in a victorious battle at Gaugamela on October 31. This victory solidifies his reputation as a formidable military leader and paves the way for the conquest of Persia.
events.name: March from Thapsacus to Gaugamela

events.enhanced_description: In 332 AD, Emperor Constantine I and his son Constantine II achieved a significant military victory against the Goths in Moesia, leading to the Goths becoming allies of Rome. This alliance was crucial for the protection of the Danube frontier against future invasions.
events.name: Emperor Constantine I and his son Constantine II defeat the Goths in Moesia

events.enhanced_description: In 332 AD, Emperor Constantine I continued the ambitious construction of a bridge across the Danube River, inspired by the earlier works of Trajan and his architect Apollodorus of Damascus. This bridge was intended to serve as a strategic point for staging military campaigns against local tribes.
events.name: Constantine I continues construction of a bridge across the Danube

events.enhanced_description: In 332 AD, Emperor Constantine I implemented a significant social policy by announcing a free distribution of food to the citizens of Constantinople, mirroring similar practices in Rome. This initiative provided approximately 80,000 rations daily from 117 distribution points throughout the city.
events.name: Constantine I announces free food distribution in Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 332 BC, King Darius III of Persia sent letters of friendship to Alexander the Great, offering a substantial ransom for his family and territorial concessions. However, Alexander rejected these overtures, choosing instead to advance into Mesopotamia, further escalating the conflict between the two powers.
events.name: Darius III sends letters to Alexander

events.enhanced_description: In 332 BC, an unidentified woman was buried in a bronze sarcophagus at the acropolis of Susa, adorned with exquisite gems and two coins dating back to 350 BC and 332 BC. This tomb remained unopened for over 22 centuries until its discovery by French archaeologist Jacques de Morgan in 1901.
events.name: Burial of an unidentified woman in Susa

events.enhanced_description: In 332 BC, Alexander the Great captured Damascus and subsequently laid siege to Tyre for seven months, resulting in widespread destruction and the enslavement of women and children. This brutal campaign solidified Alexander's control over the eastern Mediterranean.
events.name: Alexander the Great occupies Damascus and destroys Tyre

events.enhanced_description: In 332 BC, after leaving Parmenion in Syria, Alexander the Great advanced towards Gaza, facing fierce resistance that delayed his progress for two months. During this campaign, he sustained a serious shoulder wound, highlighting the challenges he faced in his conquests.
events.name: Alexander's advance to Gaza

events.enhanced_description: In 332 BC, Alexander the Great successfully conquered Egypt from the Persians, where he was welcomed as a liberator. The Persian satrap Mazaces surrendered without resistance, allowing Alexander to consolidate control over the eastern Mediterranean coast.
events.name: Alexander conquers Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 332 BC, Alexander the Great was crowned as Pharaoh of Upper and Lower Egypt, assuming divine status as both god and king. This event marked the fusion of Greek and Egyptian cultures and established Alexander's legacy in Egypt.
events.name: Alexander crowned Pharaoh of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 332 BC, Alexander the Great focused on organizing the administration of Egypt, appointing Egyptian governors while maintaining a separate Macedonian military command. This strategy aimed to stabilize his newly acquired territory.
events.name: Alexander organizes the administration of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 332 BC, Alexander the Great founded the city of Alexandria near the western arm of the Nile, strategically located between the sea and Lake Mareotis. The city was designed by the Rhodian architect Deinocrates and became a major center of culture and learning in the ancient world.
events.name: Foundation of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: After defeating the Samnites and Lucanians near Paestum in 332 BC, Alexander of Epirus negotiated a treaty with the Romans. This agreement was crucial in establishing diplomatic relations between the two powers during a time of regional instability.
events.name: Alexander's treaty with the Romans

events.enhanced_description: In 333 AD, Flavius Dalmatius and Domitius Zenofilus were appointed as consuls, marking an important political event in the Roman Empire. Their appointment reflected the ongoing consolidation of power within the imperial administration.
events.name: Flavius Dalmatius and Domitius Zenofilus appointed consuls

events.enhanced_description: In 333 AD, Emperor Constantine the Great made the strategic decision to withdraw Roman troops from Britain, effectively abandoning ongoing work on Hadrian's Wall. This marked a significant shift in Roman military focus and territorial control.
events.name: Constantine the Great pulls Roman troops out of Britain

events.enhanced_description: In 333 AD, Calocaerus revolted against Emperor Constantine I, proclaiming himself emperor. Flavius Dalmatius was dispatched to Cyprus to quell the rebellion, demonstrating the ongoing internal conflicts within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Calocaerus revolts against Constantine I

events.enhanced_description: In 333 AD, Emperor Constantine I elevated his youngest son, Constans, to the rank of Caesar in a ceremony held in Constantinople. This act was part of Constantine's broader strategy to secure his family's influence within the empire.
events.name: Constantine I elevates Constans to Caesar

events.enhanced_description: In 333 AD, Shi Hong succeeded his father, Shi Le, as the Emperor of the Later Zhao Empire during the Period of the Sixteen Kingdoms. However, real power remained with his cousin Shi Hu, leading to significant political intrigue and conflict.
events.name: Shi Hong succeeds Shi Le as Emperor of Later Zhao

events.enhanced_description: Following the capture of Byblos and Sidon, Alexander the Great laid siege to the city of Tyre, a critical stronghold for the Persian navy. This siege would become one of the most famous military operations of Alexander's campaign, lasting several months and showcasing his tactical ingenuity.
events.name: Siege of Tyre

events.enhanced_description: In 333 BC, Alexander the Great successfully conquered western Asia Minor, subduing the hill tribes of Lycia and Pisidia. This victory expanded his influence and control over the region, paving the way for further campaigns into Persia.
events.name: Alexander conquers western Asia Minor

events.enhanced_description: In 333 BC, Darius III of Persia executed Charidemus, a Greek mercenary leader, for publicly criticizing the preparations for the upcoming Battle of Issus. This act demonstrated Darius's intolerance for dissent and foreshadowed the challenges he would face against Alexander.
events.name: Execution of Charidemus by Darius III

events.enhanced_description: In 333 BC, after his conquests in Anatolia, Alexander the Great appointed Nearchus as satrap of the newly acquired regions of Lycia and Pamphylia, while his general Antigonus was made satrap of Phrygia. These appointments were crucial for maintaining control over the newly conquered territories.
events.name: Appointment of satraps in Anatolia

events.enhanced_description: After his victory at Issus, Alexander the Great marched south into Syria and Phoenicia with the strategic aim of cutting off the Persian fleet from its bases. His forces easily captured the coastal cities of Marathus and Aradus, while Parmenion was dispatched to secure the wealthy city of Damascus, which was crucial for its resources, including Darius' war chest.
events.name: Alexander's March into Syria and Phoenicia

events.enhanced_description: In response to a peace offering from Darius III, Alexander the Great demanded the Persian king's unconditional surrender, marking a significant escalation in their conflict. This bold move underscored Alexander's determination to conquer the Persian Empire and solidify his own power.
events.name: Alexander's Demand for Darius' Surrender

events.enhanced_description: In 334 AD, Flavius Dalmatius successfully suppressed a revolt in Cyprus led by Calocaerus. Following the revolt's defeat, Calocaerus was captured and executed, restoring order to the region.
events.name: Flavius Dalmatius puts down revolt in Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: In 334 AD, the Goths played a crucial role in defending the Danube frontier against an invasion by the Vandals. Their alliance with the Roman Empire proved vital in maintaining stability in the region.
events.name: The Goths protect the Danube frontier against Vandals

events.enhanced_description: In 334 AD, Emperor Constantine the Great reauthorised gladiatorial combat, a popular but controversial form of entertainment in the Roman Empire. This decision reflected the ongoing cultural dynamics and public interest in such spectacles.
events.name: Constantine the Great reauthorises gladiatorial combat

events.enhanced_description: The death of Pixodarus, the king of Caria, led to the ascension of his son-in-law Orontobates. This transition of power was pivotal as it occurred during a time of upheaval in the region, with Alexander the Great's conquests looming.
events.name: Death of Pixodarus and Succession of Orontobates

events.enhanced_description: At a war council in Zeleia, the Persian satraps debated their military strategy against Alexander the Great. Memnon of Rhodes advocated for a scorched earth policy to avoid direct confrontation, but this advice was rejected by Arsites and other satraps, leading to a critical miscalculation in their defense.
events.name: Persian War Council at Zeleia

events.enhanced_description: King Alexander III of Macedonia crossed the Dardanelles, embarking on his campaign against the Persian Empire. He left Antipater in charge of Greece, demonstrating his strategic foresight in managing both military and political affairs as he mobilized a formidable army.
events.name: Alexander Crosses the Dardanelles

events.enhanced_description: In May, Alexander the Great achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of the Granicus against the Persians, who were led by the Greek mercenary Memnon of Rhodes. This battle marked the beginning of Alexander's campaign in Asia and resulted in significant losses for Darius III's forces.
events.name: Battle of the Granicus

events.enhanced_description: After a series of victories, Alexander the Great accepted the surrender of Sardis, the provincial capital of the Persians, along with its treasury. This event was crucial as it allowed Alexander to secure a vital foothold in Asia Minor and continue his campaign down the Ionian coast.
events.name: Surrender of Sardis

events.enhanced_description: At Halicarnassus, Alexander the Great conducted a successful siege against the forces of Memnon of Rhodes and Orontobates, leading to their eventual withdrawal by sea. This marked the first of many sieges Alexander would undertake during his campaign against Persia.
events.name: Siege of Halicarnassus

events.enhanced_description: Following his victories, Alexander's reputation prompted most cities in western Asia Minor to open their gates to him. However, Miletus resisted and was subsequently besieged, illustrating the varying responses of the region to Alexander's conquests.
events.name: Cities of Western Asia Minor Open to Alexander

events.enhanced_description: Responding to a plea from the colony of Taras, Alexander of Epirus crossed into Italy to assist against the Lucanians and Bruttii. His military campaigns were marked by victories over the Samnite tribes, showcasing his military prowess.
events.name: Alexander of Epirus Aids Taras

events.enhanced_description: The rulers of the states of Wei and Qi formalized their recognition of each other as kings, marking a significant step in the political landscape of the Warring States period in ancient China. This agreement underscored the declining power of the Zhou dynasty and the rise of regional powers.
events.name: Recognition of Kings by Wei and Qi

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Emperor Constantine I consecrated the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, a significant event in the history of Christianity. This church became a major pilgrimage site and symbolized the growing influence of Christianity within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Constantine I consecrates the Church of the Holy Sepulchre

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Flavius Dalmatius was elevated to the rank of Caesar, gaining control over the regions of Thracia, Achaia, and Macedonia. This promotion underscored the importance of regional governance in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Flavius Dalmatius raised to Caesar

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Hannibalianus, the nephew of Emperor Constantine I, was appointed as Rex Regum, or 'King of Kings of the Pontic people.' This title reflected the political complexities and the hierarchical structure of power in the region.
events.name: Hannibalianus made Rex Regum

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Athanasius was banished to Trier on charges of obstructing the corn fleet from sailing to Constantinople. This event highlighted the ongoing religious and political tensions within the early Christian church.
events.name: Athanasius banished to Trier

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Samudragupta ascended to the throne as the king of the Gupta Empire, succeeding his father Chandragupta I. His reign marked a significant period of expansion and cultural development in ancient India.
events.name: Samudragupta succeeds Chandragupta I as king of the Gupta Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Tuoba Hena successfully ousted Tuoba Yihuai as the chieftain of the Tuoba Clan, marking a significant shift in leadership within the clan. This event was part of the broader power struggles during the period of the Sixteen Kingdoms in China.
events.name: Tuoba Hena ousts Tuoba Yihuai

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Emperor Shi Hu relocated the capital of the Later Zhao state to Yecheng, a strategic move that reflected the shifting political landscape during the Period of the Sixteen Kingdoms. This decision aimed to consolidate power and improve governance.
events.name: Emperor Shi Hu moves capital to Yecheng

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, the First Synod of Tyre was convened by Emperor Constantine I, gathering bishops to address the controversies surrounding Patriarch Athanasius of Alexandria. This synod was pivotal in the ongoing theological disputes of the early Christian church.
events.name: First Synod of Tyre convened by Constantine I

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Emperor Constantine I reinstated Arius, an Alexandrian priest previously declared a heretic at the First Council of Nicaea in 325. This decision occurred during a synod in Jerusalem and reflected the complex theological debates of the time.
events.name: Constantine I reinstates Arius

events.enhanced_description: In 335 AD, Pope Sylvester I passed away in Rome after a 21-year reign, making him one of the longest-serving popes of the early church. He was succeeded by Pope Mark, marking a transition in the leadership of the Catholic Church.
events.name: Pope Sylvester I dies

events.enhanced_description: After being acclaimed as 'invincible' by the Pythian priestess at Delphi, Alexander advanced into Thrace to secure the Danube as the northern boundary of his kingdom. His military campaigns included defeating the Triballi and dispersing the Getae, solidifying Macedonian control over the region.
events.name: Alexander's Campaign into Thrace

events.enhanced_description: A rumor of Alexander's death at the hands of the Illyrians incited the Thebans and Athenians to revolt against Macedonian rule. Alexander swiftly crushed the rebellion, razing Thebes and executing thousands, which served as a stark warning to other Greek city-states.
events.name: Theban and Athenian Revolt

events.enhanced_description: Following his conquest of Thebes, Alexander demanded the surrender of mercenary commanders Chares and Charidemus. While Chares escaped to the Troad, Charidemus was banished and fled to Persia, illustrating the tumultuous aftermath of Alexander's military campaigns.
events.name: Demand for Surrender of Mercenary Commanders

events.enhanced_description: Alexander the Great showed remarkable leniency towards Athens despite its rebellion against Macedonian rule, largely due to his admiration for the Athenian orator Demades. An embassy led by Phocion successfully persuaded Alexander to retract his demand for the exile of anti-Macedonian leaders, allowing Athens to maintain some degree of autonomy.
events.name: Alexander's Leniency Towards Athens

events.enhanced_description: Aristotle returned to Athens from Macedon and established the Lyceum, a peripatetic school that became a center for philosophical and scientific inquiry. This institution featured a museum, zoological gardens, and an extensive library, significantly contributing to the intellectual landscape of the time.
events.name: Aristotle Opens the Lyceum

events.enhanced_description: Marcus Valerius Corvus was elected consul of the Roman Republic for the fourth time, showcasing his significant political influence and popularity in Roman politics during this period. His repeated elections reflect the trust placed in him by the Roman populace.
events.name: Marcus Valerius Corvus Elected Consul

events.enhanced_description: The Romans captured Cales, a city in Campania, and established a colony there, marking an important step in their expansion and consolidation of power in the region. This event reflects the strategic importance of Cales in Roman territorial ambitions.
events.name: Establishment of Roman Colony at Cales

events.enhanced_description: The renowned sculptor Praxiteles concluded his active career in Athens, leaving behind a legacy that would influence generations of artists. His works, characterized by their grace and beauty, were pivotal in the development of classical sculpture.
events.name: Praxiteles Ends His Career

events.enhanced_description: In 336 AD, the military successes of Emperor Constantine I led to the reconquest of most of Dacia by the Roman Empire. This victory was a significant achievement in consolidating Roman power in the region.
events.name: Military successes of Constantine I in Dacia

events.enhanced_description: In 336 AD, the first recorded customs tariff was implemented in Palmyra, reflecting the city's importance as a trade hub in the ancient world. This tariff system marked a significant development in economic regulation and trade practices.
events.name: First recorded customs tariff in Palmyra

events.enhanced_description: In 336 AD, Pope Mark succeeded Pope Sylvester I as the 34th pope of the Catholic Church. His election marked a continuation of the leadership during a pivotal time for early Christianity.
events.name: Pope Mark succeeds Pope Sylvester I

events.enhanced_description: Pope Mark initiates the construction of the Basilica di San Marco in Venice, dedicated to St. Mark, the patron saint of the city. This iconic structure would later become a symbol of Venetian wealth and power, showcasing Byzantine architecture and art.
events.name: Construction of the Basilica of San Marco

events.enhanced_description: Arius, a prominent Alexandrian priest known for his controversial theological views, collapses in the streets of Constantinople. His teachings would later spark significant theological debates and contribute to the development of early Christian doctrine.
events.name: Arius collapses in Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: Pope Mark dies in Rome after a brief reign of 11 months, leaving the papacy vacant for a short period. His death marks a significant moment in the early history of the papacy, as the church navigates leadership transitions.
events.name: Death of Pope Mark

events.enhanced_description: The first recorded celebration of Christmas takes place in Rome, marking a pivotal moment in the Christian liturgical calendar. This event reflects the growing importance of Christmas as a major Christian holiday.
events.name: First recorded celebration of Christmas

events.enhanced_description: Arses, the young king of Persia, attempted to poison his powerful advisor Bagoas, who had significant control over the throne. However, the plot backfired, resulting in the deaths of Arses and his children, further consolidating Bagoas' power.
events.name: Arses' Attempt to Poison Bagoas

events.enhanced_description: After eliminating Arses, Bagoas sought to install Darius III, a distant relative of the royal family, as king of Persia. Darius' initial attempts to assert independence led to a dramatic confrontation where he ultimately forced Bagoas to drink poison, sealing his own fate.
events.name: Bagoas Installs Darius III

events.enhanced_description: Following the marriage of Philip II of Macedon to Eurydice, Alexander and his mother Olympias fled to Epirus, fearing for their safety. Their eventual reconciliation with Philip was pivotal in securing Alexander's position as heir to the Macedonian throne.
events.name: Alexander and Olympias Flee to Epirus

events.enhanced_description: Macedonian troops, led by Parmenion, faced a setback when they were repelled by Persian forces commanded by the Greek mercenary Memnon of Rhodes in Asia Minor. This encounter highlighted the challenges Alexander would face in his campaigns against Persia.
events.name: Macedonian Troops Driven Back

events.enhanced_description: During the wedding celebration of his daughter Cleopatra to Alexander I of Epirus, Philip II of Macedon was assassinated by his bodyguard Pausanias of Orestis, who harbored a personal grievance. This assassination dramatically altered the course of Macedonian history, paving the way for Alexander's rise.
events.name: Assassination of Philip II of Macedon

events.enhanced_description: After the assassination of Philip II, his son Alexander III ascended to the throne of Macedon. Alexander's immediate consolidation of power included executing potential rivals and leading a unified Greek army against Persia, setting the stage for his future conquests.
events.name: Alexander III Succeeds Philip II

events.enhanced_description: In a swift move to eliminate threats to his rule, Alexander III executed Amyntas IV, a cousin and potential rival. This act demonstrated Alexander's determination to secure his position as the undisputed ruler of Macedon.
events.name: Execution of Amyntas IV

events.enhanced_description: Alexander swiftly quelled a rebellion in Macedonia and defeated the Illyrians, showcasing his military prowess. Following these victories, he received the submission of Thebes and was elected as commander of the Greek forces against Persia, solidifying his leadership.
events.name: Alexander Crushes Rebellion in Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: Athens implemented a system of conscription, requiring young men to fulfill military and civic duties. This policy reflects the city's ongoing commitment to its defense and civic responsibilities during a period of political turbulence.
events.name: Conscription Introduced in Athens

events.enhanced_description: Aeschines brought a legal suit against Ctesiphon for unlawfully proposing a crown for Demosthenes, a prominent Athenian leader. This case highlighted the intense political rivalries and the significance of public recognition in Athenian democracy.
events.name: Aeschines vs. Ctesiphon

events.enhanced_description: Constantine the Great, the first Christian Roman emperor, dies in Achyron near Nicomedia at the age of 65 after being baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia. His reign significantly shaped the future of Christianity and the Roman Empire.
events.name: Death of Constantine the Great

events.enhanced_description: In September, a purge occurs within the Roman Empire targeting descendants of Constantius Chlorus and officials, reflecting the political tensions following the death of Constantine I. This event underscores the instability of imperial succession.
events.name: Purge against the sons of Constantine I

events.enhanced_description: Constantine II, Constantius II, and Constans ascend as co-emperors following the death of their father, Constantine I. This division of the Roman Empire among the three brothers sets the stage for future conflicts and power struggles.
events.name: Succession of Constantine II, Constantius II, and Constans

events.enhanced_description: King Shapur II of Persia initiates a military campaign against the Roman Empire, sending troops across the Tigris River to reclaim territories in Armenia and Mesopotamia. This conflict marks the beginning of a prolonged period of hostilities between the two empires.
events.name: Shapur II begins war against the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: Shapur II besieges the Roman fortress of Nisibis but is repulsed by Roman forces led by Lucilianus. This event highlights the ongoing military tensions between the Persian Empire and Rome.
events.name: Siege of Nisibis by Shapur II

events.enhanced_description: Murong Huang claims the title of Prince of Yan, effectively establishing the kingdom of Former Yan. This event marks a significant development in the history of the Northern Dynasties in China.
events.name: Murong Huang claims the title of Prince of Yan

events.enhanced_description: The papal vacancy following the death of Pope Mark ends with the election of Pope Julius I, marking the beginning of his leadership as the 35th pope. His papacy would be noted for its efforts to solidify the church's authority.

image.caption: Mosaic depicting Saints Peter, Cornelius, Julius I, and Calepodius in the apse of Santa Maria in Trastevere.
image.credit: Hugo DK — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image depicts a 12th-century mosaic, not the 337 papal election; the supplied image date is the photograph’s date.

events.name: Papal vacancy ends with election of Pope Julius I

events.enhanced_description: Constantius II announces the restoration of Athanasius as Patriarch of Alexandria, reversing his previous deposition. This event is significant in the ongoing theological disputes within early Christianity.
events.name: Restoration of Athanasius as Patriarch of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: Paul I is appointed as the Patriarch of Constantinople, a position of significant influence in the early Christian church. His leadership would play a crucial role in the theological and political dynamics of the time.
events.name: Paul I becomes Patriarch of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: Christianity is officially declared the state religion in Caucasian Iberia, marking a significant milestone in the spread of Christianity in the region that is now modern-day Georgia. This event reflects the growing influence of Christianity in the early medieval period.
events.name: Christianity declared official religion in Caucasian Iberia

events.enhanced_description: At a Pan-Hellenic Conference in Corinth, Philip II of Macedon announced the formation of the League of Corinth, aimed at liberating the Greek cities of Asia Minor from Persian control. This coalition, which included almost all Greek city-states except Sparta, recognized Philip as its president, consolidating his power and influence over Greece.
events.name: Formation of the League of Corinth

events.enhanced_description: Philip II of Macedon put aside his wife Olympias to marry Cleopatra, a young woman who was later renamed Eurydice. This political move effectively disowned his son Alexander, creating a significant rift in the royal family and leading to the exile of several of Alexander's companions.
events.name: Philip II's Marriage to Cleopatra

events.enhanced_description: In a significant development for the Roman Republic, a plebeian was elected as praetor for the first time, marking a crucial step towards greater political representation for the lower classes in Roman governance. This event reflected the ongoing struggle between the patricians and plebeians for political power.
events.name: First Plebeian Praetor in Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Romans, allied with the Goths, mobilize to the northern frontiers of the Roman Empire to safeguard the Danube River against potential invasions. This alliance reflects the complex relationships between the Romans and various barbarian tribes.
events.name: Romans and Goths protect the Danube frontier

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Constantius II takes military action against the Persians in Armenia, reflecting the ongoing conflict between the Roman Empire and the Sassanian Empire. This intervention is part of a broader struggle for control over the region.
events.name: Constantius II intervenes against the Persians

events.enhanced_description: Shapur II, the king of the Persian Empire, initiates a widespread persecution of Christians, enforcing conversions to Zoroastrianism. This campaign is part of his strategy to maintain control over his realm while engaging in military conflicts with Rome.
events.name: Shapur II begins persecution of Christians

events.enhanced_description: Tuoba Yihuai, the ruler of the Tuoba Dai clan, passes away and is succeeded by his brother Tuoba Shiyiqian. This transition marks a significant moment in the history of the Northern Wei dynasty in China.
events.name: Death of Tuoba Yihuai

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Church of Santa Costanza in Rome begins, representing an important development in early Christian architecture. This church would later become known for its unique circular design and mosaics.
events.name: Construction of the Church of Santa Costanza

events.enhanced_description: Eusebius of Nicomedia is appointed as the Patriarch of Constantinople following the banishment of Paul I. His leadership is significant in the context of the Arian controversy and the evolving Christian doctrine.
events.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia becomes Patriarch of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: The Roman Empire intensifies its persecution of non-Christians, targeting pagans and other religious groups. This reflects the growing dominance of Christianity and the empire's efforts to unify religious practices.
events.name: Persecution of non-Christians in the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Chaeronea, Philip II of Macedon achieved a decisive victory over the Athenian and Theban forces, with his son Alexander commanding the left wing. This battle cemented Macedonian supremacy in Greece and marked a significant turning point in the power dynamics of the region.
events.name: Battle of Chaeronea

events.enhanced_description: The Persian general Bagoas fell out of favor with King Artaxerxes III, leading him to orchestrate the king's assassination and place the young Arses on the throne. This act of political maneuvering allowed Bagoas to control the Persian Empire from behind the scenes, making Arses a puppet king.
events.name: Bagoas' Rise to Power

events.enhanced_description: After a decisive victory against the Locrians, Philip II of Macedon advanced into Phocis, seizing the city of Elateia and restoring its fortifications. This maneuver was part of Philip's broader strategy to consolidate power in central Greece and assert Macedonian dominance.
events.name: Philip II's Victory Over the Locrians

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move, Athens formed an alliance with several city-states including Thebes, under the leadership of Demosthenes. This alliance aimed to counter Macedonian influence and secure Athenian interests in the region, showcasing the intricate political landscape of ancient Greece.
events.name: Athenian Alliance with Thebes

events.enhanced_description: Philip II advanced into the Peloponnesus, defeating Thessaly and subduing Sparta, which led to the establishment of Macedonian hegemony over central Greece. This campaign was crucial in Philip's efforts to unify the Greek states under Macedonian leadership.
events.name: Philip II's Campaign in Peloponnesus

events.enhanced_description: Philip II invaded Laconia, driving out the Spartans but stopping short of capturing the city of Sparta itself. This invasion was part of his broader strategy to weaken Spartan power and assert Macedonian dominance in the region.
events.name: Philip II's Invasion of Laconia

events.enhanced_description: Lycurgus, an influential Athenian statesman and orator, was appointed to oversee the state's finances, during which he successfully doubled the annual public revenues. His reforms significantly strengthened Athens' economic position during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Lycurgus' Financial Reforms in Athens

events.enhanced_description: King Archidamus III of Sparta was killed in battle while leading a mercenary army to assist Tarentum against the Lucanians. His death marked a significant loss for Sparta, which had been struggling to maintain its influence in southern Italy.
events.name: Death of Archidamus III of Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Archidamus III, his son Agis III ascended to the throne as the Eurypontid King of Sparta. This transition in leadership came at a critical time for Sparta as it faced numerous challenges both internally and externally.
events.name: Agis III Succeeds Archidamus III

events.enhanced_description: Carthage made renewed attempts to conquer Sicily, dispatching mercenaries to escalate the conflict against Timoleon and the Sicilian tyrants. However, these efforts culminated in the defeat of Hicetas, the tyrant of Leontini, and a subsequent treaty that limited Carthaginian control to the western part of the island.
events.name: Carthaginian Efforts in Sicily

events.enhanced_description: With peace finally established with Carthage, Timoleon of Syracuse was able to depose two remaining tyrants in Sicily, leading to a more stable political environment. Following these successes, he chose to retire from public life, leaving a legacy of reform and stability.
events.name: Timoleon's Retirement After Achieving Peace

events.enhanced_description: The Latin War concluded with the dissolution of the Latin League, forcing individual Latin cities to accept terms set by Rome. This event marked a significant expansion of Roman influence and the integration of many cities into the Roman state, fostering a new era of political relationships.
events.name: End of the Latin War

events.enhanced_description: The fall of Antium marked a significant turning point in Roman expansion as the Volsci, a fierce tribe, finally surrendered their resistance and accepted an alliance with Rome. This event solidified Roman control over the region and paved the way for further territorial conquests.
events.name: Fall of Antium to the Romans

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Constantius II hastens to the eastern territories of the Roman Empire in response to renewed attacks by Shapur II of Persia. This marks the beginning of a prolonged conflict characterized by border skirmishes and military engagements.
events.name: Constantius II's military response to Persia

events.enhanced_description: Pope Julius I provides refuge in Rome to Athanasius, the Alexandrian patriarch, who had been deposed during the First Synod of Tyre. This act of support highlights the political and theological struggles within early Christianity.
events.name: Pope Julius I gives refuge to Athanasius

events.enhanced_description: Eusebius of Nicomedia is appointed as bishop of Constantinople, succeeding Paul I. His leadership is pivotal during a time of significant theological conflict within the church.
events.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia becomes bishop of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: Philip II of Macedon launched a military campaign against the Scythians, using the pretext of their refusal to allow him to dedicate a statue of Heracles. The battle resulted in the death of the Scythian king Ateas and a decisive victory for Philip, further establishing his dominance in the region.
events.name: Philip II of Macedon's Attack on the Scythians

events.enhanced_description: During a session of the Amphictyonic Council, Philip II accused the citizens of Amfissa of violating sacred grounds, leading to military actions against them. His decisive leadership resulted in a successful campaign against the Locrians, showcasing his political and military acumen.
events.name: Philip II Accuses Amfissa

events.enhanced_description: Xenocrates was elected as the head of the Academy in Athens, succeeding Speusippus. His leadership marked a significant period in the development of Platonic philosophy and education, influencing future generations of philosophers.
events.name: Xenocrates Elected Head of the Academy

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Trifanum, the Roman consul Titus Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus achieved a significant victory over the Latins, reinforcing Roman dominance in the region. This battle was part of the larger conflict between Rome and its neighboring tribes.
events.name: Battle of Trifanum

events.enhanced_description: Constantinople, under the rule of Emperor Constantius II, surpasses Rome to become the largest city in the world. This shift signifies the growing importance of Constantinople as a political and cultural center in the Roman Empire.

image.caption: Topographical map of Constantinople during the Byzantine period.

events.name: Constantinople becomes the largest city in the world

events.enhanced_description: In 340 AD, Constantine II, the emperor of the western Roman Empire, crossed the Alps to confront his brother Constans I, who ruled the central part of the Empire. The confrontation culminated in a battle at Aquileia, where Constantine was ambushed and killed, leading to Constans I becoming the sole ruler of the western territories.
events.name: Constantine II attacks Constans I

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his brother Constantine II in 340 AD, Constans I emerged as the sole ruler of the western Roman Empire, while his other brother, Constantius II, continued to govern the eastern portion. This division of power marked a significant moment in the history of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Constans becomes sole ruler

events.enhanced_description: In 340 AD, Acacius succeeded Eusebius as the bishop of Caesarea, a significant ecclesiastical position in the early Christian church. This transition marked a continuity of leadership in a pivotal region for the spread of Christianity.
events.name: Acacius succeeds Eusebius

events.enhanced_description: Wulfila, a Christian missionary, dedicated seven years to evangelizing among the Goths during the early 4th century. His efforts were instrumental in introducing Christianity to the Gothic tribes, significantly influencing their cultural and religious landscape.
events.name: Wulfila evangelizes among the Goths

events.enhanced_description: Rhodes fell to the advancing Persian forces, marking a significant event in the power dynamics of the region. This event showcased the ongoing conflicts between the Greek city-states and the Persian Empire.
events.name: Fall of Rhodes to Persian Forces

events.enhanced_description: Pixodarus, the youngest son of Hecatomnus, seized control of the satrapy of Caria by expelling his sister Ada. This power shift was significant in the political landscape of the region during the time.
events.name: Pixodarus Gains Control of Caria

events.enhanced_description: In response to Philip II of Macedon's invasion of Perinthus and Byzantium, King Artaxerxes III of Persia provided military support to these cities. This intervention highlighted the ongoing tensions between Macedonian and Persian interests in the region.
events.name: Artaxerxes III Supports Perinthus and Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: Philip II of Macedon's siege of Byzantium ended in failure, forcing him to divert his attention to threats from the Scythians. During this time, his son Alexander served as regent, marking an important moment in the succession of power in Macedon.
events.name: Philip II's Failed Siege of Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: Following Philip II's unsuccessful siege of Byzantium, the Athenian assembly publicly thanked Demosthenes for his leadership and oratory. This event underscored the importance of rhetoric in Athenian politics and the growing tensions with Macedon.
events.name: Demosthenes Receives Public Thanks

events.enhanced_description: The discovery of the Derveni papyrus in a nobleman's grave in the necropolis of Lete represents a significant archaeological find, providing insights into ancient Greek philosophy and religious practices.
events.name: Derveni Papyrus Found

events.enhanced_description: Hicetas, the tyrant of Leontini, successfully persuaded Carthage to dispatch a large army to Sicily, landing at Lilybaeum. This led to the Battle of the Crimissus, where Timoleon of Syracuse achieved a notable victory against the Carthaginian forces.
events.name: Hicetas Persuades Carthage to Send Army to Sicily

events.enhanced_description: An embassy from the Latin peoples approached the Roman Senate, proposing the formation of a single republic. However, Rome's refusal to grant political equality led to the outbreak of the Latin War, significantly altering the power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Latin Peoples Send Embassy to Roman Senate

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Vesuvius, the Roman-Samnite forces, led by consuls Publius Decius Mus and Titus Manlius Torquatus, achieved a decisive victory against the Latins and Campanians. This battle was pivotal in the ongoing conflicts in the region, solidifying Roman military strength.
events.name: Battle of Vesuvius

events.enhanced_description: The Romans successfully persuaded the Campanians to break away from their alliance with the Latins, granting citizenship to several cities including Capua and Cumae. This expansion of Roman citizenship marked a significant step in the consolidation of power in the region.
events.name: Romans Induce Campanians to Separate from Latins

events.enhanced_description: In 341 AD, Emperor Constans I issued a decree banning pagan sacrifices and magic rituals, imposing severe penalties including death for violations. This edict reflected the growing influence of Christianity and the efforts to suppress pagan practices within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Constans I bans pagan sacrifices

events.enhanced_description: In 341 AD, Constans I initiated a military campaign against the Franks, aiming to secure the borders of the western Roman Empire. This campaign was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Roman Empire and various barbarian tribes.
events.name: Constans I campaigns against the Franks

events.enhanced_description: During his reign, Samudragupta of the Gupta Empire expanded his kingdom and influence significantly, a process documented on a pillar found at Allahabad. His military conquests and diplomatic strategies solidified the Gupta Empire's power in the Indian subcontinent.

image.caption: Detail of the Allahabad stone pillar inscription of Samudragupta.

events.name: Samudragupta extends his kingdom

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Encaenia was convened in Antioch in 341 AD, addressing various theological disputes within early Christianity. This council was part of the broader efforts to establish orthodoxy and resolve conflicts among different Christian factions.
events.name: Council of Encaenia held in Antioch

events.enhanced_description: In 341 AD, Paul I was restored to his position as Patriarch of Constantinople, a significant ecclesiastical role in the early Christian church. His reinstatement was part of the ongoing power struggles within the church hierarchy during this period.
events.name: Paul I restored as Patriarch of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 341 AD, thousands of Christians were executed in Seleucia, located in Mesopotamia, as part of the broader persecution of Christians during this period. This event highlighted the tensions between the Christian community and the prevailing pagan practices.
events.name: Christian executions at Seleucia

events.enhanced_description: In 341 AD, Frumentius, a Syrian apostle, introduced Coptic Christianity to Ethiopia, significantly influencing the region's religious landscape. His efforts led to the conversion of King Ezana, who became the first Christian monarch of the Aksumite Empire.
events.name: Coptic Christianity introduced into Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: Philip II of Macedon successfully completes the annexation of Thrace, a region that poses a significant threat to Athenian security. This move heightens tensions between Macedonia and Athens, as the latter perceives Philip's expansionist policies as a direct challenge to their influence in the region.
events.name: Philip II of Macedon completes his annexation of Thrace

events.enhanced_description: In his Third Philippic, Demosthenes passionately calls for action against Philip II of Macedon, rallying the Athenian populace to resist Macedonian aggression. This speech marks a pivotal moment in Athenian politics, as Demosthenes consolidates power and undermines the pro-Macedonian faction led by Aeschines.
events.name: Demosthenes delivers his Third Philippic

events.enhanced_description: Demosthenes successfully orchestrates a coalition against Philip II, uniting former adversaries like Byzantium and Thebes. This alliance signifies a critical shift in Athenian foreign policy, as the city-state officially denounces the Peace of Philocrates, effectively declaring war on Macedonia.
events.name: Demosthenes organizes a grand alliance against Philip II

events.enhanced_description: The First Samnite War concludes with Rome emerging victorious, leading to a peace agreement with the Samnites. This conflict marks an important step in Rome's expansion into southern Italy, setting the stage for future confrontations in the region.
events.name: The First Samnite War ends

events.enhanced_description: In 342 AD, Constans I led a military campaign in Britain against the Picts, marking a significant military engagement in the Roman province of Britannia. This campaign was part of the broader Roman efforts to maintain control over the region.
events.name: Constans I campaigns in Britain

events.enhanced_description: In 342 AD, Constans I achieved a significant victory against the Franks, reinforcing Roman authority in the region. This campaign was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Roman Empire and various barbarian tribes.
events.name: Constans campaigns victoriously against the Franks

events.enhanced_description: In 342 AD, the Roman Senate enacted legislation abolishing gay marriage, reflecting the prevailing social and cultural attitudes of the time. This decision was part of the broader legal framework governing personal relationships in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Senate abolishes gay marriage

events.enhanced_description: In 342 AD, a large earthquake struck Cyprus, causing significant damage and impacting the local population. Natural disasters during this period often had profound effects on communities and their economies.
events.name: Large earthquake strikes Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: In 342 AD, Goguryeo faced an invasion by Murong Huang of the Xianbei, marking a significant military conflict in the region. This invasion was part of the broader struggles for power among various tribes and kingdoms in East Asia.
events.name: Goguryeo invaded by Murong Huang

events.enhanced_description: In 342 AD, Jin Kangdi succeeded his brother Jin Chengdi as emperor of the Jin Dynasty in China. This transition marked a continuation of the Jin Dynasty's rule during a period of significant political and social change.
events.name: Jin Kangdi succeeds Jin Chengdi

events.enhanced_description: In 342 AD, Paul I was deposed as Patriarch of Constantinople and replaced by Macedonius I, reflecting the ongoing power struggles within the early Christian church. This event was indicative of the political and theological tensions of the time.
events.name: Paul I deposed and replaced by Macedonius I

events.enhanced_description: The original Hagia Sophia was dedicated in Constantinople in 342 AD, serving as a central place of worship and a symbol of the Byzantine Empire's architectural and cultural achievements. This structure would later become one of the most significant religious buildings in history.
events.name: Original Hagia Sophia dedicated

events.enhanced_description: Philip II invites the renowned philosopher Aristotle to Pella to educate his son, Alexander. This mentorship profoundly influences Alexander's future as a military leader and ruler, shaping his approach to governance and strategy.
events.name: Aristotle is invited to tutor Alexander

events.enhanced_description: Philip II initiates military campaigns in Thrace, aiming to annex the region into Macedonia. The conflict escalates when Athenian general Diopeithes conducts raids in the area, provoking Philip's ire and leading to heightened tensions between Athens and Macedonia.
events.name: Philip begins campaigns in Thrace

events.enhanced_description: General Timoleon successfully consolidates power in Sicily, dismantling tyrannies and preparing the island for potential Carthaginian threats. His leadership marks a significant transformation in Sicilian governance and stability during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Timoleon spreads his rule over Sicily

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Mount Gaurus sees Roman forces, led by Marcus Valerius Corvus, achieve a decisive victory against the Samnites. This engagement is a key moment in the First Samnite War, showcasing Roman military prowess and strategy.
events.name: Battle of Mount Gaurus

events.enhanced_description: During the Warring States period, the state of Qi, under the command of General Sun Bin, defeats Wei at the Battle of Maling. This battle is notable for its innovative military strategies and the effective use of the handheld crossbow, marking a significant advancement in Chinese warfare.
events.name: Battle of Maling

events.enhanced_description: In 343 AD, Constans I was in Britain, possibly leading a military campaign against the Picts and Scots. This marked one of the last visits by a legitimate Roman emperor to the province, highlighting the challenges faced by the Empire in maintaining control over its territories.
events.name: Constans I in Britain against Picts and Scots

events.enhanced_description: In 343 AD, the Eastern Roman Emperor Constantius II conducted a military campaign in Adiabene, a vassal kingdom of Armenia under the influence of the Persian Empire. This campaign was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Roman Empire and Persia.
events.name: Constantius II campaigns in Adiabene

events.enhanced_description: In 343 AD, Pope Julius I convened the Council of Serdica in an effort to unite Western bishops against Arianism. Although the council acknowledged the pope's authority, it was attended only by Western and Egyptian bishops, leaving Arianism still influential.
events.name: Pope Julius I convokes the Council of Serdica

events.enhanced_description: Artaxerxes III leads a Persian invasion into Egypt, seeking control over its rich resources. The siege of Pelusium marks a critical moment in the campaign, as Pharaoh Nectanebo II is forced to retreat, leading to the eventual downfall of the 30th Dynasty.
events.name: Artaxerxes III invades Egypt

events.enhanced_description: Following the flight of Nectanebo II, Egypt succumbs to Persian rule, becoming a satrapy under Artaxerxes III. This transition marks the end of native Egyptian governance and the beginning of a period of foreign domination and exploitation.
events.name: Egypt becomes a satrapy of Persia

events.enhanced_description: Demosthenes takes a bold step by indicting Aeschines for treason, seeking to eliminate his political rival. However, Aeschines counters with damaging revelations about Demosthenes' allies, resulting in a narrow acquittal that underscores the intense political rivalries in Athens.
events.name: Demosthenes indicts Aeschines for treason

events.enhanced_description: King Philip II of Macedon engages in a series of battles against Cersobleptes, King of Thrace, ultimately defeating him and reducing him to a tributary status. This victory further solidifies Philip's control over the region and enhances Macedonian power.
events.name: Philip II defeats Cersobleptes, King of Thrace

events.enhanced_description: Phalaikos attempts to capture Kydonia on the island of Crete but ultimately fails in his siege. This event reflects the ongoing conflicts in the region during a time of shifting power dynamics among Greek city-states.
events.name: Phalaikos lays siege to Kydonia

events.enhanced_description: The Lucanians and Bruttians launch attacks on the Greek colonies of Magna Graecia, including Tarentum, prompting King Archidamus III of Sparta to respond by sending mercenaries to assist the beleaguered colonies. This intervention highlights the ongoing struggles between native tribes and Greek settlements in southern Italy.
events.name: Lucanians and Bruttians press upon Tarentum

events.enhanced_description: After his surrender to the Corinthian general Timoleon, Dionysius II, the former tyrant of Syracuse, is allowed to retire to Corinth in exile. Timoleon implements a new constitution in Syracuse aimed at preventing tyranny, while also inviting settlers from Greece to Sicily.
events.name: Dionysius II Exiled by Timoleon

events.enhanced_description: The First Samnite War begins as Rome engages in conflict with the confederated Samnites over territorial disputes in the Middle Liris Valley. This marks the beginning of a series of wars that would shape the future of Roman expansion in Italy.
events.name: First Samnite War Begins

events.enhanced_description: In 344 AD, Eastern Roman Emperor Constantius II launched a military campaign in eastern Mesopotamia against the Sassanid Persians. This conflict was part of the ongoing power struggle between the Roman Empire and Persia.
events.name: Constantius II campaigns in eastern Mesopotamia

events.enhanced_description: In 344 AD, the Battle of Singara took place, where the Roman army under Constantius II achieved a narrow victory against the forces of King Shapur II of Persia. This battle was significant in maintaining Roman control over the region and repelling the Persian siege.
events.name: Battle of Singara

events.enhanced_description: In 344 AD, King Shapur II of Persia besieged the Roman fortress of Nisibis for the second time but was repulsed by Roman forces under General Lucilianus. This event underscored the ongoing military tensions between the Roman Empire and the Sassanid Persians.
events.name: Shapur II besieges Nisibis

events.enhanced_description: At just one year old, Jin Mudi ascended to the throne of the Jin Dynasty following the death of his father, Jin Kangdi. His mother, Empress Dowager Chu, took on the role of regent, effectively ruling the empire during his infancy.
events.name: Jin Mudi succeeds his father Jin Kangdi as emperor of China

events.enhanced_description: Gye ascended to the throne of Baekje, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, marking a significant moment in the kingdom's history. His reign would contribute to the cultural and political development of Baekje during this period.

locations.name: Buyeo, South Chungcheong Province, South Korea

events.name: Gye becomes king of the Korean kingdom of Baekje

events.enhanced_description: The creation of a detail from 'Admonitions of the Imperial Instructress to Court Ladies,' attributed to the renowned painter Gu Kaizhi, began during the Six Dynasties period. This artwork reflects the cultural values and aesthetics of the time and is now housed in the British Museum.
events.name: Creation of Admonitions of the Imperial Instructress to Court Ladies begins

events.enhanced_description: According to a 12th-century legend, Bishop Eustorgius I of Milan brought the relics of the Three Magi from Constantinople to Milan, enhancing the city's religious significance and attracting pilgrims.
events.name: Bishop Eustorgius I brings relics of the Three Magi to Milan

events.enhanced_description: Idrieus, the king of Caria, dies and bequeaths his satrapy to his sister Ada, who was also his wife. This succession reflects the dynastic practices of the time and the complex political landscape of the Persian Empire.
events.name: Idrieus of Caria Dies

events.enhanced_description: Philip II of Macedon lays siege to Perinthus, a city that has resisted his rule and leaned towards the Athenians. The siege is supported by allies of Perinthus, including Byzantium and the Achaemenid Empire, highlighting the geopolitical tensions of the era.
events.name: Philip II of Macedon Besieges Perinthus

events.enhanced_description: Philip II of Macedon strategically divides his army, sending part to continue the siege of Perinthus while taking the remainder to besiege Byzantium. This maneuver demonstrates his military acumen and ambition to consolidate power in the region.
events.name: Philip Divides His Army

events.enhanced_description: The Athenian statesman Demosthenes embarks on a mission to the Peloponnesus to persuade cities to break away from Macedonian influence. His efforts largely fail, leading to a backlash from local leaders who view Philip II as a protector of their autonomy.
events.name: Demosthenes' Mission to Peloponnesus

events.enhanced_description: The aristocracy of Syracuse seeks assistance from their mother city, Corinth, against the tyrant Dionysius II. Corinthian general Timoleon leads a liberation force that successfully occupies Syracuse after defeating Dionysius and Hicetas' armies.
events.name: Syracuse Appeals to Corinth

events.enhanced_description: Following Timoleon's successful invasion of Syracuse, Dionysius II is exiled once more, marking the end of his tyrannical rule. This event signifies a shift in power dynamics in Sicily and the influence of Corinthian leadership.
events.name: Dionysius II Exiled Again

events.enhanced_description: The philosopher and scientist Aristotle travels from Assus to Lesbos to conduct studies in natural history, with a particular focus on marine biology. This journey reflects his commitment to empirical observation and the study of the natural world.
events.name: Aristotle Studies Natural History

events.enhanced_description: Merchant Knai Thomman, along with 400 followers, arrived at the Malabar Coast in Kerala, India, where they played a crucial role in assisting the local Christian church, marking an important moment in the region's religious history.
events.name: Merchant Knai Thomman visits the Malabar Coast

events.enhanced_description: Mayurasharma established the Kadamba Dynasty in the region of present-day Karnataka, India. This dynasty would become significant in the history of South India, known for its contributions to culture and governance.
events.name: The Kadamba Dynasty is founded by Mayurasharma

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Constans I commissioned the construction of the Basilica di Santa Tecla in Milan, reflecting the growing importance of Christianity in the Roman Empire during his reign.
events.name: Constans orders the construction of the Basilica di Santa Tecla

events.enhanced_description: With support from Thebes and Thessaly, Macedonia successfully takes over the votes of Phocis in the Amphictyonic League, a religious council. This maneuver strengthens Philip II's influence in Greek affairs, despite resistance from Athenian leaders.
events.name: Macedonia Takes Over Phocis' Votes

events.enhanced_description: The Nanda Empire is established in Magadha, marking a significant development in Indian history. This empire would later play a crucial role in the political landscape of ancient India.
events.name: Nanda Empire Founded

events.enhanced_description: Carthaginian forces ravage and blockade the town of Entella, demonstrating their military strength and influence in Sicily during this period. This event is part of the larger context of Carthaginian expansion and conflict with Greek cities.
events.name: Carthaginians Blockade Entella

events.enhanced_description: The Buyeo Kingdom, located in present-day South Korea, was absorbed by Goguryeo, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in the Korean peninsula during this period.

locations.name: Buyeo, South Chungcheong Province, South Korea

events.name: Buyeo Kingdom absorbed by Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: Geunchogo ascended to the throne of Baekje, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, and his reign is noted for military conquests and cultural advancements.

locations.name: Buyeo, South Chungcheong Province, South Korea

events.name: Geunchogo becomes king of the Korean kingdom of Baekje

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Constans I intervened to restore Athanasius as Patriarch of Alexandria, highlighting the political and religious tensions of the time, particularly concerning Arianism.

locations.name: Monastery of St. Macarius, Wadi El Natrun

events.name: Emperor Constans I secures the return of Athanasius

events.enhanced_description: Macedonius I, the Patriarch of Constantinople, was deposed by Paul I, reflecting the ongoing struggles for power within the church and the political implications of these religious leadership changes.
events.name: Macedonius I is deposed by Paul I

events.enhanced_description: Julius Firmicus Maternus authored 'De erroribus profanarum religionum,' a significant work critiquing pagan religions and reflecting the theological debates of the time.
events.name: Julius Firmicus Maternus writes De erroribus profanarum religionum

events.enhanced_description: Wulfila, a bishop and missionary, played a pivotal role in converting the Visigoths to Arianism, significantly influencing the religious landscape of the Gothic tribes.
events.name: The Visigoths are converted to Arianism by Wulfila

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Philocrates is signed between Macedonia and Athens, restoring the status quo but allowing Philip II to retain punitive rights against the Phocians for their role in the Sacred War. This treaty reflects the ongoing tensions and fragile peace in the region.
events.name: Peace of Philocrates Signed

events.enhanced_description: Athenian politicians Demosthenes and Timarchus prepare to prosecute Aeschines for treason due to his attempts to reconcile Athens with Macedonian expansion. This political strife highlights the deep divisions within Athenian society regarding foreign policy.
events.name: Demosthenes Prepares to Prosecute Aeschines

events.enhanced_description: Demosthenes, while critical of the terms of the Peace of Philocrates, argues that it must be honored to maintain stability. His stance reflects the complexities of Athenian politics and the challenges of navigating relations with Macedonia.
events.name: Demosthenes on the Peace of Philocrates

events.enhanced_description: After the Peace of Philocrates, which temporarily eased tensions between Athens and Macedon, Philip II of Macedon strategically moved his forces through the Thermopylae Pass to assert control over Phocis, a region that had resisted Macedonian influence. This maneuver demonstrated Philip's military prowess and the political fragility of Athens, which chose not to intervene in support of Phocis.
events.name: Following the conclusion of the Peace of Philocrates, Philip II's army moves through the pass of Thermopylae and subdues Phocis

events.enhanced_description: Dionysius II, the son of the earlier tyrant Dionysius I, was restored to power in Syracuse, marking a significant moment in the city's tumultuous political history. His return to power reflected the ongoing struggles for control in the region, influenced by both internal factions and external pressures.
events.name: Dionysius II is restored to power in Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: Li Shi, the ruler of Cheng Han, was unable to stop a military expedition led by Huan Wen of the Jin Dynasty. Following his defeat, he fled to Chengdu and surrendered, but was spared by Emperor Jin Mudi.
events.name: Li Shi fails to halt Jin expedition under Huan Wen

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Sardica convened in an effort to address the Arian controversy, establishing guidelines for bishops and attempting to unify the Christian church amidst growing theological divisions.
events.name: Council of Sardica attempts to resolve Arian controversy

events.enhanced_description: Following the departure of Eastern bishops from the Council of Sardica, the Council of Philippopolis was held, where they excommunicated Pope Julius, further entrenching the divisions within the church regarding Arianism.
events.name: Council of Philippopolis held after Eastern bishops leave Sardica

events.enhanced_description: Following the Macedonian victory at Olynthus, Athens, under the influence of Eubulus, sought to negotiate peace with Philip II of Macedon. This shift in policy indicated a strategic retreat from aggressive posturing, as the Athenian leadership recognized the futility of continued conflict with a resurgent Macedonian power.
events.name: In the wake of the Macedonian victory at Olynthus, Athens seeks to make peace with Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: An official Athenian delegation, including prominent figures such as Demosthenes and Aeschines, was dispatched to Pella to negotiate a peace treaty with Philip II of Macedon. The negotiations highlighted the political divisions within Athens, particularly as Aeschines advocated for a conciliatory approach towards Macedon, contrasting with Demosthenes' more hawkish stance.
events.name: An Athenian delegation is sent to Pella to negotiate a peace treaty with Philip II

events.enhanced_description: The introduction of coinage in Rome marked a significant advancement in the city’s economic development and facilitated trade and commerce. This innovation laid the groundwork for Rome's future as a dominant economic power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Coinage is introduced into Rome for the first time

events.enhanced_description: The death of Plato signified the end of an era for philosophical thought in ancient Greece, as his nephew Speusippus succeeded him as the head of the Academy. This transition marked a pivotal moment in the development of Western philosophy, influencing subsequent generations of thinkers.
events.name: Plato dies and his nephew Speusippus is named as head of the Academy

events.enhanced_description: In response to the growing anti-Macedonian sentiment in Athens following Philip II's conquest of Olynthus, Aristotle departed the city along with fellow philosopher Xenocrates. They established a new center of learning in Assus, reflecting the shifting intellectual landscape of the time.
events.name: Aristotle leaves Athens due to the anti-Macedonian sentiment

events.enhanced_description: Wulfila, fleeing religious persecution, obtained permission from Emperor Constantius II to migrate with his flock of Arian converts to Moesia, settling near Nicopolis ad Istrum, where he continued his missionary work.
events.name: Wulfila migrates to Moesia with converts

events.enhanced_description: In a notable development in ancient Persia, women were enrolled in the army to perform auxiliary services, reflecting the evolving roles of women in military contexts during this period.
events.name: Women enrolled in the army in Persia

events.enhanced_description: Samudragupta of the Gupta Empire achieved a significant military victory over Rudrasena, consolidating his power and expanding the influence of the Gupta dynasty in northern India.
events.name: Samudragupta defeats Rudrasena in battle

events.enhanced_description: Sidon, a prominent city in the Phoenician region, fell to the Persian forces of King Artaxerxes III after a prolonged siege. The capture of Sidon was marked by severe reprisals against its population, illustrating the harsh realities of Persian imperial power during this period.
events.name: Sidon is taken by Persian forces after a siege

events.enhanced_description: Amidst a revolt in Euboea, instigated by Philip II of Macedon, Athenian support for its allied cities in Macedonia was significantly hindered. This event underscored the shifting power dynamics in the region as Philip expanded his influence at the expense of Athenian authority.
events.name: The Athenian help to its cities in Macedonia is diverted by a revolt in Euboea

events.enhanced_description: The city of Eretria on the island of Euboea successfully revolted against Athenian control, declaring independence. Athenian general Phocion played a crucial role in attempting to manage the conflict, showcasing the challenges faced by Athens in maintaining its influence over its territories.
events.name: Eretria successfully rebels against Athenian rule

events.enhanced_description: After leaving Athens and the Academy founded by Plato, Aristotle established himself in Assus, where he continued his philosophical work. This move was partly a response to the political climate in Athens, reflecting the tensions of the time regarding Macedonian influence.
events.name: Aristotle leaves Athens and Plato's Academy for Assus

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move, Rome and Carthage entered into a trade agreement that prohibited Carthage from attacking Latin states loyal to Rome. This agreement illustrated Rome's rising dominance within the Latin League and its growing influence in the region.
events.name: Rome and Carthage make a trade agreement

events.enhanced_description: After a brief reign of just 183 days, Emperor Shi Zun and his mother, Empress Zheng Yingtao, were executed, leading to the ascension of his son, Shi Jian, as the new emperor of the Jie state Later Zhao.
events.name: Emperor Shi Zun and Empress Zheng Yingtao executed

events.enhanced_description: The Mou-jong, considered proto-Mongols, seized control of North China, marking a significant shift in the region's power dynamics and foreshadowing future Mongol influences.
events.name: Mou-jong take control of North China

events.enhanced_description: Sidon, a key city in Phoenicia, was besieged by the forces of King Artaxerxes III of Persia, reflecting the ongoing conflicts in the region during the Persian Empire's expansion. The siege highlighted the strategic importance of Sidon in the struggle for control over the eastern Mediterranean.
events.name: Sidon is besieged by Persian forces

events.enhanced_description: After recovering from an illness, Philip II of Macedon refocused his military efforts on the remaining Athenian-controlled cities in Macedonia, particularly targeting Olynthus. This shift in focus underscored Philip's determination to consolidate his power in the region and diminish Athenian influence.
events.name: Philip II of Macedon turns his attention to Athenian cities in Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: Western Roman Emperor Constans I faced growing unpopularity, leading to his general Magnentius being proclaimed emperor at Augustodunum, supported by the army stationed on the Rhine frontier.
events.name: Constans I becomes unpopular; Magnentius proclaimed emperor

events.enhanced_description: In January, Constans I fled towards Spain, where he was ultimately assassinated at Castrum Helenae, leading to a power shift as Magnentius took control of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Constans I flees to Spain and is assassinated

events.enhanced_description: Vetranio was encouraged by Constantina, sister of Constantius II, to proclaim himself Caesar, a move that would lead to further political complexities within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Vetranio is proclaimed Caesar

events.enhanced_description: Nepotianus, a Roman usurper, boldly proclaimed himself emperor and entered Rome with a group of gladiators, reflecting the political turmoil and power struggles of the time.
events.name: Nepotianus proclaims himself emperor

events.enhanced_description: Nepotianus, a claimant to the Roman throne, is defeated and killed by Marcellinus, a general loyal to the usurper Magnentius. Following his death, his severed head is displayed on a spear, symbolizing the brutal nature of Roman power struggles during this period.
events.name: Nepotianus is defeated and killed by Marcellinus

events.enhanced_description: Vetranio, a Roman general, meets with Emperor Constantius II at Naissus, where he ultimately aligns himself with Constantius. Following this meeting, Vetranio is compelled to abdicate his title, living out his days as a private citizen under state pension.
events.name: Vetranio meets Constantius II at Naissus

events.enhanced_description: King Pushyavarman establishes the Varman Dynasty in Assam, marking a significant development in the region's political landscape. This dynasty would play a crucial role in the history of Assam and its cultural heritage.
events.name: King Pushyavarman establishes the Varman Dynasty in Assam

events.enhanced_description: Around this time, the Huns initiate their invasions into the Sassanid Empire, marking the beginning of a series of conflicts that would significantly impact the region's stability and power dynamics.
events.name: Huns begin to invade the Sassanid Empire

events.enhanced_description: The city of Anbar is founded by King Shapur II, serving as a significant urban center in the Sassanid Empire. This establishment reflects the empire's expansion and its efforts to enhance trade and military presence in the region.
events.name: City of Anbar is founded by Shapur II

events.enhanced_description: The Ran Wei-Later Zhao war erupts in North China, marking a period of intense conflict between these two states. This war is part of the larger fragmentation of power during the Three Kingdoms period.
events.name: Ran Wei-Later Zhao war breaks out in North China

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Church of Santa Constanza in Rome is completed, showcasing the architectural and artistic achievements of early Christian builders. This church remains a significant example of early Christian architecture.
events.name: Church of Santa Constanza is finished

events.enhanced_description: During a revolt against Persian rule, Sidon reached out for assistance from its sister city Tyre and Egypt, although the support received was minimal. This plea for help illustrated the desperation of Sidon amid the overwhelming power of the Persian Empire.
events.name: Sidon seeks help from Tyre and Egypt during a revolt

events.enhanced_description: Idrieus, the second son of Hecatomnus, ascends to the throne of Caria following the death of Artemisia II, his brother Mausolus's widow. Shortly after his reign begins, he responds to a request from the Persian king Artaxerxes III by equipping a fleet of 40 triremes and assembling an army of 8,000 mercenaries to launch an expedition against Cyprus, commanded by the Athenian general Phocion.
events.name: Idrieus Succeeds to the Throne of Caria

events.enhanced_description: With the assistance of his brother-in-law Philip II of Macedon, Alexander I successfully ousts the previous king Arymbas to become the ruler of Epirus. This event marks a significant shift in power dynamics within the region, as Macedonian influence begins to grow.
events.name: Alexander I Becomes King of Epirus

events.enhanced_description: Philip II of Macedon orders the sacking of Abdera, a city in Thrace, as part of his broader campaign to expand Macedonian influence in the region. This act of aggression exemplifies the militaristic strategies employed by Philip to consolidate power and assert dominance over neighboring territories.
events.name: Philip II Sacks Abdera

events.enhanced_description: In a decisive confrontation, an army composed of Roman forces and their allies successfully defeats the Gauls, who had once again threatened the city of Rome. This victory not only secures Rome's safety but also reinforces the military prowess of the Roman Republic during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Gauls Defeated by Roman Allies

events.enhanced_description: Philosopher Aristotle presents arguments supporting the concept of a spherical Earth, utilizing observations from lunar eclipses among other logical reasoning. His work contributes significantly to the field of astronomy and the understanding of the cosmos in ancient philosophy.
events.name: Aristotle Argues for a Spherical Earth
