events.name: Vision of Lè Zūn leading to the creation of the Mogao Caves

events.enhanced_description: In 366 AD, Pope Liberius passed away after a 14-year reign, leading to the election of Damasus I as the 37th pope. His election was met with discontent among some Romans, who subsequently elected the antipope Ursicinus.
events.name: Death of Pope Liberius and succession of Damasus I

events.enhanced_description: In 366 BC, several satraps under King Artaxerxes II initiated a revolt in Persia, forming alliances with Athens, Sparta, and Egypt. This conflict, which persisted until 358 BC, reflected the instability within the Persian Empire and the rising power of Greek city-states.
events.name: Revolt of Persian Satraps

events.enhanced_description: In 366 BC, Athens established the town of Kos on the island of Kos in the Aegean Sea. This foundation was part of Athens' broader strategy to expand its influence and control over the Aegean islands.
events.name: Foundation of Kos

events.enhanced_description: In 366 BC, Theban leader Epaminondas made his third return to the Peloponnesus, aiming to secure alliances with the Achaean states. Despite his initial successes, the democratic governments he established were soon overturned by pro-Spartan factions.
events.name: Epaminondas Returns to the Peloponnesus

events.enhanced_description: In 366 BC, Thebes negotiated peace with Sparta, redirecting its focus towards Athens, which was attempting to re-establish its maritime empire. This shift in attention was indicative of the complex political landscape of ancient Greece during this period.
events.name: Thebes Makes Peace with Sparta

events.enhanced_description: In 366 BC, Thebes successfully captured the city of Oropus, further asserting its influence in the region. This military action was part of Thebes' broader strategy to expand its territory and power in Greece.
events.name: Thebes Captures Oropus

events.enhanced_description: In 366 BC, the philosophical experiment led by Dion and Plato to educate the tyrant Dionysius II of Syracuse in the principles of governance failed, resulting in their banishment from the city. This event underscored the challenges of applying philosophical ideals in practical politics.
events.name: Dion and Plato's Educational Experiment Fails

events.enhanced_description: In 366 BC, the Roman Republic permanently abandoned the use of military tribunes with consular power, restoring the dual consulship. This change led to the establishment of the praetorship, a new magistracy responsible for civil matters, allowing consuls to focus on military leadership.
events.name: The abandonment of military tribunes with consular power

events.enhanced_description: In 366 BC, the Roman political structure was expanded with the introduction of two additional curule aediles, who were initially patricians. This role alternated between patricians and plebeians, reflecting the evolving dynamics of Roman governance and representation.
events.name: Creation of curule aediles in Rome

events.enhanced_description: Around 366 BC, the wall painting known as 'The Abduction of Persephone' was created in Tomb I (Small Tomb) in Vergina, Macedonia. This artwork reflects the rich cultural and artistic heritage of ancient Macedonian society.
events.name: Creation of the wall painting 'The Abduction of Persephone'

events.enhanced_description: In April 366 AD, the Battle of Thyatira saw Emperor Valens decisively defeat the forces of Procopius, effectively quelling Procopius's revolt. The battle resulted in the deaths of key commanders Serenianus and Marcellus, while Procopius fled but was later executed by Valens.
events.name: Battle of Thyatira

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 366 AD, Emperor Valentinian I appointed Jovinus as his Master of the Horse and general of the army. Jovinus successfully led campaigns against the Alamanni, achieving victory in three consecutive battles and driving them out of Gaul.
events.name: Winter – Emperor Valentinian I appoints Jovinus

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, Emperor Valentinian I launched a punitive expedition against the Alamanni in the Battle of Solicinium, responding to crises in Britannia and Gaul. The Alamanni were forced to retreat across the Rhine, leading to the plundering of Moguntiacum (modern Mainz).
events.name: Battle of Solicinium

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, Emperor Valentinian I issued a decree stating that Christians would not be compelled to enter gladiator training schools. This decision reflected the growing influence of Christianity within the Roman Empire and its leaders.
events.name: Valentinian I declares Christians will not be forced into gladiator training schools

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, the Great Conspiracy unfolded as the Roman garrison stationed at Hadrian's Wall revolted, allowing Picts from Caledonia to ravage Britain. This rebellion coincided with invasions by the Attacotti, Scotti from Ireland, and Saxons from Germania, leading to widespread devastation.
events.name: Great Conspiracy: Roman garrison on Hadrian's Wall revolts

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, Eunomius of Cyzicus was banished to Mauretania for harboring the usurper Procopius. This event highlights the political and religious tensions of the time within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Eunomius of Cyzicus is banished

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, Gratian was bestowed the title of Augustus by his father, Emperor Valentinian I. This event marked Gratian's formal recognition as co-emperor, setting the stage for his future role in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Gratian receives the title of Augustus

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, the first Korean envoy arrived in Japan as an emissary of the government of Kudara. This event marked an important moment in the diplomatic relations between Korea and Japan.
events.name: First Korean envoy arrives in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, St. Athanasius of Alexandria compiled the first listing of the New Testament, which played a crucial role in the formation of the Christian biblical canon. This listing helped to define the texts considered authoritative by the Christian community.
events.name: First Listing of the New Testament by St. Athanasius

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, Antipope Ursicinus was banished by the praefecti to Gaul. This event was part of the ongoing power struggles within the early Christian church, reflecting the tensions between different factions.
events.name: Antipope Ursicinus is banished

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, Epiphanius was appointed as the bishop of Salamis in Cyprus. His leadership would influence the Christian community in the region during a time of theological disputes.
events.name: Epiphanius of Salamis becomes bishop

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, Emperor Valens was baptized by Eudoxius of Antioch, marking a significant moment in his reign as he embraced Christianity. This act reflected the growing influence of Christianity within the Roman imperial structure.
events.name: Emperor Valens is baptized

events.enhanced_description: In 367 AD, a star in the constellation Perseus, now known as GK Persei, exploded in a nova. This astronomical event, not visible to the naked eye, was later detected on Earth in 1901.
events.name: Nova in Perseus

events.enhanced_description: In 367 BC, Theban general Epaminondas led an invasion into the Peloponnesus, successfully gaining the allegiance of Sicyon to Thebes. Despite this minor victory, he faced legal repercussions upon returning to Thebes, where he was acquitted.
events.name: Epaminondas invades the Peloponnesus

events.enhanced_description: In 367 BC, Archidamus III, the Spartan king, commanded a Spartan army that achieved a significant victory over the Arcadians. This battle reinforced Spartan dominance in the region during a time of political strife in Greece.
events.name: Archidamus III's victory over the Arcadians

events.enhanced_description: In 367 BC, Theban leader Pelopidas embarked on an embassy to the Persian king Artaxerxes II, persuading him to propose a settlement for the disputes among Greek states. However, the edict issued by Artaxerxes II was largely ignored by the Greeks.
events.name: Pelopidas' embassy to Artaxerxes II

events.enhanced_description: In 367 BC, Dionysius I, the tyrant of Syracuse, died and was succeeded by his son Dionysius II. Due to Dionysius II's inexperience, his uncle Dion took control, seeking the guidance of philosopher Plato to train the young tyrant.
events.name: Death of Dionysius I of Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: In 367 BC, Dionysius II of Syracuse negotiated peace with Carthage, reverting to the terms established after his father's previous defeat. This agreement aimed to stabilize relations following a tumultuous period in Sicilian politics.
events.name: Dionysius II's peace with Carthage

events.enhanced_description: From 376 BC to 367 BC, Gaius Licinius Stolo served as tribune in Rome, enacting significant reforms to ease tensions between patricians and plebeians. His proposals, including the Lex Licinia Sextia, ultimately restored the consulship to the plebeians and regulated land ownership.
events.name: Gaius Licinius Stolo's reforms in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 367 BC, the Temple of Concordia was built on the Forum Romanum in Rome by Marcus Furius Camillus. This temple symbolized the importance of unity and harmony in Roman society during a period of political reform.
events.name: Construction of the Temple of Concordia

events.enhanced_description: In 367 BC, the philosopher Aristotle arrived in Athens to study at Plato's Academy. His time there would profoundly influence his later work and the development of Western philosophy.
events.name: Aristotle's arrival at Plato's Academy

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 367 AD, Emperor Valentinian I mobilized a substantial army for his campaign against the Alamanni and the Franks. He summoned legions from Italy and Illyria to prepare for a spring offensive.
events.name: Winter – Valentinian I mobilizes a massive army

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 368 AD, Emperor Valentinian I, accompanied by his 8-year-old son Gratian, crossed the Rhine River with an army into Alamannic territory. Following a series of victories, he returned to his capital, Augusta Treverorum (modern Trier), after signing a temporary peace with Macrian, king of the Bucinobantes.
events.name: Spring – Emperor Valentinian I crosses the Rhine

events.enhanced_description: In 368 AD, during the Great Conspiracy, Picts, Scotti, and Saxons invaded and plundered Roman London. General Theodosius was dispatched from Richborough, Kent, to confront the invaders and restore order.
events.name: Great Conspiracy: Picts, Scotti and Saxons plunder Roman London

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 368 AD, Roman forces successfully drove the invading barbarians back to their homelands, retaking Hadrian's Wall and restoring order to the Roman diocese. Theodosius reorganized the abandoned forts and initiated punitive expeditions into Hibernia (Ireland).
events.name: Winter – Barbarians driven back to their homelands

events.enhanced_description: In 368 AD, an earthquake struck Nicaea, a significant city in the Roman Empire located in modern-day Turkey. This event would have had considerable impacts on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: Earthquake strikes Nicaea

events.enhanced_description: In 368 BC, after the Macedonian intervention in Thessaly, Alexander of Pherae resumed his harsh treatment of subjects, prompting the Thessalians to seek assistance from Thebes. This led to a series of military and political maneuvers involving Theban leaders.
events.name: Alexander of Pherae's cruel rule in Thessaly

events.enhanced_description: In 368 BC, after being captured, Pelopidas was rescued by Epaminondas, who led the Theban army into Thessaly. This strategic maneuver allowed for Pelopidas' release without engaging in battle, showcasing Epaminondas' military acumen.
events.name: Epaminondas secures Pelopidas' release

events.enhanced_description: In 368 BC, Alexander II of Macedon was assassinated during a festival, orchestrated by his brother-in-law Ptolemy of Aloros. Following his death, Alexander's underage brother Perdiccas III ascended to the throne, with Ptolemy acting as regent.
events.name: Assassination of Alexander II of Macedon

events.enhanced_description: Zhou Xian Wang ascended to the throne of the Zhou dynasty, marking a significant moment in Chinese history as the dynasty was in decline. His reign would be characterized by attempts to consolidate power and address the challenges posed by rival states during the Warring States period.
events.name: Zhou Xian Wang becomes king of the Zhou dynasty of China

events.enhanced_description: Plato completed his seminal work, 'The Republic', which outlines his vision of an ideal society governed by philosopher-kings. This text has had a profound influence on Western political thought and philosophy, advocating for justice and the role of education in governance.

image.caption: A manuscript page from Codex Parisinus graecus 1807 containing the beginning of Plato’s Politeia.

events.name: Plato's Republic is completed

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 369 AD, Emperor Valens crossed the Danube River to engage the Gothic tribes, specifically the Greuthungi and Tervingi. Following military confrontations, Valens and the Gothic king Athanaric eventually signed a treaty, highlighting the complexities of Roman-Gothic relations.
events.name: Spring – Emperor Valens attacks Gothic tribes

events.enhanced_description: Fritigern ascends as king of the Visigoths during a tumultuous period marked by internal strife against his rival Athanaric. Seeking stability, he appeals to the Roman Emperor Valens for military assistance, which ultimately leads to the cessation of the civil war and Fritigern's conversion to Christianity.
events.name: Fritigern becomes king of the Visigoths

events.enhanced_description: Count Theodosius successfully re-establishes Roman control over Britain following the Great Conspiracy of 367, a significant uprising that threatened the stability of Roman rule in the region. His efforts mark a pivotal moment in the Roman Empire's attempts to maintain its influence in Britain.
events.name: Count Theodosius brings Britain fully back to the Empire

events.enhanced_description: King Shapur II of the Sassanian Empire launches a military campaign to occupy the pro-Roman kingdom of Armenia, besieging the fortress of Artogerassa. The defense is led by Papas, the son of King Arsaces II, who valiantly protects the royal treasure against the Persian forces.
events.name: King Shapur II occupies the pro-Roman kingdom of Armenia

events.enhanced_description: In a significant military engagement, the troops of the Jin Dynasty face defeat at the hands of the Former Yan, a state ruled by the Xianbei people. This battle reflects the ongoing power struggles in northern China during this period.
events.name: Chinese troops of the Jin Dynasty are defeated by Former Yan of the Xianbei

events.enhanced_description: The kingdom of Goguryeo launches an invasion against its rival Baekje, marking a significant military conflict in the Three Kingdoms period of Korea. This invasion is part of the broader struggle for dominance among the Korean states.
events.name: Goguryeo invades Baekje

events.enhanced_description: Wulfila, a prominent Gothic bishop, develops a unique Gothic alphabet that incorporates elements from Greek and Roman scripts, alongside Germanic runes. This innovation not only aids in the literacy of the Gothic people but also facilitates the spread of Arian Christianity among them.
events.name: Wulfila creates a Gothic alphabet

events.enhanced_description: After defeating the Spartan army threatening Mantinea, Theban general Epaminondas made a bold move by crossing the Evrotas River, a significant territorial boundary for Sparta. This act demonstrated the growing power of Thebes and marked a pivotal moment in the conflict with Sparta.
events.name: Epaminondas crosses the Evrotas River

events.enhanced_description: Following his campaign in Arcadia, Epaminondas marched into Messenia, a territory long held by Sparta. He initiated the reconstruction of the city of Messene, signaling a strategic effort to reclaim lost territory and bolster Theban influence in the region.
events.name: Epaminondas marches to Messenia

events.enhanced_description: Upon returning to Thebes, Epaminondas faced trial for allegedly overstepping his military command. His defense, emphasizing the necessity of his actions to safeguard Thebes, ultimately led to the dismissal of the charges, reflecting his significant political influence.
events.name: Epaminondas put on trial in Thebes

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move to counter the rising power of Thebes, Athens chose to ally with its historical rival, Sparta. This alliance marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Greece, as former enemies united against a common threat.
events.name: Athens allies with Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his father, Amyntas III, Alexander II ascended to the throne of Macedon. He faced immediate challenges, including invasions from Illyrian forces and a rival claimant, which tested his leadership and military capabilities.
events.name: Alexander II becomes king of Macedon

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of his father, Alexander of Pherae assumed control over Thessaly, establishing a tyrannical rule that prompted local leaders to seek assistance from Alexander II of Macedon. His actions significantly impacted the political dynamics in the region.
events.name: Alexander of Pherae becomes tyrant of Thessaly

events.enhanced_description: Pelopidas, a prominent Theban general, exerted pressure on Alexander of Pherae, compelling him to shift his allegiance from Athens to Thebes. This realignment of power dynamics was crucial for Thebes in its ongoing struggle against Spartan influence.
events.name: Pelopidas forces Alexander to abandon alliance with Athens

events.enhanced_description: Cleomenes II ascended to the throne of Sparta following the death of his brother, Agesipolis II. His reign would be marked by the challenges of maintaining Spartan power amidst the shifting alliances and conflicts of the Greek city-states.
events.name: Cleomenes II succeeds Agesipolis II as king of Sparta

events.enhanced_description: During the Germanic Invasions, various Germanic tribes encircle the northern borders of the Roman Empire, while the Huns wreak havoc across the region, destroying settlements and destabilizing existing powers. This period marks a significant threat to Roman authority and territorial integrity.
events.name: Germanic Invasions

events.enhanced_description: In a bid to maintain Roman cultural integrity, a law is enacted by Emperors Valentinian I and Valens prohibiting marriages between Romans and barbarian peoples, imposing severe penalties for violations. This reflects the growing tensions between the Roman Empire and the various tribes at its borders.
events.name: Law banning marriages between Romans and barbarians

events.enhanced_description: An edict issued by Emperors Valentinian I and Valens prohibits the importation of wine and olive oil from regions controlled by barbarian tribes, aiming to curb economic ties with these groups. This reflects the increasing isolationist policies of the Roman Empire during this period.
events.name: Edict banning importation of wine and olive oil

events.enhanced_description: The Huns begin their westward migration from the Volga River into Europe, subjugating the Alans and Ostrogoths along the way. This migration introduces new military tactics, including the use of composite bows, significantly impacting the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Huns migrate westward from the Volga

events.enhanced_description: Athanaric, the Gothic leader of the Tervingi, moves eastward and establishes a defensive position along the banks of the Dniester River. This strategic maneuver is part of his efforts to protect his people from external threats.
events.name: Athanaric advances eastwards

events.enhanced_description: The Former Qin state successfully conquers Former Yan, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in northern China. This conquest is part of the broader conflicts that characterized the era of the Sixteen Kingdoms.
events.name: Former Qin conquers Former Yan

events.enhanced_description: Basil the Great is appointed as the bishop of Caesarea, a significant ecclesiastical position in the early Christian church. His leadership and theological contributions would later have a profound impact on Christian doctrine and monasticism.
events.name: Basil the Great becomes bishop of Caesarea

events.enhanced_description: Demophilus is appointed as the Patriarch of Constantinople, although his position is contested by Evagrius. This dispute highlights the theological and political tensions within the early Christian church.
events.name: Demophilus becomes Patriarch of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: John Chrysostom, later known for his eloquence and theological contributions, is baptized in Antioch. His early life and education in this vibrant city would shape his future role as a prominent church leader.
events.name: John Chrysostom is baptized

events.enhanced_description: Under King Agesilaus II, the Spartans launched an invasion of Arcadia, seeking to assert their dominance. However, after failing to secure assistance from Athens, they faced a counter-offensive led by Epaminondas of Thebes.
events.name: Spartans invade Arcadia

events.enhanced_description: With support from Thebes, the new capital of Arcadia, Megalopolis, was completed, establishing a democratic government featuring an Assembly of Ten Thousand. This development represented a significant shift towards democracy in the region.
events.name: Megalopolis completed with democratic system

events.enhanced_description: Jason of Pherae, a powerful leader in Thessaly, passed away, leaving behind a significant political legacy. His leadership had transformed Thessaly into a formidable force in Greek politics, influencing the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Death of Jason of Pherae

events.enhanced_description: The renowned sculptor Praxiteles began his artistic career in Athens, where he would go on to create some of the most celebrated works of ancient Greek sculpture. His contributions significantly shaped the artistic landscape of the time.
events.name: Praxiteles begins career in Athens

events.enhanced_description: Eudoxus of Cnidus made significant advancements in mathematics by developing the method of exhaustion, a precursor to integral calculus. This method allowed for the determination of areas and volumes, influencing future mathematical thought.
events.name: Eudoxus develops method of exhaustion

events.enhanced_description: The fortified cities along the Danube, particularly Sirmium, play a crucial role in halting an invasion by the Quadi. This defense underscores the strategic importance of these cities in protecting the Roman Empire's northern frontier.
events.name: Fortified cities of the Danube stop Quadi invasion

events.enhanced_description: Under King Shapur II, the neo-Persian Empire reaches the height of its power, coinciding with renewed hostilities against the Romans. This period marks a significant escalation in the long-standing Roman-Persian conflicts.
events.name: Neo-Persian Empire attains zenith under Shapur II

events.enhanced_description: Forces from Baekje successfully storm the capital of Goguryeo, P'yongyang, in a significant military engagement during the Three Kingdoms period of Korea. This attack highlights the ongoing conflicts and power struggles among the Korean states.
events.name: Baekje forces storm Goguryeo capital

events.enhanced_description: Sosurim ascends to the throne as king of Goguryeo, a pivotal moment in the history of this ancient Korean kingdom. His reign would be marked by efforts to consolidate power and strengthen the state.
events.name: Sosurim becomes king of Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: The Roman poet Ausonius composes 'Mosella', a poetic work that reflects on his experiences during a voyage along the Rhine and Moselle rivers. This piece is notable for its vivid imagery and celebration of the natural beauty of the region.
events.name: Roman poet Ausonius writes 'Mosella'

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 17, Augustine of Hippo travels to Carthage to pursue his education in rhetoric. This journey marks a significant turning point in his life, leading to his eventual conversion to Christianity and influential theological writings.
events.name: Augustine of Hippo travels to Carthage

events.enhanced_description: Martin of Tours is appointed as the bishop of Tours, a significant ecclesiastical role that would see him become one of the most revered saints in Christianity. His leadership and commitment to the poor would leave a lasting legacy.
events.name: Martin of Tours becomes bishop of Tours

events.enhanced_description: In 371 BC, a peace congress convened in Sparta aimed at resolving ongoing conflicts among Greek city-states. Spartan King Agesilaus II, supported by Athens, denied Thebes the right to sign the treaty on behalf of Boeotia, leading to heightened tensions and the exclusion of Thebes from the peace agreement.
events.name: A fresh peace congress is summoned at Sparta

events.enhanced_description: The actions of Thebes at the peace congress ignited a conflict with Sparta, culminating in the pivotal Battle of Leuctra. The Theban generals, Epaminondas and Pelopidas, executed a groundbreaking military strategy, defeating the Spartan forces led by Cleombrotus I, who was killed in the battle, thereby altering the balance of power in Greece.
events.name: Thebes' actions at the peace congress lead to a war between Sparta and Thebes

events.enhanced_description: Following the Theban victory at Leuctra, Athens expressed concern over Thebes' increasing power and aggressiveness. This apprehension led to the restoration of the alliance between Thebes and Persia, further complicating the political landscape of Greece.
events.name: Athens does not welcome the Theban victory, fearing the rising aggressiveness of Thebes

events.enhanced_description: The Theban victory over Sparta at Leuctra prompted the Arcadians to reclaim their independence, leading to the establishment of the Arcadian League and the founding of a new city, Megalopolis. This shift marked a significant change in the political dynamics of the region.
events.name: With the unexpected defeat of Sparta by the Thebans, the Arcadians decide to re-assert their independence

events.enhanced_description: In 371 BC, Agesipolis II ascended to the throne of Sparta following the death of his father, Cleombrotus I. His reign would be marked by the challenges posed by Thebes and the shifting alliances among the Greek city-states.
events.name: Agesipolis II succeeds his father Cleombrotus I as king of Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Around 371 BC, it is believed that the original comet of the Kreutz Sungrazers family passed perihelion, possibly observed by notable figures such as Aristotle and Ephorus. This event contributed to the understanding of celestial phenomena in ancient Greece.
events.name: It is suggested that the original comet associated with the Kreutz Sungrazers family of comets passes perihelion at this time

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Valentinian I is actively engaged in military operations against various tribes, including the Alamanni, Quadi, and Sarmatians, while also addressing threats from usurpers in Africa and the Picts in Britain. His reign is characterized by constant military challenges.
events.name: Emperor Valentinian I engaged in operations

events.enhanced_description: The Huns launch a devastating attack on the Tervingi along the Dniester River, utilizing their superior light cavalry tactics to overwhelm the Gothic forces. King Athanaric is ultimately defeated and seeks refuge in the Carpathian Mountains, highlighting the Huns' growing threat in the region.
events.name: Huns attack the Tervingi

events.enhanced_description: In response to the increasing threats from the Alans and Huns, Athanaric initiates the construction of new defensive fortifications to protect his people. This strategic move reflects the dire circumstances faced by the Goths during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Athanaric builds new defensive works

events.enhanced_description: In 372, Jin Feidi was dethroned as emperor of the Eastern Jin Dynasty, marking a significant shift in power. His granduncle, Sima Yu, was installed as Jin Jianwendi, indicating a change in leadership amidst the turmoil of the Sixteen Kingdoms period.
events.name: Jin Feidi is dethroned as emperor of the Eastern Jin Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 372, Jin Xiaowudi ascended to the throne at the tender age of 10, following the death of his father, Jin Jianwendi. Empress Chu Suanzi served as regent, while high officials Xie An and Wang Tanzhi effectively guided the young emperor's decisions during this politically volatile time.
events.name: Jin Xiaowudi succeeds his father Jin Jianwendi

events.enhanced_description: In 372, the Korean kingdom of Baekje established its first diplomatic ties with the Jin Dynasty of China, marking a significant step in international relations in East Asia. This event laid the groundwork for future interactions and exchanges between the two regions.
events.name: First diplomatic ties between Baekje and the Jin Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 372, the national academy of Chinese learning, known as Taehak, was established in the kingdom of Goguryeo. This institution played a crucial role in the promotion of Confucian education and Chinese cultural influence in Korea.
events.name: Establishment of Taehak in Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: In 372, Basil the Great founded the Basileias near Caesarea Mazaca, which is considered one of the earliest hospitals in history. This establishment was part of his broader efforts to provide care for the poor and sick, reflecting the early Christian commitment to social welfare.
events.name: Basil the Great establishes the Basileias

events.enhanced_description: In 372, Gregory of Nyssa was appointed as the bishop of Nyssa, a significant position that allowed him to influence early Christian theology and church governance. His contributions would later be pivotal in the development of Christian doctrine.
events.name: Gregory of Nyssa becomes bishop of Nyssa

events.enhanced_description: In 372, Goguryeo officially adopted Buddhism as its state religion, marking a significant cultural and religious transformation. This decision facilitated the spread of Buddhist teachings and practices throughout the Korean peninsula.
events.name: Buddhism adopted as the official religion of Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: In 372, Saint Augustine, a prominent theologian, adopted Manichaeism, a dualistic religious system that influenced his later thoughts and writings. This period of exploration into various philosophies would shape his eventual conversion to Christianity.
events.name: Saint Augustine adopts Manichaeism

events.enhanced_description: In 372, Emperor Valentinian I issued a ban on Manichaean meetings, reflecting the growing tension between different religious groups in the Roman Empire. This action was part of a broader effort to consolidate Christian orthodoxy and suppress heretical movements.
events.name: Valentinian I bans Manichaean meetings

events.enhanced_description: In 372 BC, Jason of Pherae, a prominent ruler in Thessaly, initially formed an alliance with Athens before shifting his allegiance to Macedon. His political maneuvers played a crucial role in the power dynamics of the region during this period.
events.name: Jason of Pherae allies himself first with Athens and then with Macedon

events.enhanced_description: Troilus of Elis achieved notable success at the Olympic Games in 372 BC by winning two equestrian events. His victories led to significant changes in the rules of the Games, including the banning of referees from competing, reflecting the evolving nature of this ancient sporting tradition.
events.name: Troilus of Elis wins two equestrian events at the Olympic Games

events.enhanced_description: In 373, Emperor Valens converted to Arianism, a controversial Christian doctrine that denied the full divinity of Christ. His conversion led to the persecution of Trinitarian Christians in the Eastern Roman Empire, exacerbating religious tensions.
events.name: Emperor Valens converts to Arianism

events.enhanced_description: In 373, Quintus Aurelius Symmachus was appointed proconsul of Africa, a position that placed him in charge of one of the most important provinces of the Roman Empire. His role included managing local governance and maintaining order in a region marked by political unrest.
events.name: Quintus Aurelius Symmachus becomes proconsul of Africa

events.enhanced_description: In 373, Count Theodosius was appointed commander of an expedition to suppress the rebellion of Firmus in Mauretania. This military action was part of the Roman Empire's efforts to maintain control over its North African territories.
events.name: Count Theodosius appointed commander against Firmus

events.enhanced_description: In 373, the Valens Aqueduct was inaugurated in Constantinople, a remarkable feat of engineering that extended over 971 meters. This aqueduct was crucial for supplying water to the growing population of the city, showcasing the advanced infrastructure of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Valens Aqueduct inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: In 373, the Battle of the Tanais River saw the Huns defeat the Alans near the Don River, forcing the remnants of the Alan forces to flee westward. This battle was part of the larger conflicts involving nomadic tribes and the Roman Empire's borders.
events.name: Battle of the Tanais River

events.enhanced_description: In 373, King Shapur II of Persia declared war against the Roman Empire, prompted by Emperor Valens' support of Armenia. This conflict marked a significant escalation in hostilities between the two powers, with Valens establishing Antioch as his military base for the campaign.
events.name: King Shapur II declares war

events.enhanced_description: In 373, Saint Martin of Tours undertook significant efforts to Christianize Gaul, spreading the teachings of Christianity throughout the region. His work laid the foundation for the establishment of Christianity as a dominant faith in France.
events.name: Saint Martin of Tours Christianizes Gaul

events.enhanced_description: In 373 BC, Persian King Artaxerxes II initiated an invasion of Egypt, aiming to reassert Persian control over the region. Despite initial successes, the invasion ultimately faltered as Egyptian King Nectanebo I successfully repelled the Persian forces, showcasing the resilience of Egyptian resistance.
events.name: The Persian King Artaxerxes II launches an invasion of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 373 BC, Athenian general Iphicrates led a successful expedition to relieve the island of Corcyra from a Spartan siege. This military action demonstrated Athenian naval strength and strategic capabilities during the ongoing conflicts with Sparta.
events.name: Iphicrates leads an Athenian expedition to relieve Corcyra

events.enhanced_description: In 373 BC, the ancient city of Helike was devastated by a catastrophic earthquake and subsequent tsunami, leading to its complete destruction. This event was significant in ancient Greek history, as Helike was known for its cultural and economic contributions to the region.
events.name: The ancient Greek city of Helike is destroyed by a massive earthquake and tsunami

events.enhanced_description: In 373 BC, a powerful earthquake struck Delphi, leading to the destruction of the Temple of Apollo, one of the most significant religious sites in ancient Greece. This disaster had profound implications for the oracle and the worship practices associated with Apollo.
events.name: The Temple of Apollo in Delphi is destroyed by an earthquake

events.enhanced_description: In 374, the Quadi crossed the Danube River and began ravaging the province of Pannonia. Their incursions targeted the unprotected countryside, avoiding fortified cities, which highlighted the vulnerabilities of the Roman frontier.
events.name: The Quadi cross the Danube

events.enhanced_description: In 374, Spearthrower Owl ascended to the throne of Teotihuacan, a major Mesoamerican city. His reign is noted for its cultural and political developments during a time of significant growth for the civilization.
events.name: Spearthrower Owl ascends to the throne of Teotihuacan

events.enhanced_description: In 374, the people of Milan acclaimed Ambrosius, the governor of Aemilia-Liguria, as their bishop. His subsequent leadership would significantly influence the relationship between church and state in the medieval period.
events.name: Ambrosius acclaimed bishop by the people of Milan

events.enhanced_description: In 374 BC, Athens sought to withdraw from the ongoing Theban-Spartan war by negotiating a peace treaty with Sparta. However, this peace was short-lived, as hostilities resumed shortly after, reflecting the volatility of Greek alliances during this period.
events.name: Athens tries to retire from the Theban-Spartan war and makes peace with Sparta

events.enhanced_description: In 374 BC, Sparta launched an attack on Corcyra, seeking assistance from Syracusan forces. The Athenian general Timotheus intervened, capturing the island and defeating the Spartan navy in a decisive naval battle off Alyzia, showcasing Athenian military prowess.
events.name: Sparta attacks Corcyra, enlisting Syracusan help

events.enhanced_description: In 374 BC, Evagoras, the King of Salamis in Cyprus, was assassinated, leading to the ascension of his son, Nicocles. Nicocles continued his father's policies of Hellenization, influenced by the philosopher Isocrates, who provided guidance through his writings.
events.name: The King of Salamis, Evagoras, is assassinated

events.enhanced_description: In 375, Emperor Valentinian I negotiated a lasting peace with the Alamanni in Germany before marching into Illyricum to confront the Quadi and Sarmatians. His reign was marked by both military conflict and efforts to stabilize the empire.
events.name: Valentinian I concludes peace with the Alamanni

events.enhanced_description: In 375, the Quadi accepted a precarious peace from Merobaudes, the Magister militum, which granted them land to settle along the Danube. This agreement was a temporary solution to ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: The Quadi accept peace from Merobaudes

events.enhanced_description: In 375, 16-year-old Gratian assumed control of the government in Augusta Treverorum, while his half-brother Valentinian II was proclaimed co-emperor. This political maneuvering was aimed at securing loyalty from the Illyrian army amidst fears of usurpation.
events.name: Gratian takes over government at Augusta Treverorum

events.enhanced_description: In 375, Gratian initiated a systematic persecution of pagans, confiscating temple wealth to bolster the Imperial Treasury. His actions reflected the growing influence of Christianity and the desire to suppress competing beliefs.
events.name: Gratian begins persecution of pagans

events.enhanced_description: In 375, the dissident Berber prince Firmus was delivered to the Romans by his brother Gildon, a significant event that underscored the internal strife within the Berber tribes and the Roman Empire's efforts to maintain control over North Africa.
events.name: Firmus delivered to Romans by Gildon

events.enhanced_description: In 375, Chandragupta II ascended to the throne of the Gupta Empire, following in the footsteps of his father, Samudragupta. His reign is noted for its military conquests and cultural achievements, marking a golden age in Indian history.
events.name: Chandragupta II becomes ruler of the Gupta Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 375 AD, Geungusu ascended to the throne of Baekje, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His reign marked a significant period of cultural and political development in the kingdom, which was known for its advanced metallurgy and trade relations with neighboring states.

locations.name: Buyeo, South Chungcheong Province, South Korea

events.name: Geungusu becomes king of the Korean kingdom of Baekje

events.enhanced_description: In 375 AD, two of the earliest known books, a school textbook and an account book with bound wooden leaves, were lost in the sands of the Dakhla Oasis in Egypt. These artifacts, preserved by the desert environment, provide invaluable insights into ancient Egyptian literacy and administrative practices.

locations.name: Dakhla Oasis, New Valley Governorate, Egypt

events.name: The earliest extant books are lost at the Dakhla Oasis in western Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 375 AD, the first two Buddhist temples were constructed in Korea, marking the introduction of Buddhism to the region. This event laid the foundation for the spread of Buddhist culture and philosophy throughout the Korean Peninsula.
events.name: The first two Korean Buddhist temples are built

events.enhanced_description: In 375 AD, Saint Jerome, a prominent Christian scholar and translator, retired to the desert of Chalcis in Syria. This period of solitude allowed him to focus on his biblical translations, including the Vulgate, which would become the standard Latin version of the Bible.
events.name: Saint Jerome retires to the desert of Chalcis (Syria)

events.enhanced_description: In 375 AD, Saint Maron founded the Maronite Church in Lebanon, which became a significant branch of Christianity. The Maronite community has maintained its distinct identity and traditions throughout centuries, contributing to the religious diversity of Lebanon.
events.name: The Maronite Church is founded by Saint Maron in Lebanon

events.enhanced_description: In 375 AD, Rav Ashi completed the Talmud of Babylon, a comprehensive compilation of Jewish oral law and commentary. This monumental work has had a lasting impact on Jewish scholarship and law, shaping the practices of Jewish communities worldwide.

image.caption: A volume displaying pages from Tractate Eruvin in the Jewish Museum of Switzerland.

events.name: The Talmud of Babylon is written by Rav Ashi

events.enhanced_description: In 375 BC, the Theban general Pelopidas was appointed as the leader of the Sacred Band, an elite infantry unit of 300 men known for their bravery and loyalty. This formation played a crucial role in Theban military successes against Sparta, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in ancient Greece.
events.name: Pelopidas Becomes Leader of the Sacred Band

events.enhanced_description: In 375 BC, Pelopidas led the Sacred Band of Thebes in a daring attempt to seize the city of Orchomenus while its Spartan garrison was away. Despite initially retreating upon discovering reinforcements for the Spartans, Pelopidas and his forces engaged in the Battle of Tegyra, where they achieved a stunning victory over a larger Spartan contingent, solidifying Theban military reputation.
events.name: Battle of Tegyra

events.enhanced_description: In 375 BC, Zhou Lie Wang ascended to the throne of the Zhou dynasty, a significant event in the history of ancient China. His reign marked a continuation of the Zhou dynasty's influence, despite the increasing fragmentation of power among regional states during the Warring States period.
events.name: Zhou Lie Wang Becomes King

events.enhanced_description: In 376 AD, during the Gothic War, Emperor Valens allowed the Visigothic chieftain Fritigern and his people to cross the Danube River into Roman territory. This decision was made under the condition that the Visigoths would provide soldiers for the Roman legions, setting the stage for future conflicts.
events.name: Gothic War: Emperor Valens permits the Visigothic chieftain Fritigern to cross the Danube

events.enhanced_description: In 376 AD, the Greuthungi, led by chieftains Alatheus and Saphrax, sought asylum within the Roman Empire due to pressures from the Huns and Alans. Their request was denied, leading them to cross the Danube and join forces with the Visigoths.
events.name: The Greuthungi request asylum within the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 376 AD, the Roman authorities failed to effectively disarm the Visigoths and mishandled the administration of the refugees, leading to rising tensions. The Goths, feeling mistreated, began to break out of their containment area along the Danube, moving towards the fertile lands near Marcianople.
events.name: The Romans fail to disarm the Visigoths

events.enhanced_description: In 376 AD, Lupicinus, the count of Thrace, attempted to regain control over the Visigoths by inviting their leaders to a banquet. However, his plan to assassinate the Gothic delegation failed when Fritigern escaped, leading to widespread looting and violence in the region.
events.name: Lupicinus tries to bring the Visigoths back under control

events.enhanced_description: In 376 AD, Lupicinus launched an attack against the Visigoths just outside Marcianople with a hastily assembled force. The battle resulted in a devastating defeat for the Romans, allowing the Goths to seize Roman armor and weapons, further escalating the conflict.
events.name: Lupicinus attacks the Visigoths outside Marcianople

events.enhanced_description: In 376 AD, fearing that Gothic troops stationed in Adrianople might join Fritigern, Emperor Valens ordered them to move east. The refusal of local officials to provide necessary provisions led to open rebellion among the Gothic soldiers, further destabilizing the region.
events.name: Roman troops of Gothic origin are ordered to move east

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 376 AD, Fritigern attempted to besiege Adrianople but was unsuccessful. His forces, unable to maintain a sustained assault, resorted to foraging in smaller groups, while Roman prisoners provided valuable intelligence to the Goths.
events.name: Winter – Fritigern attempts an unsuccessful siege of Adrianople

events.enhanced_description: In 376 AD, Zhang Tianxi, the ruler of Former Liang, submitted to Fu Jiān of Former Qin, effectively ending the state of Former Liang. This submission marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region during the period of the Sixteen Kingdoms.
events.name: Zhang Tianxi submits to Fu Jiān of Former Qin

events.enhanced_description: In 376 AD, China was politically fragmented, with the Former Qin controlling the north and the Eastern Jin governing the south. This division was a result of the chaotic period known as the Sixteen Kingdoms, characterized by constant warfare and shifting allegiances.
events.name: China is divided between the Former Qin and the Eastern Jin

events.enhanced_description: In 376 BC, the Athenian admiral Chabrias achieved a decisive naval victory against the Spartan fleet off the coast of Naxos. This battle was pivotal for Athens, as it helped to break the Spartan blockade and secure vital grain supplies from the Black Sea, strengthening Athenian naval power during the ongoing conflict with Sparta.

events.name: Battle of Naxos

events.enhanced_description: In 376 BC, the Thracian city of Abdera was sacked by the Triballi, a significant event that highlighted the ongoing conflicts in the region. The sacking contributed to the instability and decline of Abdera as a prominent city in Thrace during this turbulent period.
events.name: Sacking of Abdera

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, famine struck Lower Moesia, where the Goths were settled, leading to severe suffering and starvation among the population. Despite appeals for help from Fritigern, the Roman governors Lupicinus and Maximus offered little assistance, exacerbating the crisis.
events.name: Gothic War: Famine in Lower Moesia takes a fearsome toll

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, Emperor Valens sought military assistance from his nephew Gratian to combat the Goths. Gratian responded by sending General Frigeridus along with elite reinforcements, highlighting the growing threat posed by the Gothic incursions.
events.name: Emperor Valens requests troops against the Goths

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, during the Battle of the Willows, the Romans abandoned their guerrilla tactics and faced a direct attack from the Goths. The battle resulted in heavy casualties for both sides, further weakening the Roman military position in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Willows: The Romans are attacked by the Goths

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, Emperor Valens dispatched Saturninus to the Balkan Mountains to secure the passes against the Goths. This strategic move aimed to prevent the Goths from consolidating their forces and launching further attacks into Roman territory.
events.name: Valens sends Saturninus to the Balkan Mountains

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, the Goths forged an alliance with some of the Huns and Alans along the Danube River, significantly altering the balance of power in the region. This coalition posed a greater threat to the Roman Empire, as they coordinated their efforts against Roman forces.
events.name: The Goths make an alliance with the Huns and Alans

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, the Goths sought to force the Roman army led by Frigeridus out of Beroea. Frigeridus retreated over the Succi Pass, indicating the growing pressure the Goths were exerting on Roman forces in the region.
events.name: The Goths aim to dislodge the army of Frigeridus from Beroea

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, Emperor Valens successfully negotiated a peace treaty with the Persian Empire, allowing him to focus on the Gothic threat. However, this peace was soon challenged by a revolt led by Queen Mavia, which devastated territories from Phoenicia to Sinai.
events.name: Valens concludes a peace with the Persian Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, Persian king Shapur II successfully repelled the Huns from the Caucasus region, demonstrating the strength of the Persian military during this tumultuous period. This victory helped stabilize the eastern front for the Persian Empire.
events.name: Persian king Shapur II pushes the Huns back across the Caucasus

events.enhanced_description: In 377 AD, renowned Chinese painter Gu Kaizhi created his famous work "The Nymph of the Luo River," which is celebrated for its intricate detail and poetic expression. This painting is considered a masterpiece of Chinese art and reflects the cultural richness of the period.
events.name: Chinese painter Gu Kaizhi paints "The Nymph of the Luo River"

events.enhanced_description: In 377 BC, Mausolus was appointed as the Persian satrap of Caria, a position that allowed him to wield significant power in the region. His rule is noted for the cultural and architectural developments that took place, including the construction of the famous Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, which became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
events.name: Mausolus Appointed Satrap of Caria

events.enhanced_description: In 377 BC, the Athenian general Timotheus successfully secured alliances with the Acarnanians and Molossians, strengthening Athens' influence in the region. This diplomatic success was crucial for Athens as it sought to expand its power and counter Spartan dominance during the ongoing conflicts in Greece.
events.name: Timotheus Wins Over Acarnanians and Molossians

events.enhanced_description: In 377 BC, Athens undertook a major reorganization of its financial system in preparation for the Spartan-Theban struggle. This reform mandated that wealthier citizens collect taxes from their less affluent counterparts, reflecting a shift in fiscal responsibility and governance in the city-state.
events.name: Athens Financial Reorganization

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 377 AD, various bands of 'barbarians' roamed the province in search of food and supplies. With most Roman troops confined to towns, skirmishes occurred between elite units and the Goths, leading to significant losses for the Roman cavalry.
events.name: Autumn – Bands of predatory "barbarians" spread throughout the province

events.enhanced_description: During the Gothic War in 378, Emperor Valens dispatched Sebastian with a select force of 2,000 troops to Thrace, renewing guerrilla warfare against the Goths. This strategic move aimed to counter the Gothic threat by targeting small raiding parties.
events.name: Gothic War: Valens sends Sebastian to Thrace

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Fritigern, the Gothic leader, concentrated his forces at Cabyle, located in present-day Kavala, Greece. The Goths were primarily situated in the river valleys south of the Balkan Mountains, preparing for further confrontations with the Roman Empire.

locations.name: Kavala, Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, Greece

events.name: Fritigern concentrates his army at Cabyle

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Emperor Gratian departed from Lauriacum, present-day Austria, with a contingent of lightly armed troops. His journey down the Danube was interrupted by illness, forcing him to halt for several days at Sirmium.
events.name: Gratian sets out from Lauriacum

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Fritigern led his forces south from Cabyle, following the Tundzha River towards Adrianople, with the intent of disrupting Roman supply lines to Constantinople. This maneuver was part of the larger Gothic War against the Roman Empire.

locations.name: Kavala, Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, Greece

events.name: Fritigern strikes south from Cabyle

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Roman reconnaissance successfully detected Gothic movements. In response, Emperor Valens, who was already west of Adrianople, turned back to establish a fortified camp outside the city, preparing for an impending confrontation.
events.name: Roman reconnaissance detects the Goths

events.enhanced_description: In 378, the Goths, realizing their vulnerable position with families and wagons, withdrew northward. Roman scouts, however, failed to detect the Greuthungi cavalry foraging further up the Tundzha valley, which could have posed a significant threat.
events.name: The Goths withdraw back to the north

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Fritigern sent a Christian priest to the Roman camp with an offer of peace terms and a letter for Emperor Valens. However, these overtures were ultimately rejected, escalating tensions between the Goths and the Roman Empire.
events.name: Fritigern sends a Christian priest to the Roman camp

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Emperor Valens led an elite Roman army into Thrace to confront revolts and the Gothic threat. This campaign culminated in the disastrous Battle of Adrianople, where Valens faced a significant defeat.
events.name: Valens leads an elite Roman army to Thrace

events.enhanced_description: In 378, the Goths launched an assault on Adrianople, attempting to scale the city walls with ladders. The defenders successfully repelled the attack by dropping heavy stones and masonry on the attackers.
events.name: The Goths attack Adrianople

events.enhanced_description: In 378, the Goths, bolstered by Hunnic support, advanced towards Constantinople. Their progress was halted by the Saracens, who were recruited from Arab tribes controlling the eastern fringes of the Roman Empire.
events.name: The Goths move on to Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Siyaj K'ak', a prominent figure in the Maya region, began replacing local kings with relatives of Spearthrower Owl, the emperor of Teotihuacan. This political maneuver significantly influenced the power dynamics within the Mayan city-states.
events.name: Siyaj K'ak' begins to replace Mayan kings

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Siyaj K'ak' conquered Uaxactun, further extending the reach of Teotihuacan into the Maya region. This victory was part of a series of military campaigns that reshaped the political landscape of Mesoamerica.
events.name: Siyaj K'ak' conquers Uaxactun

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Emperor Valens completed the construction of the aqueduct of Constantinople, which had been initiated by Constantine I. This engineering feat was crucial for supplying the growing city with fresh water.
events.name: Valens completes the aqueduct of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Gregory of Nazianzus was ordained as the bishop of Constantinople. His leadership would play a significant role in the theological debates and ecclesiastical politics of the early Christian church.
events.name: Gregory of Nazianzus is ordained bishop of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 378, Pope Damasus I faced accusations of adultery but was exonerated by Emperor Gratian. This incident highlighted the intertwining of religious authority and imperial power during this period.
events.name: Pope Damasus I is exonerated by Gratian

events.enhanced_description: In 378 BC, Epaminondas, a prominent Theban general and statesman, took command of Thebes, marking a pivotal moment in Theban history. His leadership, alongside Pelopidas as boeotarch, initiated a series of military reforms and strategies that would challenge Spartan supremacy in Greece.
events.name: Epaminondas Takes Command of Thebes

events.enhanced_description: In 378 BC, Timotheus, the son of the renowned Athenian general Conon, was elected strategos of Athens. His leadership was crucial during a period of military and political restructuring in Athens as it sought to reassert its influence in the Greek world.
events.name: Timotheus Elected Strategos

events.enhanced_description: In 378 BC, a Spartan attempt to seize Piraeus led to a significant confrontation between Athenian forces, commanded by Chabrias, and the larger army of Agesilaus II. Chabrias' unconventional tactics and command style not only thwarted the Spartan advance but also strengthened the alliance between Athens and Thebes.
events.name: Spartan Attempt to Seize Piraeus

events.enhanced_description: In 378 BC, Athens allied itself with Thebes to form the Second Athenian League, a confederation that included most Boeotian cities and several Ionian islands. This alliance was a strategic response to Spartan aggression and aimed to restore Athenian influence in the region.
events.name: Formation of the Second Athenian League

events.enhanced_description: In 378 BC, Dionysius I of Syracuse suffered a disastrous defeat in his third war against Carthage at Cronium. This loss forced him to pay a substantial indemnity and cede significant territory to the Carthaginians, marking a low point in his military campaigns.
events.name: Dionysius I's Third War with Carthage

events.enhanced_description: In 378 BC, the Servian Wall was constructed around Rome as a defensive measure against potential invasions. This fortification represented a significant development in Roman military architecture and urban planning, laying the groundwork for future expansions of the city.
events.name: Construction of the Servian Wall

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 378, Siyaj K'ak' successfully conquered the city of Waka, marking a significant expansion of influence for Teotihuacan in the Maya region. This conquest was part of a broader campaign to assert control over the area.
events.name: Siyaj K'ak' conquers Waka

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 378, Siyaj K'ak' achieved a pivotal victory by conquering Tikal, one of the most powerful city-states in the Maya region. This conquest further solidified Teotihuacan's influence over the Maya civilization.
events.name: Siyaj K'ak' conquers Tikal

events.enhanced_description: In February 378, the Lentienses, a group of the Alemanni, crossed the frozen Rhine River to raid the surrounding countryside. They were met with resistance from the Roman auxilia palatina, who successfully defended the western frontier against the invaders.
events.name: The Lentienses cross the frozen Rhine and raid the countryside

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 378, Emperor Valens returned to Constantinople to mobilize a significant military force of 40,000 men. He appointed Sebastianus as magister militum to reorganize the Roman armies in Thrace, preparing for the escalating conflicts with the Goths.
events.name: Emperor Valens returns to Constantinople and mobilises an army

events.enhanced_description: In May 378, the Battle of Argentovaria took place, where Emperor Gratian was compelled to recall his army from the East. The Lentienses were defeated by Roman general Mallobaudes near Colmar, leading Gratian to earn the title Alemannicus Maximus.
events.name: Battle of Argentovaria

events.enhanced_description: In July 378, Roman general Frigeridus fortified the Succi Pass, located near modern Ihtiman, Bulgaria, to prevent barbarian incursions into the northwest territories of Pannonia. This strategic defense was crucial in maintaining Roman control over the region.
events.name: Frigeridus fortifies the Succi Pass

events.enhanced_description: In August 378, Emperor Gratian advanced down the Danube to the Camp of Mars, a frontier fortress near modern Niš, Serbia. There, he faced an ambush by Alans, resulting in significant losses for his forces.
events.name: Gratian continues to the Camp of Mars

events.enhanced_description: In October 378, the Greuthungi, facing food shortages, split from the main Gothic group and moved westward into Pannonia. Accompanied by their families, they began raiding local villages and farmland.
events.name: Greuthungi split off and move west into Pannonia

events.enhanced_description: In 379, Emperor Gratian elevated Flavius Theodosius at Sirmium, granting him the title of Augustus and authority over the eastern provinces. Theodosius would later negotiate with the Visigoths, settling them in the Balkans as military allies.
events.name: Emperor Gratian elevates Flavius Theodosius

events.enhanced_description: In 379, Emperor Gratian declined the title of Eastern Emperor, a significant political decision that reflected his focus on the Western Roman Empire and its challenges. This refusal would shape the future governance of the empire.
events.name: Gratian refuses the title of Eastern Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In a significant political and religious move, Emperor Gratian renounced the title of Pontifex Maximus, which had been a symbol of pagan authority in Rome. This act marked a shift towards Christianity as the dominant religion in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Gratian renounces the title Pontifex Maximus

events.enhanced_description: During this period, Britain faced relentless raids from various barbarian tribes, leading to significant instability and decline in Roman control over the region. These incursions contributed to the eventual withdrawal of Roman forces from Britain.
events.name: Britain is forced to endure fierce Barbarian raids

events.enhanced_description: Niall, a prominent figure in Irish history, ascended to the position of High King of Ireland, a title that would solidify his power and influence over the various tribes of the island. His reign is often associated with the expansion of Irish influence and the establishment of early Christian missions.
events.name: Niall becomes High King of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: King Shapur II of the Persian Empire died after a remarkable 69-year reign, during which he expanded the empire's territories and founded the city of Nishapur. His death marked a significant transition in Persian leadership as his brother Ardashir II ascended to the throne.
events.name: Death of King Shapur II

events.enhanced_description: During this time, Buddhism was officially recognized as a state religion, reflecting its growing influence and the patronage it received from rulers. This declaration helped to solidify Buddhism's role in the cultural and spiritual life of the region.
events.name: Buddhism is declared to be a state religion

events.enhanced_description: The War of the Feishui, a significant conflict in ancient China, took place during this year, showcasing the ongoing struggles for power among various factions. This war had lasting implications for the political landscape of the region.
events.name: The War of the Feishui is fought in China

events.enhanced_description: Yax Nuun Ayiin (I) ascended to power as the ruler of Tikal, one of the most significant city-states of the Maya civilization. His reign marked an important period in the history of Maya politics and culture.
events.name: Yax Nuun Ayiin (I) becomes ruler of Tikal

events.enhanced_description: Gregory Nazianzus was appointed as the Patriarch of Constantinople, a pivotal role in the early Christian church. His tenure was marked by conflict, including an attack by heretical mobs, reflecting the intense theological disputes of the time.
events.name: Gregory Nazianzus becomes Patriarch of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: John Chrysostom, a prominent early Church Father, authored a significant work focused on the Christian education of children. His writings contributed to the development of Christian pedagogy and moral instruction.
events.name: John Chrysostom writes a book on the Christian education of children

events.enhanced_description: The Edict of Thessalonica was a pivotal decree issued by Theodosius I, along with co-emperors Gratian and Valentinian II, declaring trinitarian Christianity as the official state religion of the Roman Empire. This edict effectively marginalized Arianism and set the stage for the Christianization of the empire.
events.name: Edict of Thessalonica

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move, the Roman Empire began integrating its former enemies, including Germans, Sarmatians, and Huns, into its military service. This decision marked a significant shift in the dynamics of power within the empire and allowed barbarian leaders to gain influence.
events.name: Integration of barbarian leaders into Roman service

events.enhanced_description: Theodosius I made his formal entry, or adventus, into Constantinople, marking a significant moment in his reign. This event symbolized his consolidation of power and the importance of the city as the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire.
events.name: Theodosius I's adventus into Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: Queen Mavia, leading her Saracen forces, achieved a notable victory against the Roman army in southern Syria. This battle underscored the challenges faced by the Roman Empire in maintaining control over its territories amidst rising local powers.
events.name: Queen Mavia defeats the Roman army

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Theodosius I was baptized, marking a significant personal and political commitment to Christianity. His conversion had profound implications for the Roman Empire, influencing its religious policies and alignment.
events.name: Emperor Theodosius I is baptized

events.enhanced_description: Fritigern, the Visigothic chieftain, died after a campaign of devastation across the Balkans, leading to the ascension of his rival Athanaric as king of the entire Gothic nation. This transition marked a pivotal moment in Gothic leadership and their interactions with the Roman Empire.
events.name: Death of Fritigern and rise of Athanaric

events.enhanced_description: Chandragupta II expanded his empire through the annexation of western provinces, enhancing trade relations with Europe and Egypt. This expansion played a crucial role in the economic and cultural exchanges of the time.
events.name: Chandragupta II's annexation of western provinces

events.enhanced_description: Neolithic seafarers, led by Hotu Matu'a, began to occupy and fortify Easter Island, establishing one of the most remote human settlements in the world. This early colonization laid the groundwork for the island's unique cultural and historical development.
events.name: Occupation of Easter Island by Neolithic seafarers

events.enhanced_description: During this period, significant advancements in mathematics and astronomy were made in India, with important texts being composed in Sanskrit. These works contributed to the foundation of mathematical concepts and astronomical observations that would influence future generations.
events.name: Important works on mathematics and astronomy are written in Sanskrit

events.enhanced_description: Ticonius, a North African theologian, authored a commentary on the Book of Revelation, contributing to the early Christian understanding of eschatology. His insights provided a framework for interpreting biblical prophecy during a time of theological turmoil.
events.name: Ticonius writes a commentary on the Bible's Book of Revelation

events.enhanced_description: A significant cathedral was constructed in Trier, Germany, reflecting the growing influence of Christianity in the region. This architectural achievement symbolized the establishment of Christian worship and community in the heart of the Roman Empire.
events.name: A cathedral is built in Trier

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Saragossa convened, where bishops from Spain and Aquitaine condemned the teachings of Priscillianism, a movement considered heretical by the mainstream church. This council was part of the broader struggle against heresy within early Christianity.
events.name: The Council of Saragossa

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Gratian made the pivotal decision to relocate the capital of the Western Roman Empire to Mediolanum (modern-day Milan). This move was influenced by his Christian beliefs and marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the empire.
events.name: Emperor Gratian moves the capital to Mediolanum

events.enhanced_description: In recognition of Emperor Gratian's establishment of a bishopric, the Gallic city of Cularo was renamed Gratianopolis, which would later become known as Grenoble. This renaming reflected the intertwining of political and religious authority during Gratian's reign.
events.name: Cularo is renamed Gratianopolis

events.enhanced_description: Athanaric, the Visigothic chieftain, made history by becoming the first foreign king to visit Constantinople. His visit included negotiations with Emperor Theodosius I, resulting in a peace treaty that recognized the Goths as foederati, integrating them into the Roman military structure.
events.name: Athanaric visits Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 381 AD, the Sciri and Huns launched a coordinated attack against the Roman Empire along the lower Danubian frontier, challenging the authority of Emperor Theodosius I. This incursion was part of the larger context of barbarian invasions that pressured the Roman borders during this period.
events.name: The Sciri together with the Huns attack along Rome's lower Danubian frontier

events.enhanced_description: The First Council of Constantinople, convened by Emperor Theodosius I in 381 AD, aimed to affirm and extend the Nicene Creed while denouncing Arianism and Apollinarism. This ecumenical council played a crucial role in shaping Christian doctrine and the authority of the Church.
events.name: First Council of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 381 AD, the Council of Aquileia, led by Ambrose, resulted in the deposition of Arian bishops Palladius of Ratiaria and Secundianus of Singidunum. This event underscored the ongoing conflict between Arianism and Nicene Christianity within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Council of Aquileia

events.enhanced_description: In 381 AD, Flavian succeeded Meletius as the Patriarch of Antioch, marking a significant transition in the leadership of one of the early Christian centers. This change occurred during a period of theological disputes and political challenges within the Church.
events.name: Flavian succeeds Meletius as Patriarch of Antioch

events.enhanced_description: In 381 AD, Timothy became the Patriarch of Alexandria, succeeding Peter II. This leadership change occurred amidst significant theological debates and the consolidation of Christian doctrine in the region.
events.name: Timothy succeeds Peter II as Patriarch of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: In 381 AD, Nectarius succeeded Gregory Nazianzus as the Archbishop of Constantinople, taking on a pivotal role in the early Christian Church during a time of doctrinal conflict and political intrigue.
events.name: Nectarius succeeds Gregory Nazianzus as Archbishop of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 381 AD, John Chrysostom was ordained as a deacon in Antioch, marking the beginning of his significant ecclesiastical career. His later contributions to Christian theology and homiletics would earn him the title 'Chrysostom', meaning 'Golden Mouth'.
events.name: John Chrysostom becomes a deacon

events.enhanced_description: In 382 AD, Emperor Theodosius I ordered General Saturninus to negotiate a peace treaty with the Visigoths, allowing them to settle south of the Danube as foederati. This treaty was significant in establishing a temporary peace and integrating the Visigoths into the Roman military structure.
events.name: Emperor Theodosius I commands his general Saturninus to conclude a peace treaty with the Visigoths

events.enhanced_description: In 382 AD, Emperor Gratian made a significant political statement by refusing the divine attributes associated with the Imperial cult and removing the Altar of Victory from the Senate. This act reflected the growing influence of Christianity in Roman politics.
events.name: Emperor Gratian refuses the divine attributes of the Imperial cult

events.enhanced_description: In 382 AD, the Council of Rome, under Pope Damasus I, established the Biblical canon for the Catholic Church, commissioning a revision of the Vetus Latina that would eventually lead to the Vulgate. This council was pivotal in defining the scriptures recognized by the Church.
events.name: The Council of Rome establishes Biblical canon in the Catholic Church

events.enhanced_description: In 382 AD, the Council of Rome adopted Trinitarianism as a core doctrine, condemning Apollinarism. This decision was part of the broader theological battles of the time, reflecting the Church's efforts to unify Christian beliefs.
events.name: The same council adopts Trinitarianism as doctrine, condemning Apollinarism

events.enhanced_description: In 382 AD, John Chrysostom delivered his first sermons emphasizing the virginity of Mary, contributing to the theological discourse surrounding her role in Christianity. His eloquence and theological insights would later establish him as a prominent Church Father.
events.name: The first sermons declaring the virginity of Mary are given by John Chrysostom

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, Niall of the Nine Hostages was recognized as the first High King of Ireland, a title that symbolized his dominance over various tribes. His reign marked the beginning of a more centralized authority in early Irish history.
events.name: Niall of the Nine Hostages becomes the first High King of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, Hadrian's Wall, the northern frontier of the Roman Empire in Britain, was reportedly overrun by the Picts, leading to its decline and eventual ruin. This event highlighted the increasing pressures faced by Roman Britain from northern tribes.
events.name: Hadrian's Wall is overrun by the Picts

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, the Roman legions withdrew from Wales, marking a significant retreat from their control over the region. This departure signaled the beginning of the end for Roman influence in Britain.
events.name: The Romans leave the region of Wales

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, Arcadius was elevated to the position of Emperor, becoming a key figure in the Eastern Roman Empire. His reign would be marked by challenges, including internal strife and external threats.
events.name: Arcadius is elevated to Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, Roman troops in Britain proclaimed Magnus Maximus as Emperor, leading him to cross to the continent and establish Trier as his capital. This event marked a significant power shift within the Roman Empire and set the stage for further conflicts.
