events.name: Roman troops in Britain proclaim Magnus Maximus Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, Emperor Gratian was assassinated in Lugdunum (modern-day Lyon), leaving a power vacuum and a young widow, Laeta. His death marked a turning point in the political landscape of the Roman Empire, particularly affecting the allegiance of provinces.
events.name: Emperor Gratian is assassinated at Lugdunum

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, Emperor Theodosius I ceded the provinces of Dacia and Macedonia to Valentinian II, recognizing Magnus Maximus as Augustus. This political maneuver was part of the complex power dynamics within the Roman Empire during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Emperor Theodosius I cedes Dacia and Macedonia to Valentinian II

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, Emperor Theodosius I dispatched Flavius Stilicho to the Persian court of King Shapur III in Ctesiphon to negotiate a peace settlement regarding the partition of Armenia. This diplomatic effort was crucial in maintaining stability along the eastern frontier of the Empire.
events.name: Theodosius I sends Flavius Stilicho as an envoy to the Persian court

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, the Jin Dynasty achieved a decisive victory over the Former Qin dynasty at the Battle of Feishui in Anhui. This battle was a pivotal moment in the struggle for power during the Sixteen Kingdoms period in China.
events.name: Battle of Feishui

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, King Ardashir II of Persia died after a brief four-year reign, leading to the ascension of his son, Shapur III. This transition marked a significant moment in the Sasanian Empire's history.
events.name: King Ardashir II dies after a 4-year reign

events.enhanced_description: The First Council of Constantinople, convened by Emperor Theodosius I, aimed to affirm and extend the Nicene Creed while denouncing Arianism and Apollinarism. This ecumenical council played a crucial role in shaping Christian doctrine and the authority of the Church.
events.name: First Council of Constantinople (some authorities date this council to 381)

events.enhanced_description: In 383 AD, Emperor Theodosius I ordered the banishment of Eunomius of Cyzicus to Moesia, reflecting the ongoing theological conflicts within the Church and Theodosius's commitment to Nicene orthodoxy.
events.name: By the order of Theodosius I, Eunomius of Cyzicus is banished to Moesia

events.enhanced_description: In 383 BC, the Spartan commander Phoebidas seized the opportunity presented by civil unrest in Thebes to infiltrate the city. Once inside, he captured the Cadmeia, the citadel of Thebes, and established a pro-Spartan government, leading to the exile of many anti-Spartan leaders, although Epaminondas remained.
events.name: Phoebidas Takes Thebes

events.enhanced_description: In 383 BC, the Babylonian calendar was reformed to incorporate a lunar cycle, aligning the months with the phases of the moon. This change was significant for agricultural and religious practices in ancient Babylonian society.
events.name: Introduction of the Lunar Calendar in Babylon

events.enhanced_description: The Second Buddhist Council was convened in 383 BC by King Kalasoka in Vaisali, aiming to address various issues within the Buddhist community and to preserve the teachings of the Buddha. This council played a crucial role in the development of Buddhist doctrine and monastic discipline.
events.name: Second Buddhist Council

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, Magnus Maximus elevated his son Flavius Victor to the rank of Augustus, solidifying his family's power within the Roman Empire. This act was part of the broader political maneuvers during a time of fragmentation and conflict.
events.name: Magnus Maximus elevates his son Flavius Victor to the rank of Augustus

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, Magnus Maximus returned to Britain to assist the Roman army against barbarian raids that had intensified following his earlier withdrawal of troops to the continent. His return was part of the broader struggle to maintain Roman control over the province amidst increasing external pressures.
events.name: Magnus Maximus returns to Britain

events.enhanced_description: The Forum of Theodosius, also known as the Forum of the Bull, was constructed in Constantinople around 384 AD. This monumental complex served as a central public space, reflecting the grandeur of the Roman Empire and the authority of Emperor Theodosius I.
events.name: The Forum of Theodosius is built

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, Quintus Aurelius Symmachus was appointed as the urban prefect of Rome, a significant political position in the late Roman Empire. His tenure was marked by efforts to maintain the traditional Roman religious practices amidst the growing influence of Christianity.
events.name: Quintus Aurelius Symmachus becomes urban prefect of Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, an edict issued by Theodosius I led to the closure of pagan temples in the Nile Valley, marking a significant moment in the Christianization of the Roman Empire. This action reflected the emperor's commitment to establishing Christianity as the dominant faith.
events.name: Theodosius I closes pagan temples in Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, Stilicho, a prominent general of the Western Roman Empire, married Serena, the adopted niece of Emperor Theodosius I. This marriage strengthened political ties and alliances within the imperial court.
events.name: Stilicho marries Serena

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, King Shapur III of Persia signed a treaty with Emperor Theodosius I, which divided Armenia into two vassal kingdoms. This treaty established a period of relative peace and cooperation between the Roman Empire and Persia for the next 36 years.
events.name: King Shapur III signs a treaty with Theodosius I

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, King Chimnyu ascended to the throne of Baekje, an ancient Korean kingdom. He welcomed the Indian Buddhist monk Marananta into his court, later declaring Buddhism the official religion of his kingdom, which significantly influenced Korean culture.
events.name: King Chimnyu ascends to the throne of Baekje

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, Gogugyang ascended to the throne of Goguryeo, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His rule marked a significant period in the kingdom's history, characterized by military expansion and cultural development.
events.name: Gogugyang becomes ruler of Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Fei River in 384 AD saw the numerically inferior Eastern Jin army defeat the forces of Former Qin, preserving the Jin state in southern China. This victory was pivotal in altering the balance of power in the region and led to the eventual downfall of Former Qin.
events.name: The Battle of Fei River

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, Pope Siricius succeeded Damasus I as the 38th pope of the Roman Catholic Church. His papacy was marked by the assertion of papal authority and the promotion of clerical celibacy.
events.name: Pope Siricius succeeds Damasus I

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, Jerome, a prominent Christian scholar, wrote his celebrated letter 'De custodia virginitatis' to Eustochium, emphasizing the vow of virginity. At this time, he had also completed his Vulgate translation of the Gospels, which would have a lasting impact on Christian theology.
events.name: Jerome writes letter to Eustochium

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, Ambrosius, the Bishop of Milan, refused the request of Empress Justina to build a church in Milan for Arian worship. This incident highlighted the growing tensions between Arianism and Nicene Christianity during this period.
events.name: Ambrosius refuses Empress Justina's request

events.enhanced_description: In 384 AD, a synod was convened in Bordeaux, France, to address various ecclesiastical matters. This synod was part of the broader efforts to consolidate Christian doctrine and address heretical teachings.
events.name: A synod is held in Bordeaux

events.enhanced_description: Around 384 AD, Egeria, a Gallic woman, concluded her Christian pilgrimage to the Holy Land. Her narrative, the Itinerarium Egeriae, is considered one of the earliest surviving writings by a woman in Western European culture, providing valuable insights into early Christian practices.
events.name: Egeria concludes her pilgrimage

events.enhanced_description: In 384 BC, the Athenian orator Lysias delivered a powerful speech during the Olympiad, criticizing the Greek states for their subjugation under the Syracusan tyrant Dionysius I and the Persian Empire. His words highlighted the political tensions and the struggle for autonomy among the Greek city-states.
events.name: Lysias Rebukes Greeks

events.enhanced_description: In 384 BC, Greek settlers founded the colony of Pharos at the site of modern-day Stari Grad on the island of Hvar, overcoming local Iadasinoi warriors. This settlement marked an important expansion of Greek influence in the Adriatic region.
events.name: Foundation of Pharos Colony

events.enhanced_description: In 385 AD, the Roman synod exiled Jerome, a significant Christian scholar, due to his incorporation of ideas from Cicero into his teachings. This exile led him to travel to Egypt, Bethlehem, and Jerusalem, where he would continue his influential work on the Bible.
events.name: The Roman synod exiles Jerome

events.enhanced_description: In 385 AD, Jinsa ascended to the throne as the 16th king of Baekje, an ancient Korean kingdom. His reign contributed to the cultural and political development of Baekje during a crucial period in Korean history.
events.name: Jinsa of Baekje becomes king

events.enhanced_description: In 385 AD, Ammianus Marcellinus began writing a comprehensive history covering the years AD 96-378, modeled after the works of Tacitus. His writings provide critical insights into the late Roman Empire and its challenges.
events.name: Ammianus Marcellinus begins writing history

events.enhanced_description: In 385 AD, the Serapeum of Alexandria, one of the largest Greek temples in Egypt, was destroyed by a Christian mob. This event marked a significant moment in the decline of paganism and the rise of Christianity in the region.
events.name: The Serapeum of Alexandria is destroyed

events.enhanced_description: In 385 AD, Theophilus was appointed as the Patriarch of Alexandria, a position of great influence in the early Christian church. His tenure was marked by significant theological disputes and the consolidation of Christian authority in Egypt.
events.name: Theophilus becomes Patriarch of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: In 385 AD, Pope Siricius issued the Directa Decretal, which proclaimed the primacy of the Roman see and emphasized the obligation of celibacy for priests. This decree reinforced the authority of the papacy in the early church.
events.name: Pope Siricius issues the Directa Decretal

events.enhanced_description: In 385 AD, Priscillian, a Spanish bishop, was accused of Manichaeism and magic, leading to his execution by beheading at Trier. This event marked him as the first person in Christian history to be executed for heresy, highlighting the tensions within early Christianity.
events.name: Priscillian is executed at Trier

events.enhanced_description: In 385 AD, Aurelios Zopyros became the last reported athlete to compete in the Ancient Olympic Games, winning in the event of junior boxing (pankration). His victory marked the end of an era for the Olympic Games, which would not be held again for centuries.
events.name: Aurelios Zopyros at the Ancient Olympic Games

events.enhanced_description: In 385 BC, Jason of Pherae rose to power as the tyrant of Thessaly, consolidating control over the region and influencing Greek politics. His rule was marked by military campaigns and attempts to unify Thessaly under his leadership.
events.name: Jason of Pherae Becomes Tyrant

events.enhanced_description: In 385 BC, Dionysius I of Syracuse sought to restore Alcetas I to the throne of Epirus, reflecting the complex political dynamics and power struggles in the region during this period. This attempt was part of Dionysius's broader ambitions to expand his influence.
events.name: Dionysius I Attempts Restoration of Alcetas I

events.enhanced_description: In 385 BC, Bardyllis ascended to the throne as king of Illyria, establishing the Bardyllian Dynasty. His reign marked significant developments in Illyrian power and territorial expansion in the Balkans.
events.name: Bardyllis Becomes King of Illyria

events.enhanced_description: In 385 BC, Mantinea was destroyed by Spartan forces along with their Theban allies. This event underscored the ongoing conflicts between the city-states of Greece and the military dominance of Sparta during this period.
events.name: Destruction of Mantinea by Sparta

events.enhanced_description: In 385 BC, the philosopher Plato established his Academy in Athens, a pioneering institution dedicated to the study of philosophy, mathematics, and sciences. This marked a significant development in the history of education and intellectual thought in the Western world.
events.name: Plato Forms His Academy

events.enhanced_description: In 385 BC, the philosopher Democritus proposed that the Milky Way is composed of numerous stars, contributing to early astronomical thought. His ideas laid the groundwork for future explorations of the cosmos.
events.name: Democritus Announces Composition of the Milky Way

events.enhanced_description: In 386 AD, Emperor Theodosius I signed a peace treaty with King Shapur III of Persia, which divided Armenia into two vassal kingdoms. This treaty established a long-lasting peace between the Roman Empire and Persia, significantly influencing regional politics.
events.name: Theodosius I signs peace treaty with Shapur III

events.enhanced_description: In 386 AD, the Greuthungi crossed the Danube River to raid Roman garrisons on the northern frontier. They were met by a well-armed Roman fleet, resulting in a disastrous defeat for the raiders, with many being killed or captured.
events.name: Greuthungi raid Roman garrisons

events.enhanced_description: In 386 AD, Magnus Maximus invaded Italy, targeting Novara for its support of his rival, Valentinian II. This military action underscored the political instability within the Western Roman Empire during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Magnus Maximus invades Italy

events.enhanced_description: In 386, Emperor Theodosius I initiated the reconstruction of the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, a significant Christian site that honors Saint Paul the Apostle. This rebuilding effort was part of a broader movement to establish and reinforce Christian architecture and worship spaces throughout the Roman Empire.

locations.historical_name: Basilica di San Paolo fuori le Mura
locations.name: Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls

events.name: Theodosius I begins to rebuild the present-day Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls

events.enhanced_description: In 386, a monumental column was erected in Constantinople to honor Emperor Theodosius I, featuring reliefs that celebrated his military victories over barbarian tribes in the Balkans. This column served not only as a tribute to Theodosius but also as a symbol of imperial power and the city's growing significance.
events.name: A column is constructed at Constantinople in honour of Theodosius I

events.enhanced_description: The Northern Wei Dynasty was established in 386 by the Tuoba clan of the Xianbei tribe, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in northern China. Under the rule of the young emperor Dao Wu Di, the dynasty became known for its strong support of Buddhism and efforts to integrate various cultures within its territory.
events.name: The Northern Wei Dynasty begins in China

events.enhanced_description: In 386, Saint Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan, became a prominent defender of the Catholic Church's rights against state interference. His advocacy for the church's autonomy highlighted the growing tensions between ecclesiastical authority and imperial power during this period of religious transformation.
events.name: Saint Ambrose defends the rights of the Catholic Church with respect to those of the State

events.enhanced_description: In 386, John Chrysostom was ordained as a presbyter in Antioch, where he began to write influential homilies, including 'Adversus Iudaeos,' which addressed Jewish practices and beliefs. His eloquent preaching and theological insights would later earn him the title of 'Chrysostom,' meaning 'Golden Mouth.'
events.name: John Chrysostom becomes a presbyter; he also writes eight Homilies entitled "Adversus Iudaeos" ("Against the Jews")

events.enhanced_description: In 386, Augustine of Hippo experienced a profound conversion to Christianity after hearing a sermon on the life of Saint Anthony. This pivotal moment led him to abandon his previous lifestyle and ultimately become one of the most influential theologians in Christian history.
events.name: Augustine converts to Christianity

events.enhanced_description: By 386, the Roman Empire's efforts to suppress pagan practices were increasingly met with resistance, highlighting the growing tensions between the traditional pagan beliefs and the rising influence of Christianity. This struggle marked a significant cultural shift within the empire.
events.name: The fight in the Roman Empire against anti-pagan laws becomes increasingly futile

events.enhanced_description: In 386, the Sumela Monastery was established in the Pontic Mountains of Asia Minor, dedicated to the Virgin Mary. This site became a significant center for Orthodox Christian worship and pilgrimage, renowned for its stunning frescoes and dramatic cliffside location.
events.name: Sumela Monastery is established in Asia Minor

events.enhanced_description: In 386 BC, following the Peace of Antalcidas, Persia shifted its focus from Spartan conflicts to consolidating power in Cyprus and Egypt. The military efforts, led by King Evagoras of Cyprus and the Greek general Chabrias, faced prolonged resistance and challenges.
events.name: Persia Turns to Cyprus and Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 386 BC, Dionysius I of Syracuse expanded his influence and trade networks to the Adriatic Sea, establishing colonies in key locations such as Adria, Ancona, and Issa. This expansion was part of his broader strategy to enhance Syracuse's power in the region.
events.name: Dionysius I Expands Influence to the Adriatic

events.enhanced_description: In 386 BC, the State of Zhao founded the city of Handan, which would become an important cultural and political center in ancient China. This establishment played a significant role in the development of the region during the Warring States period.
events.name: Foundation of Handan by Zhao

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 387, Emperor Theodosius I raised taxes in Antioch, leading to widespread discontent among the populace. This unrest culminated in a violent riot, prompting Theodosius to dispatch troops to restore order and enforce his authority.
events.name: Spring – Emperor Theodosius I increases the taxes in Antioch

events.enhanced_description: In 387, Magnus Maximus, the usurper emperor of the Western Roman Empire, launched an invasion of Italy, forcing the young Emperor Valentinian II to flee Rome. This conflict underscored the political instability and power struggles within the Roman Empire during this period.
events.name: Magnus Maximus, usurping emperor of the West, invades Italy

events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 387, Emperor Theodosius I took the young Valentinian II under his protection, solidifying his political alliance by marrying Valentinian's sister, Flavia Galla. This union aimed to stabilize the Western Roman Empire amidst ongoing conflicts and power struggles.

image.caption: Bust of Theodosius I, found at Aphrodisias, Aydın, Turkey.

events.name: Winter – The widowed emperor Theodosius I takes Valentinian II under his protection, and marries his sister Flavia Galla

events.enhanced_description: In 387, King Shapur III of Persia signed the Peace of Acilisene with Emperor Theodosius I, which resulted in the partitioning of Armenia into two kingdoms. This treaty established Armenia as a vassal state under both the Roman Empire and Persia, reflecting the geopolitical complexities of the era.

image.caption: Map of the Roman–Sasanian frontier after the treaty of 384.

events.name: Peace of Acilisene: King Shapur III signs a treaty with Theodosius I

events.enhanced_description: In 387, Oribase, a Greek physician, published a significant treatise addressing medical conditions such as paralysis and bleeding. His work contributed to the understanding of medical practices in the Roman Empire and influenced subsequent generations of physicians.
events.name: Oribase, Greek doctor, publishes a treatise on paralysis and bleedings

events.enhanced_description: On Easter Vigil in 387, Augustine of Hippo was baptized by Saint Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan, marking a transformative moment in his spiritual journey. This event not only solidified Augustine's commitment to Christianity but also established Ambrose as a pivotal figure in the early Church.
events.name: Augustine is baptized on Easter Vigil by Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Antalcidas, also known as the King's Peace, was a treaty brokered by Persian King Artaxerxes II in 387 BC. It established Persian control over the Asiatic mainland and Cyprus while granting autonomy to other Greek states, significantly influencing Greek political dynamics and marking a pivotal moment in the power struggle among Greek city-states.
events.name: Peace of Antalcidas

events.enhanced_description: The Corinthian War, a conflict involving several Greek city-states against Sparta, came to an end in 387 BC. This resolution marked a significant shift in the balance of power in ancient Greece, leading to the establishment of the King's Peace.
events.name: End of the Corinthian War

events.enhanced_description: In 387 BC, under the threat of Spartan military intervention, Thebes disbanded its league, a significant political shift in the region. This decision led to the reintegration of Corinth into Sparta's Peloponnesian League, further consolidating Spartan power in Greece.
events.name: Thebes Disbands its League

events.enhanced_description: In 387 BC, Plato founded the Platonic Academy in Athens, which became one of the earliest institutions of higher learning in the Western world. The Academy was notable for being the place where Plato taught Aristotle, shaping the foundations of Western philosophy and science.
events.name: Founding of the Platonic Academy

events.enhanced_description: In 387 BC, with the assistance of the Lucanians, Dionysius I of Syracuse launched a devastating campaign against the territories of Thurii, Crotone, and Locri in Southern Italy. This military success allowed him to solidify his power in the region and expand his influence further into the Adriatic Sea by founding new colonies.
events.name: Dionysius I's Campaign in Southern Italy

events.enhanced_description: In 387 BC, Plato was forced to leave Syracuse after expressing his views too freely under the rule of Dionysius I. This experience influenced Plato's philosophical writings and led him to return to Athens, where he established a school that would become central to Western philosophy.
events.name: Plato's Expulsion from Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: Following the devastating invasion by the Gauls under Brennus, 387 BC marked the beginning of Rome's extensive rebuilding efforts. This period was crucial for the city's recovery and eventual rise as a dominant power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Rebuilding of Rome after Gaul Invasion

events.enhanced_description: In 387 BC, Marcus Furius Camillus introduced the Capitoline Games (Ludi Capitolini) in honor of Jupiter Capitolinus. This festival commemorated the survival of Rome's Capitol during the Gaul invasion, marking a significant cultural event in the city's history.
events.name: Introduction of the Capitoline Games

events.enhanced_description: In 388, the Battle of the Save took place near Emona, where Emperor Theodosius I achieved a decisive victory over Magnus Maximus. This battle was crucial in restoring Valentinian II to the throne and reaffirming Theodosius's control over the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Battle of the Save: Emperor Theodosius I defeats Magnus Maximus near Emona (modern Slovenia)

events.enhanced_description: In 388, a coalition of rebellious Franks led by Marcomer, Sunno, and Genobaud invaded the Roman Empire, targeting the city of Cologne. Their incursion posed a significant threat to Roman territories, prompting military responses from the empire to defend its borders.

events.name: Frankish invasion of 388: Rebellious Franks led by Marcomer, Sunno and Genobaud invade the Roman Empire with plunder and threaten Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium (Cologne)

events.enhanced_description: In 388, Magnus Maximus surrendered to Theodosius I at Aquileia, leading to his execution. This event marked the end of Maximus's challenge to Theodosius's authority and solidified Theodosius's position as the sole ruler of the Roman Empire.

image.caption: Aureus of Magnus Maximus bearing the inscription “DN MAG MAXIMVS PF AVG.”

events.name: Magnus Maximus surrenders at Aquileia, and is executed

events.enhanced_description: In 388, King Shapur III of Persia passed away after a reign marked by the partitioning of Armenia with the Roman Empire. His death led to the ascension of his son Bahram IV, who would continue the Sassanid dynasty's legacy.
events.name: King Shapur III dies after a reign in which he has partitioned Armenia with the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 388, Emperor Chandragupta II of the Gupta Empire initiated military campaigns against the Shaka Dynasty in western India. This conflict was part of Chandragupta's broader strategy to expand his empire and consolidate power in the region.
events.name: Emperor Chandragupta II, ruler of the Gupta Empire, begins a war against the Shaka Dynasty in West India

events.enhanced_description: In 388, Paternus was appointed as the bishop of Braga, a significant ecclesiastical position in the region. His leadership contributed to the spread of Christianity in what is now Portugal.
events.name: Paternus becomes bishop of the Episcopal see of Braga (Portugal)

events.enhanced_description: In 388, Isaac was appointed as the Catholicos of the Armenian Apostolic Church, becoming the spiritual leader of the Armenian Christians. His leadership played a crucial role in the development of the church and its influence in the region.
events.name: Isaac, age 50, is named Catholicos (spiritual head) of the Armenian Apostolic Church

events.enhanced_description: In 388, Jerome relocated to Bethlehem, where he chose to live as a hermit. This period of solitude allowed him to focus on his scholarly work, including the translation of the Bible into Latin, known as the Vulgate.
events.name: Jerome moves to Palestine, where he spends the rest of his life as a hermit near Bethlehem

events.enhanced_description: In 388, a violent incident occurred in Callinicum when a group of Christians stormed the local synagogue, reflecting the rising tensions between different religious communities in the Roman Empire. This event highlighted the growing conflicts as Christianity became more dominant.
events.name: A group of Christians storms the synagogue of the city Callinicum (Syria), at the Euphrates

events.enhanced_description: In 388 BC, King Agesipolis I of Sparta led a military campaign against Argos, plundering its countryside without facing significant opposition. However, after receiving unfavorable omens, he chose to return to Sparta, reflecting the superstitious nature of Spartan leadership.
events.name: King Agesipolis I's Campaign against Argos

events.enhanced_description: In 388 BC, Athenian general Thrasybulus achieved a significant victory against Spartan forces on the island of Lesbos, aided by local Mytileneans. Despite his success, Thrasybulus was later killed by raiders from Aspendus, highlighting the dangers faced by military leaders during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Thrasybulus' Victory in Lesbos

events.enhanced_description: In 388 BC, Persian King Artaxerxes II formed an alliance with King Agesilaus II of Sparta in response to the perceived threat from Athenian imperial ambitions. This alliance also included support from Dionysius I of Syracuse, illustrating the complex political landscape of ancient Greece.
events.name: Alliance between Artaxerxes II and Agesilaus II

events.enhanced_description: In 388 BC, Athens secured a notable victory over Sparta, marking a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between these two powerful city-states. This victory contributed to the shifting balance of power in ancient Greece during this period.
events.name: Athenian Victory over Sparta

events.enhanced_description: In 388 BC, following the death of Socrates, Plato traveled to Syracuse at the invitation of Dionysius I's brother-in-law, Dion. This journey was significant as it represented Plato's engagement with the political landscape of Sicily and his philosophical pursuits beyond Athens.
events.name: Plato's Journey to Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: In 388 BC, Aristophanes' play 'Plutus' was performed in Athens, showcasing the playwright's sharp wit and commentary on wealth and society. This performance contributed to the rich tradition of Greek theater and reflected the social dynamics of the time.
events.name: Performance of Aristophanes' Plutus

events.enhanced_description: In 389, a catastrophic fire consumed all pagan buildings in Alexandria, including the renowned library. This destruction marked a significant loss of cultural heritage and knowledge, reflecting the broader decline of paganism in the face of rising Christianity.
events.name: All pagan buildings in Alexandria, including the library, are destroyed by fire

events.enhanced_description: In 389 BC, a Spartan expeditionary force under King Agesilaus II crossed the Gulf of Corinth to attack Acarnania, a key ally of the anti-Spartan coalition. The campaign culminated in a pitched battle that resulted in a decisive victory for Agesilaus, reinforcing Spartan dominance in the region.
events.name: Agesilaus II's Expedition to Acarnania

events.enhanced_description: In 389 BC, Athenian general Thrasybulus led a naval campaign to levy tribute from Aegean cities and support Rhodes against Spartan influence. His successful capture of Byzantium and imposition of duties on ships passing through the Hellespont underscored Athens' continued maritime power during this period.
events.name: Thrasybulus' Campaign in the Aegean

events.enhanced_description: In response to threats from Akarnania, the city of Kalydon fortified its defenses by garrisoning troops from the Achaean League. This strategic move was aimed at deterring potential attacks and maintaining regional stability during a time of heightened tensions.
events.name: Due to threats of attack from Akarnania, Kalydon garrisons the Achaeans

events.enhanced_description: Isaeus, a prominent Athenian orator, delivered his earliest known speech titled 'Dicaeogenes'. This speech marked a significant contribution to the art of rhetoric in ancient Greece, showcasing Isaeus's skill in legal oratory and influencing future generations of speakers.
events.name: The orator Isaeus gives his earliest known speech, the Dicaeogenes

events.enhanced_description: In a decisive military engagement, Dionysius I of Syracuse led his forces to victory at the Battle of the Elleporus, resulting in the capture of the city of Kroton. This victory was part of Dionysius's broader campaign to expand his influence over southern Italy and assert Syracuse's dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Elleporus and the capture of Kroton by Dionysius I of Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: Wu Qi, the prime minister of the State of Chu, implemented a series of significant reforms aimed at reducing corruption and consolidating power within the state. His aggressive policies, however, led to widespread resentment among the aristocracy, ultimately culminating in his assassination.
