events.name: Wu Qi enacts reforms in the State of Chu

events.enhanced_description: The Zuo Zhuan, a historical text attributed to the blind historian Zuo Qiuming, is believed to have been compiled around this time. This work is crucial for understanding the history and culture of ancient China, providing insights into the events and philosophies of the Spring and Autumn period.
events.name: Compilation of the Zuo Zhuan

events.enhanced_description: In April 390, the citizens of Thessalonica erupted in violence following the arrest of a beloved charioteer, leading to the murder of Butheric, the military commander. In retaliation, Emperor Theodosius I ordered a brutal crackdown, resulting in the massacre of over 7,000 inhabitants, despite pleas for mercy from Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan.
events.name: April – Massacre of Thessalonica: Resentment among the citizens of Thessalonica (Macedonia) breaks out into violence after the arrest of a popular charioteer

events.enhanced_description: Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan, famously refused to celebrate a mass in the presence of Emperor Theodosius I until the emperor repented for the massacre he ordered in Thessalonica. This event highlighted the growing power of the church over the state, as Theodosius humbled himself before Ambrose in the cathedral, stripping off his royal purple as a sign of penitence.
events.name: Ambrose retires to Milan

events.enhanced_description: The Visigoths and Huns, under the leadership of Alaric, launched an invasion into Thrace, prompting a military response from Stilicho, a high-ranking Roman general. This conflict marked a significant escalation in the tensions between the Roman Empire and the barbarian tribes, foreshadowing the eventual fall of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Visigoths and Huns invade Thrace

events.enhanced_description: In a display of imperial power and cultural significance, Theodosius I transported an ancient Egyptian obelisk to the Hippodrome of Constantinople. This act not only symbolized the grandeur of the Roman Empire but also served to connect the city with its ancient past.
events.name: Theodosius I brings an obelisk to Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: Rudrasena II ascended to the throne of the Vakataka dynasty, succeeding his father Prthivisena I. His reign marked a significant period in Indian history, characterized by cultural and political developments, including his marriage to Prabhavatigupta, the daughter of the Gupta king Chandragupta II.
events.name: Rudrasena II of Vakataka succeeds his father

events.enhanced_description: The late Antiquity ivory diptych known as the Priestess of Bacchus documents the relationship between senators Quintus Aurelius Symmachus and Virius Nicomachus Flavianus. This exquisite piece of art commemorates their families' union and reflects the cultural richness of the period.
events.name: Priestess of Bacchus ivory diptych

events.enhanced_description: After completing the Latin translation of the New Testament, Jerome began his monumental task of translating the Old Testament. His work would go on to influence Christian theology and the development of the Latin Vulgate, which became the standard Bible for the Western Church.
events.name: Jerome begins translating the Old Testament

events.enhanced_description: The Kama Sutra, an ancient Indian text on love and relationships, was revised by the philosopher Vatsyayana. This work has been influential in both literature and the understanding of human sexuality, remaining a significant cultural artifact to this day.
events.name: The Kama Sutra is revised by Vatsyayana

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Allia marked a significant defeat for the Romans, as Brennus, a chieftain of the Senones, led a successful invasion of the city. The Romans were forced to pay a hefty ransom in gold to the Gauls to spare the city from further destruction, except for the Capitoline Hill, which remained under Roman control.
events.name: Battle of the Allia

events.enhanced_description: Pharaoh Hakor of Egypt forged a strategic tripartite alliance with Evagoras, the king of Cyprus, and Athens. This alliance aimed to strengthen their positions against common threats and enhance their political influence in the eastern Mediterranean during a time of shifting power dynamics.
events.name: Tripartite alliance between Hakor, Evagoras, and Athens

events.enhanced_description: The Temple of Asclepius, dedicated to the Greek god of healing, was constructed in Epidaurus, becoming a significant religious site. This temple not only served as a place of worship but also as a center for healing practices, attracting pilgrims from across the Greek world.
events.name: Construction of the Temple of Asclepius at Epidaurus

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Theodosius I declared Christianity the official state religion of the Roman Empire, leading to the closure of non-Christian temples and the disbanding of the Vestal Virgins. This pivotal moment marked a significant shift in the religious landscape of the empire and the rise of Christian dominance.
events.name: Theodosius I establishes Christianity as the state religion

events.enhanced_description: Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, the urban prefect of Rome, made a passionate plea to Emperor Theodosius I to reopen the pagan temples, advocating for the preservation of traditional cult practices. His efforts were met with strong opposition from Ambrose, reflecting the intense religious conflicts of the time.
events.name: Quintus Aurelius Symmachus pleads for traditional cult practices

events.enhanced_description: Saint Telemachus, a Christian monk, was stoned to death for attempting to stop a gladiatorial contest in Rome. His martyrdom is often cited as a pivotal moment in the decline of gladiatorial games and the rise of Christian values in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Saint Telemachus dies after being stoned to death

events.enhanced_description: In a significant battle, Heduohan, a chief of the Rouran, was defeated and killed by the Toba Northern Wei Dynasty. This defeat forced the surviving Rouran to move westward, led by Heduohan's son Shelun, marking a shift in power dynamics in Northern China.
events.name: Heduohan defeated in battle

events.enhanced_description: Gwanggaeto the Great ascended to the throne of Goguryeo, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His reign would later be marked by significant military conquests and territorial expansion, solidifying Goguryeo's power in the region.
events.name: Gwanggaeto the Great ascends to the throne

events.enhanced_description: The great Library of Alexandria, a center of knowledge and learning in the ancient world, was destroyed by flames, resulting in the loss of countless works, including significant scientific texts. This event marked a tragic turning point in the preservation of ancient knowledge and culture.
events.name: Library of Alexandria destroyed

events.enhanced_description: Under the orders of Emperor Theodosius I, Patriarch Theophilus led a campaign to destroy all pagan temples in Alexandria, including the Temple of Serapis. This act of iconoclasm was part of a broader movement to eradicate pagan practices and establish Christianity as the dominant faith.
events.name: Patriarch Theophilus destroys pagan temples

events.enhanced_description: Struthas, a Persian satrap, initiated an anti-Spartan policy that prompted the Spartans to dispatch their governor, Thibron, to Ionia. Thibron's campaign initially met with success, but he ultimately fell victim to an ambush, illustrating the volatile nature of Persian-Greek relations during this period.
events.name: Struthas's anti-Spartan policy and Thibron's campaign

events.enhanced_description: Evagoras of Salamis engaged in a fierce struggle against Persian forces for control of Cyprus. With the support of Athenian and Egyptian allies, he managed to extend his rule significantly, highlighting the geopolitical tensions in the region during this era.
events.name: Evagoras's struggle for control of Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: In a groundbreaking military engagement, Athenian general Iphicrates achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Lechaeum, employing a force primarily composed of light infantry. This battle marked a pivotal moment in military tactics, demonstrating the effectiveness of light troops against traditional hoplite formations.
events.name: Battle of Lechaeum

events.enhanced_description: General Iphicrates led a successful campaign against the cities of Phlius and Arcadia, decisively defeating their armies. His victories not only showcased Athenian military prowess but also set the stage for further territorial consolidation in the Peloponnese.
events.name: Iphicrates campaigns against Phlius and Arcadia

events.enhanced_description: Dionysius I of Syracuse initiated a campaign to extend his influence over the Greek cities of southern Italy, beginning with an unsuccessful siege of Rhegium. This military endeavor reflected his ambitions to expand Syracuse's power and control in the region.
events.name: Dionysius I's attempts to extend rule in southern Italy

events.enhanced_description: The Roman dictator Marcus Furius Camillus faced accusations of unfairly distributing the spoils from his victory at Veii, leading to his voluntary exile. This incident highlights the political tensions and challenges faced by leaders in the early Roman Republic.
events.name: Marcus Furius Camillus's exile

events.enhanced_description: In a critical diplomatic mission, Roman ambassadors, including Quintus Fabius Ambustus, were dispatched to negotiate with the Celtic chieftain Brennus, who was advancing on Rome. The mission escalated into conflict when the ambassadors were involved in a skirmish, leading to increased tensions between the Romans and the Gauls.
events.name: Roman ambassadors sent to Brennus

events.enhanced_description: Roman general Stilicho achieved a significant victory against the Visigoths and Huns in Thrace, a crucial moment in the ongoing conflict between the Roman Empire and barbarian tribes. Following the battle, Emperor Theodosius I allowed Alaric to remain free, requiring him to serve the empire as a foederati.
events.name: Stilicho defeats the Visigoths and Huns

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Valentinian II, at the young age of 21, was found dead under mysterious circumstances in his residence at Vienne while advancing against the Frankish usurper Arbogast. His untimely death marked a significant turning point in the power dynamics of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Emperor Valentinian II dies

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Valentinian II, Arbogast, a powerful general, nominated Eugenius, a Roman teacher of rhetoric, as the new emperor of the Western Roman Empire. This political maneuvering highlighted the instability and power struggles within the empire during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Arbogast nominates Eugenius as emperor

events.enhanced_description: Theodosius I became the last emperor to rule the entire Roman Empire, issuing edicts that reinforced the prohibition of pagan practices and the destruction of non-Christian temples. His reign marked the culmination of the Christianization of the empire and the decline of traditional Roman religious practices.
events.name: Theodosius I becomes the last emperor to rule the whole Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: Asin ascended to the throne of the Korean kingdom of Baekje, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His reign would contribute to the rich cultural and political history of the region during this period.
events.name: Asin becomes king of Baekje

events.enhanced_description: Struthas, a Persian general, is appointed by King Artaxerxes II to replace Tiribazus as the satrap of Sardis, aiming to implement an anti-Spartan policy during a tumultuous period in Greek history. This move reflects Persia's strategic interests in countering Spartan influence in the region.
events.name: Struthas Takes Command of Sardis

events.enhanced_description: In the context of the Corinthian War, Spartan ambassador Antalcidas seeks to sway the Persian satrap Tiribazus against the Athenian allies by revealing Conon's use of the Persian fleet to restore Athenian power. This diplomatic maneuvering highlights the intricate alliances and conflicts of the period, culminating in Conon's arrest by Tiribazus.
events.name: Spartan Diplomacy During the Corinthian War

events.enhanced_description: A peace conference convenes in Sparta, where Athenian orator Andocides and his colleagues attempt to negotiate an end to hostilities among the Greek city-states. The conference ultimately fails, leading to the exile of the Athenian ambassadors and the continuation of conflict.
events.name: Peace Conference in Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Dionysius I of Syracuse faces a renewed threat from Carthage as they launch a second expedition against him. In a strategic alliance with the Sicels, Dionysius successfully repels the Carthaginian forces led by Mago II, resulting in a favorable peace treaty for Syracuse.
events.name: Dionysius I's Conflict with Carthage

events.enhanced_description: The renowned orator and educator Isocrates founds a school of rhetoric on the island of Chios, contributing to the development of rhetorical education in ancient Greece. His teachings would influence generations of speakers and writers in the Hellenistic world.
events.name: Isocrates Establishes a Rhetoric School

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Theodosius I proclaimed his young son Honorius as co-ruler of the Western Roman Empire, a strategic move to secure his dynasty's future. This decision would have lasting implications for the governance of the empire as it faced increasing external pressures.
events.name: Theodosius I proclaims Honorius as co-ruler

events.enhanced_description: Theodosius I issued a decree demanding the destruction of pagan temples and holy sites throughout the Roman Empire, further solidifying the Christian faith's dominance. This act was part of a broader campaign against paganism and marked a significant turning point in the empire's religious landscape.
events.name: Theodosius I demands destruction of pagan temples

events.enhanced_description: In a decisive move to establish Christianity as the central cultural force, Theodosius I abolished the ancient Greek Olympic Games, which had been celebrated for nearly a millennium. This decision reflected the broader Christian policy of the time and marked the end of a significant cultural tradition.
events.name: Theodosius I abolishes the Greek Olympic Games

events.enhanced_description: Gao Zu succeeded Tai Zu as the emperor of the Later Qin Empire, continuing the legacy of his predecessor. This transition of power was crucial for the stability and governance of the empire during a time of significant change.
events.name: Gao Zu succeeds Tai Zu as emperor of the Later Qin Empire

events.enhanced_description: Chinese astronomers documented the appearance of a guest star, known as SN 393, marking a significant event in the history of astronomy. This observation contributed to the understanding of celestial phenomena in ancient China.
events.name: Chinese astronomers observe guest star SN 393

events.enhanced_description: The Synod of Hippo was a significant council hosted by the Church at Hippo Regius, where bishops approved a canon of Sacred Scripture that would correspond to the Roman Catholic Church. This event played a crucial role in the development of Christian doctrine and the establishment of the biblical canon.
events.name: Synod of Hippo

events.enhanced_description: Athenian general Conon, in collaboration with Persian satrap Pharnabazus, leads a naval expedition against the coast of Laconia, successfully capturing the strategically important island of Cythera. This operation marks a significant moment in the struggle for control over the Aegean Sea.
events.name: Conon and Pharnabazus Raid Laconia

events.enhanced_description: Pharnabazus provides Conon with resources to aid in the reconstruction of the Long Walls connecting Athens to its port at Piraeus, a project initiated by Thrasybulus. This strategic fortification enhances Athenian military capabilities and facilitates their resurgence in the region.
events.name: Rebuilding of the Long Walls

events.enhanced_description: Violence erupts in Corinth as the democratic faction, supported by Argos, clashes with the oligarchs. The ensuing conflict leads to the oligarchs seeking Spartan assistance while the democrats receive backing from Athens and Boeotia, highlighting the internal strife within Greek city-states.
events.name: Conflict in Corinth

events.enhanced_description: In a coordinated night attack, Spartan forces alongside exiled oligarchs successfully capture Lechaeum, the vital port of Corinth, defeating a local army that attempts to respond. This strategic victory underscores the ongoing power struggles in the region during the Corinthian War.
events.name: Spartan Seizure of Lechaeum

events.enhanced_description: Amyntas III ascends to the throne of Macedonia amidst political turmoil following the death of King Archelaus I. His reign marks a significant period in Macedonian history, setting the stage for future developments in the region.
events.name: Amyntas III Becomes King of Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of King Nepherites I, Egypt experiences a succession crisis as factions vie for control, backing either Muthis, the king's son, or Psammuthes. Ultimately, Psammuthes claims the throne but faces challenges to his rule.
events.name: Succession Crisis in Egypt

events.enhanced_description: Hakor successfully overthrows Psammuthes, claiming to be the grandson of Nepherites I, and establishes himself as King of Egypt. His rise to power marks the continuation of the 29th Dynasty amidst the political turmoil of the time.
events.name: Hakor Overthrows Psammuthes

events.enhanced_description: The comedic play 'The Ecclesiazusae' by Aristophanes is performed, showcasing the playwright's sharp wit and commentary on Athenian society and politics. This work reflects the cultural vibrancy of Athens during the classical period.
events.name: Performance of The Ecclesiazusae

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Frigidus was a decisive confrontation in which Emperor Theodosius I defeated the usurper Eugenius, solidifying his control over the Roman Empire. Theodosius's forces included a significant contingent of Visigoth federates led by Alaric, while the Frankish general Arbogast, who had supported Eugenius, ultimately took his own life after the defeat.
events.name: Battle of the Frigidus

events.enhanced_description: The Notitia Dignitatum is a crucial document that outlines the military organization of the late Roman Empire, detailing the deployment of approximately 200,000 soldiers along its borders and a reserve force of 50,000. This document reflects the increasing reliance on non-Roman soldiers from various Germanic tribes, indicating a significant shift in the empire's military structure.
events.name: Notitia Dignitatum

events.enhanced_description: During a harsh winter, the Huns crossed the frozen Danube River, launching devastating attacks on Gothic settlements. This incursion highlighted the vulnerability of the Roman Empire's northern frontier, as Theodosius I was unable to provide reinforcements from Italy to defend against the Huns.
events.name: Huns cross the frozen Danube

events.enhanced_description: The extinguishing of the sacred fire in Rome marked a significant moment in the decline of traditional Roman religious practices. This event symbolized the waning influence of the Vestal Virgins and the old pagan traditions in the face of the rising prominence of Christianity.
events.name: Sacred fire stops burning in Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Graffito of Esmet-Akhom represents the last known hieroglyphic inscription, marking the end of an era for ancient Egyptian writing. This inscription was found on the island of Philae, a significant religious site dedicated to the goddess Isis, indicating the gradual decline of traditional Egyptian culture.
events.name: Last hieroglyphic inscription

events.enhanced_description: Fu Chong, the last ruler of the Former Qin dynasty, was killed in battle against the forces of Western Qin, leading to the collapse of his regime. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics during the tumultuous period of the Sixteen Kingdoms in China.
events.name: Death of Fu Chong

events.enhanced_description: Epiphanius of Salamis launched a vehement attack against the followers of Origen, urging John II, the Bishop of Jerusalem, to condemn Origen's writings. This conflict highlights the theological disputes within early Christianity and the struggle for orthodoxy during this period.
events.name: Epiphanius of Salamis attacks Origen's followers

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Bagaï convened 310 Donatist bishops, reflecting the significant schism within Christianity in North Africa. This gathering was part of the ongoing conflict between the Donatists and the Catholic Church, which sought to unify Christian doctrine and practice.
events.name: Council of Bagaï

events.enhanced_description: The allies of Athens, Thebes, Corinth, and Argos assemble a large force at Corinth, leading to a confrontation with the Spartans at the Nemea River. The resulting Battle of Nemea sees a decisive Spartan victory, further solidifying their dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Nemea

events.enhanced_description: In a pivotal naval engagement, Athenian general Conon, Persian satrap Pharnabazus, and Evagoras of Salamis achieve a significant victory over Spartan forces at the Battle of Cnidus. This battle marks a turning point in the struggle for control of the Aegean Sea, diminishing Spartan influence.
events.name: Battle of Cnidus

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Coronea, the armies of Sparta, led by King Agesilaus II, faced off against their adversaries in Theban territory. The Spartans emerged victorious once again, solidifying their military prowess in the region before Agesilaus sailed back to Sparta with his forces.
events.name: Battle of Coronea

events.enhanced_description: The temple of Athena Alea in Tegea was burned down but was quickly rebuilt according to the designs of the renowned architect Scopas of Paros. This reconstruction marked a significant cultural revival in the region, showcasing the resilience and dedication of the Tegeans to their patron goddess.
events.name: Destruction and Reconstruction of the Temple of Athena Alea

events.enhanced_description: The ancient Greek Olympic Games, a series of athletic competitions held in honor of Zeus, came to an end in 394 AD when Emperor Theodosius I banned them as part of his efforts to promote Christianity and suppress pagan practices. This marked a significant cultural shift in the Roman Empire, as the games had been a central part of Greek culture for nearly a millennium.
events.name: End of the ancient Greek Olympic Games

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Theodosius I died in Milan at the age of 48, succumbing to a disease characterized by severe edema. His death resulted in the final division of the Roman Empire into Eastern and Western halves, with his sons Arcadius and Honorius assuming control over their respective territories.
events.name: Death of Theodosius I

events.enhanced_description: Arcadius married Aelia Eudoxia, the daughter of the Frankish general Flavius Bauto, without the consent of Rufinus, the Praetorian prefect of the East. This politically significant union would have implications for the power dynamics within the Eastern Roman Empire.
events.name: Marriage of Arcadius and Aelia Eudoxia

events.enhanced_description: Alaric I, the Visigothic leader, renounced his allegiance to Rome and was declared king, initiating a war against both halves of the Roman Empire. His campaign led to the devastation of Thrace and Macedonia, culminating in the imposition of tribute on Athens and a significant shift in the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Revolt of Alaric I

events.enhanced_description: Rufinus, the Praetorian prefect of the East, was assassinated by Gothic mercenaries under Gainas, marking a significant turning point in the power struggles within the Eastern Roman Empire. His death created a power vacuum that would have lasting implications for the region.
events.name: Murder of Rufinus

events.enhanced_description: Alaric I besieged Constantinople, the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, as part of his campaign against Roman authority. This siege was a critical moment in the conflict between the Visigoths and the Roman Empire, showcasing the vulnerability of the imperial capital.
events.name: Alaric besieges Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: Stilicho, the Roman general, arrived with his army to confront the Goths led by Alaric. However, political machinations led to the cancellation of his campaign against Alaric, reflecting the complex interplay of military and political power in the Eastern Roman Empire.
events.name: Stilicho arrives to fight the Goths

events.enhanced_description: The Goths, under the leadership of Alaric I, invaded and ravaged the regions of Thrace and Macedonia, imposing a tribute on Athens. This incursion marked a significant escalation in the conflict between the Visigoths and the Roman Empire, contributing to the empire's eventual decline.
events.name: Goths invade Thrace and Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Canhe Slope saw the Later Yan defeated by its former vassal, Northern Wei, during the Southern and Northern Dynasties period of China. This battle was part of the larger struggle for dominance among the various states in northern China.
events.name: Battle of Canhe Slope

events.enhanced_description: The Huns initiated a large-scale invasion of the Eastern Roman Empire, targeting regions such as Armenia and Cappadocia, and threatening the city of Antioch. This aggressive expansion marked a significant threat to the stability of the Eastern Roman Empire.
events.name: Huns attack Eastern Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: King Rudrasimha III, the ruler of the Western Satraps, was defeated by the Gupta Empire, marking a significant shift in power in ancient India. This defeat contributed to the rise of the Gupta Empire as a dominant force in the region.
events.name: Defeat of Rudrasimha III

events.enhanced_description: An estimated 330,000 acres of farmland in Campania were abandoned due to a combination of malaria outbreaks and imprudent agricultural practices. This decline in agricultural productivity reflects the broader socio-economic challenges facing the Roman Empire during this period.
events.name: Abandonment of farmland in Campania

events.enhanced_description: Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius is believed to have published his work 'Saturnalia' around this time, contributing to the literary and philosophical discourse of the late Roman Empire. This work reflects the cultural and intellectual currents of the period.

image.caption: Title page of a 1560 Lyon humanistic edition of Macrobius’s works, including Saturnalia.
image.credit: Macrobious, Ambrosius Aurelius Theodosius — Old book
image.date_qualification: Depicts a 1560 edition, not the original composition or publication date. The article excerpt says the work was written after c. 431 CE.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Saturnalia

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 40, Augustine was appointed bishop of Hippo Regius, where he focused on the reunification of the Roman Catholic Church in Africa, particularly addressing the challenges posed by the Donatist movement. His leadership would have a lasting impact on Christian theology and practice.
events.name: Augustine becomes bishop of Hippo Regius

events.enhanced_description: Russian astronomer Nikolai Alexandrovich Morozov proposed that the Book of Revelation could be astronomically dated to September 30, 395. This claim reflects the intersection of astronomy and biblical scholarship during this period.
events.name: Astronomical dating of Revelation

events.enhanced_description: Parysatis, the mother of Cyrus, successfully persuaded King Artaxerxes II to execute the Persian satrap Tissaphernes at Colossae. This political maneuvering highlighted the intense rivalries within the Persian court and the influence of familial ties in matters of state.
events.name: Execution of Tissaphernes

events.enhanced_description: Following the execution of Tissaphernes, Tithraustes was appointed as the new satrap. He quickly negotiated an armistice with Agesilaus and sought to bribe Spartan forces to shift their focus northward, indicating the shifting political landscape in the region.
events.name: Tithraustes Replaces Tissaphernes

events.enhanced_description: Unable to defeat Agesilaus's forces directly, Persian satrap Pharnabazus devised a strategy to incite unrest among the Greek city-states. He sent Timocrates of Rhodes to Athens, Thebes, Corinth, and Argos to persuade them to adopt an anti-Spartan stance, effectively stirring conflict on the Greek mainland.
events.name: Pharnabazus's Strategy Against Agesilaus

events.enhanced_description: The Corinthian War commenced as a coalition of Athens, Thebes, Corinth, and Argos, supported by Persia, rose against Sparta. This conflict marked a significant shift in power dynamics in ancient Greece, leading to a series of military engagements that would reshape alliances.
events.name: Beginning of the Corinthian War

events.enhanced_description: The Spartans coordinated an attack on the Boeotian city of Haliartus, with two armies led by General Lysander and King Pausanias. The campaign, however, ended tragically for Lysander, who was killed during the assault, highlighting the perils of Spartan military endeavors.
events.name: Spartan Attack on Haliartus

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Haliartus between Spartan and Theban forces concluded without a clear victor. Following the battle, Pausanias faced trial for his leadership and fled to Tegea, marking a significant moment in Spartan politics and military history.
events.name: Battle of Haliartus

events.enhanced_description: King Agesilaus II of Sparta organized a cavalry force over the winter and launched a successful military incursion into Lydia in the spring. This campaign demonstrated Sparta's ongoing military ambitions and its ability to project power into Asia Minor.
events.name: Agesilaus II's Incursion into Lydia

events.enhanced_description: Stilicho, a prominent Roman general, effectively became the ruler of the Western Roman Empire as he served as regent for the young emperor Honorius. His military strategies included enlisting various barbarian tribes to defend the empire's borders.
events.name: Stilicho becomes ruler of the Western Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: During the Revolt of Alaric I, the Visigoths rampaged through Greece, plundering cities such as Corinth, Argos, and Sparta. This destructive campaign culminated in the destruction of the Temple of Eleusis and marked a significant moment in the decline of Roman influence in the region.
events.name: Revolt of Alaric I in Greece

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 14, Emperor Jǐn Ān Dì ascended to the throne of the Eastern Jin dynasty following the assassination of his father, Emperor Xiaowu, by his concubine Honoured Lady Zhang. This event marked a significant transition in leadership during a tumultuous period in Chinese history.
events.name: Emperor Jǐn Ān Dì succeeds his father Emperor Xiaowu

events.enhanced_description: Lü Guang declared himself 'Heavenly Prince' (Tian Wang), asserting his claim to the Later Liang Kingdom, a significant step in the fragmentation of the Northern dynasties during the Sixteen Kingdoms period. This title symbolized his ambition and the shifting power dynamics in northern China.
events.name: Lü Guang claims the title "Heavenly Prince"

events.enhanced_description: The Persians orchestrated a naval campaign, assembling a fleet of Phoenician, Cilician, and Cypriot ships under the command of Athenian admiral Conon, successfully seizing control of Rhodes. This operation underscored the strategic importance of naval power in the ongoing conflicts of the era.
events.name: Persian Naval Campaign Against Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: The Carthaginians, besieging Syracuse, were forced to abandon their efforts due to a devastating plague, while they successfully destroyed Messina. This marked a significant victory for Dionysius of Syracuse, consolidating his power in the region and diminishing Carthaginian influence.
events.name: Carthaginian Siege of Syracuse Ends

events.enhanced_description: In 397 BC, Agesilaus II of Sparta launched a military campaign in Asia Minor to assist the Ionians against the Persian King Artaxerxes II. This campaign marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between Greek city-states and the Persian Empire, showcasing Sparta's military ambitions and influence in the region.
events.name: Agesilaus II's Campaign in Asia Minor

events.enhanced_description: Marcus Furius Camillus was appointed dictator by the Romans, leading to the destruction of the Etruscan city of Veii after a prolonged siege. This victory marked a pivotal moment in Roman expansion, effectively doubling the territory of Rome.
events.name: Marcus Furius Camillus Becomes Dictator

events.enhanced_description: Plato published his work 'Apologia', a defense of his mentor Socrates, which has since become a foundational text in Western philosophy. This publication reflects the enduring legacy of Socratic thought and the philosophical inquiries that shaped ancient Greek intellectual life.
events.name: Plato Publishes Apologia

events.enhanced_description: Kyniska made history by becoming the first woman to win an event at the Olympic Games, sponsoring a victorious horse-drawn chariot despite the prohibition against women competing. Her triumph challenged societal norms and highlighted the evolving role of women in ancient Greek culture.
events.name: Kyniska Wins Olympic Event

events.enhanced_description: During the Revolt of Alaric I, Roman general Stilicho managed to trap the Visigoths under King Alaric in the Peloponnese but ultimately chose to abandon the campaign, allowing Alaric to escape to Epirus with his plunder. This decision reflected the complexities of Roman military strategy and the pressures of impending threats elsewhere.
events.name: Revolt of Alaric I: Stilicho traps the Visigoths

events.enhanced_description: In a bid to maintain Roman cultural identity, Emperor Honorius enacted a law prohibiting the wearing of barbarian styles of dress in Rome. This law, which banned boots, trousers, animal skins, and long hair, was a response to the growing influence of barbarian fashions among the Roman populace.
events.name: Emperor Honorius passes a law against barbarian dress

events.enhanced_description: The Xiongnu, a confederation of nomadic tribes, occupied the economically vital Gansu area, a key region along the Silk Road. This occupation had significant implications for trade and the geopolitical landscape of northern China.
events.name: Xiongnu occupy the Gansu area

events.enhanced_description: Ambrose, a pivotal figure in early Christianity and Archbishop of Milan, passed away after 23 years of influential leadership. His tenure was marked by significant theological contributions and his role in shaping the political landscape of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Death of Ambrose, Archbishop of Milan

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Carthage convened to definitively declare the biblical canon, establishing the texts that would be recognized as scripture in Christianity. This event was crucial in the formation of Christian doctrine and the consolidation of church authority.
events.name: Council of Carthage declares biblical canon

events.enhanced_description: The First Council of Toledo was convened, where Hispanic bishops, including Lampius, condemned Priscillianism, a Christian sect viewed as heretical. This council played a significant role in the consolidation of orthodox Christian beliefs in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: First Council of Toledo condemns Priscillianism

events.enhanced_description: John Chrysostom was appointed Archbishop of Constantinople, a position that would allow him to influence the Christian church and society significantly. His tenure was marked by his eloquent preaching and reformative zeal.
events.name: John Chrysostom appointed Archbishop of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: The Mor Gabriel Monastery was founded on the Tur Abdin plateau near Midyat, becoming one of the oldest surviving monasteries in the world. It has served as a significant center for Syriac Christianity and monastic life.
events.name: Foundation of Mor Gabriel Monastery

events.enhanced_description: Sulpicius Severus authored the earliest biography of Martin of Tours, marking it as the first known 'life of a saint' ever written. This work played a crucial role in the development of hagiography and the veneration of saints in Christianity.
events.name: Sulpicius Severus writes biography of Martin of Tours

events.enhanced_description: Augustine of Hippo commenced writing his 'Confessions', an autobiographical work that explores his intellectual and spiritual journey. This text is considered one of the foundational works of Western literature and Christian theology.
events.name: Augustine of Hippo begins his Confessions

events.enhanced_description: Ninian, a Scottish missionary, established a church known as Candida Casa at Whithorn, marking a significant step in the spread of Christianity among the Picts. His work laid the foundation for the Christianization of Scotland.
events.name: Scottish missionary Ninian establishes Candida Casa

events.enhanced_description: In 397 BC, the Carthaginians established the town of Lilybaeum in Sicily to replace the earlier settlement of Motya, which had been lost. This strategic move was part of Carthage's efforts to maintain control over its territories in Sicily amidst ongoing conflicts with the Greeks.
events.name: Establishment of Lilybaeum

events.enhanced_description: Following Stilicho's return to Italy, the Eastern Roman Empire negotiated a peace treaty with Alaric I, granting the Visigoths a settlement area in Illyricum. This agreement marked a significant moment in the shifting alliances and conflicts of the late Roman Empire.
events.name: Revolt of Alaric I: Peace treaty with Alaric

events.enhanced_description: Gildo, a Berber official in Mauretania, instigated a revolt against the Western Roman Empire, aiming to cut off the grain supply to Rome. His rebellion prompted a military response from Flavius Stilicho, leading to a brief but intense conflict in North Africa.
events.name: Gildonic Revolt: Gildo rebels against the Western Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: Eutropius, a Roman general, celebrated his victory over the Huns in a grand parade through Constantinople, showcasing the military successes of the Eastern Roman Empire. This event highlighted the ongoing conflicts with barbarian tribes and the importance of military prowess in maintaining imperial authority.
events.name: Eutropius celebrates victory over the Huns

events.enhanced_description: An imperial edict mandated that Roman landowners with plantations yield one-third of their fields to the 'barbarians' settled within the empire. This policy reflected the changing demographics and the integration of barbarian groups into Roman society.
events.name: Imperial edict obliges landowners to yield fields to barbarians

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Honorius married Maria, the daughter of his powerful general Stilicho, strengthening the political alliance between the emperor and his military commander. This marriage was significant in the context of the power struggles within the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Emperor Honorius marries Stilicho's daughter Maria

events.enhanced_description: The Second Pictish War is believed to have occurred around this time, marking a significant conflict between the Picts and the Romans. This war was part of the broader struggles for control over the British Isles during the late Roman period.
events.name: Possible date for the Second Pictish War

events.enhanced_description: John Chrysostom, the Archbishop of Constantinople, met with a delegation of clergy advocating for the closure of pagan temples in Gaza, where worshippers were openly defying the law. His influence led to an imperial edict aimed at suppressing pagan practices.

locations.name: Gaza City, Gaza Strip, State of Palestine

events.name: John Chrysostom receives clergy delegation in Gaza

events.enhanced_description: Augustine of Hippo completed his influential work 'Confessions', an introspective autobiography that explores his spiritual journey and philosophical reflections. This text is regarded as a cornerstone of Christian literature and has had a lasting impact on Western thought.
events.name: Augustine of Hippo completes his Confessions

events.enhanced_description: In 398 BC, Dionysius I of Syracuse broke a peace treaty with Carthage and launched attacks against Carthaginian cities in western Sicily, taking advantage of their weakened state due to a plague. His forces captured Motya, leading to significant casualties among the Carthaginian population.
events.name: Syracuse's Attack on Carthaginian Cities

events.enhanced_description: At just 15 years old, Emperor Honorius officially closed the gladiatorial schools in Rome, effectively ending the practice of munera, or gladiatorial games. This decision reflected the changing values of the Roman Empire and the influence of Christian morality.
events.name: Emperor Honorius closes gladiatorial schools

events.enhanced_description: Flavius Mallius Theodorus was appointed as Roman consul and took on an official role at the imperial court of Emperor Arcadius. His appointment was part of the ongoing political maneuvering within the Eastern Roman Empire.
events.name: Flavius Mallius Theodorus becomes consul

events.enhanced_description: Gainas, a Gothic leader, was appointed magister militum and formed an alliance with deserters of Tribigild along the Bosphorus. His rise to power marked a significant shift in military and political dynamics within the Eastern Roman Empire.
events.name: Gainas becomes magister militum

events.enhanced_description: King Bahram IV of the Sassanid Empire died after an 11-year reign, leading to the ascension of Yazdegerd I as the thirteenth Sassanid Emperor of Persia. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Sassanid dynasty.
events.name: Death of King Bahram IV

events.enhanced_description: Fa-Hien, a Chinese Buddhist monk, undertook a significant pilgrimage to India, Sri Lanka, and Kapilavastu, where he sought to collect Buddhist texts and understand the practices of Buddhism in its homeland. His travels contributed to the spread of Buddhism in China and provided valuable insights into the religious landscape of the time.
events.name: Fa-Hien travels to India, Sri Lanka and Kapilavastu

events.enhanced_description: In 399 AD, the Xianbei kingdom of Southern Yan successfully conquered Qing Province from the Eastern Jin dynasty, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in the region. This conquest was part of the larger context of the fragmentation of the Jin dynasty and the rise of various northern kingdoms during the period.
events.name: Xianbei kingdom of Southern Yan conquers Qing Province

events.enhanced_description: Pope Siricius, who served as the Bishop of Rome for 15 years, died in 399 AD. His papacy was marked by significant reforms, including the enforcement of celibacy among priests and the assertion of papal authority over the Western Church, which laid the groundwork for future ecclesiastical governance.
events.name: Death of Pope Siricius

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Pope Siricius in 399 AD, Anastasius I was elected as the 39th pope. His papacy focused on reconciling the churches of Rome and Antioch and addressing theological disputes, particularly condemning the teachings of Origen.
events.name: Anastasius I succeeds Siricius as Pope

events.enhanced_description: In 399 AD, Flavian I was officially recognized as the legitimate bishop of Antioch by the Church of Rome. This acknowledgment was significant in establishing the authority of the bishopric in the early Christian Church and reinforcing the connection between Rome and Antioch.
events.name: Flavian I acknowledged as bishop of Antioch

events.enhanced_description: In 399 BC, the philosopher Socrates was sentenced to death by the Athenian court for impiety and corrupting the youth. He chose to accept his sentence rather than flee, ultimately dying by consuming hemlock, an event that has had a lasting impact on Western philosophy.
events.name: Socrates' Death Sentence

events.enhanced_description: In 399 BC, the Spartan admiral Lysander attempted to initiate political reforms in Sparta by suggesting that the leadership of the army should not automatically be given to the king. His proposals were ultimately unsuccessful, leading to his fall from favor with King Agesilaus II.
events.name: Lysander's Political Reforms Attempt

events.enhanced_description: In 399 BC, King Archelaus I of Macedon was killed during a hunting trip by his lover, Craterus. This assassination marked a significant turning point in Macedonian politics, leading to instability in the region.
events.name: Death of King Archelaus I of Macedon

events.enhanced_description: In 399 BC, King Amyrtaeus of Egypt was defeated in battle by his successor Nepherites I of Mendes and subsequently executed at Memphis. This event marked the beginning of the Twenty-ninth dynasty of Egypt, with Mendes becoming the new capital.
events.name: Battle of Memphis

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 399 BC, Sparta successfully forced the city of Elis to surrender, demonstrating its military strength in the region. This victory contributed to Sparta's dominance in Greece during this period.
events.name: Sparta's Victory Over Elis

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, Emperor Arcadius officially bestowed the title of Augusta upon his wife, Aelia Eudoxia, marking her prominence in the Byzantine court. This title allowed her to wear the purple paludamentum, a symbol of imperial authority, and she was also depicted on Roman currency, signifying her status and influence.
events.name: Emperor Arcadius gives his wife Aelia Eudoxia the official title of Augusta

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, Anthemius, the praetorian prefect of the East, was dispatched on a diplomatic mission to Ctesiphon to congratulate King Yazdegerd I on his ascension to the throne. This embassy highlighted the ongoing diplomatic interactions between the Eastern Roman Empire and the Sassanian Empire.
events.name: Anthemius sent on an embassy to Ctesiphon

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, a violent riot erupted in Constantinople, resulting in the destruction of the Great Palace. The Gothic leader Gainas attempted to evacuate his troops, but they were trapped and massacred by imperial orders, leading to further conflict and the eventual downfall of Gainas.
events.name: Riot in Constantinople and the burning of the Great Palace

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 400 AD, Gainas led the remaining Gothic forces back across the Danube River after suffering significant losses. They encountered the Huns, who defeated them, and Gainas's head was sent to Constantinople as a grim diplomatic gift to Emperor Arcadius.
events.name: Gainas leads Goths back across the Danube

events.enhanced_description: Around 400 AD, the Paeonians, an ancient people of Illyricum, began to lose their distinct cultural identity, likely due to the pressures of surrounding civilizations and the expansion of the Roman Empire. This marked a significant cultural transformation in the region.
events.name: The Paeonians lose their identity

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, Richū ascended to the throne as the 17th Emperor of Japan, succeeding his father, Emperor Nintoku. His reign is noted for the continuation of the Yamato dynasty and the consolidation of imperial power in Japan.
events.name: Richū becomes the 17th Emperor of Japan

events.enhanced_description: Around 400 AD, the diptych panel titled "Two Marys with Angel near the Empty Tomb" was created in Rome, showcasing early Christian art. This piece reflects the artistic and religious developments of the time and is now housed in Castello Sforzesco, Milan.
events.name: Creation of the diptych panel "Two Marys with Angel near the Empty Tomb"

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, the Vergilius Vaticanus, an illuminated manuscript containing fragments of Virgil's works, was produced in Rome. This manuscript is significant for its artistic merit and its role in preserving classical literature through the ages.
events.name: The Vergilius Vaticanus manuscript is created

events.enhanced_description: Around 400 AD, the Yoga Sutras, attributed to the sage Patanjali, were composed in India. This foundational text laid the groundwork for the philosophical and practical aspects of yoga, influencing generations of practitioners and scholars.
events.name: Composition of the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, the Roman physician Caelius Aurelianus was active in practicing and writing about medicine, particularly his work "De morbis acutis et chronicis". His contributions to medical literature provided insights into the understanding of diseases in ancient Rome.
events.name: Caelius Aurelianus practices medicine

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, Hypatia, a prominent Greek philosopher, distinguished herself as one of the earliest female scientists by becoming the head of the Neo-Platonist school in Alexandria. Her work in mathematics and philosophy made her a significant figure in the intellectual history of the ancient world.
events.name: Hypatia becomes head of the Neo-Platonist school

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, the mausoleum of Galerius in Thessaloniki was converted into a church, reflecting the growing influence of Christianity in the Roman Empire. This transformation marked a significant shift in the use of monumental architecture from pagan to Christian purposes.
events.name: Conversion of the mausoleum of Galerius into a church

events.enhanced_description: In 400 AD, bishops from Gaza traveled to Constantinople to petition Emperor Arcadius for the closure of the pagan temple of Marnas. This event underscores the tensions between emerging Christianity and traditional pagan practices in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Bishops from Gaza petition Arcadius

events.enhanced_description: In 400 BC, Artaxerxes II, the king of Persia, appointed Tissaphernes to govern the districts in Asia Minor that had previously been under his brother Cyrus's control. This decision was part of Artaxerxes' efforts to consolidate power following the internal strife within the Persian Empire.
events.name: Artaxerxes II Appoints Tissaphernes

events.enhanced_description: In 400 BC, Tamôs, the satrap of Ionia, fled to Egypt seeking refuge from King Artaxerxes II's retribution. However, he was executed by Psammetichus, the Egyptian king, who seized his possessions and fleet, demonstrating the political turmoil of the era.
events.name: Tamôs Flees to Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 400 BC, the Greek cities of Ionia, fearing retribution from Artaxerxes II after Cyrus' defeat, sent embassies to Sparta requesting military assistance. The Spartans responded by sending Thibron, who recruited soldiers to aid the Ionian Greeks against Persian forces.
events.name: Ionian Greek Cities Seek Spartan Assistance

events.enhanced_description: In 400 BC, Thibron embarked with his army from the Isthmus of Corinth to Ephesus on the Ionian coast, where he recruited additional soldiers for his campaign against Tissaphernes. This military action was part of the broader conflict between Sparta and Persia.
events.name: Thibron's Campaign Against Tissaphernes

events.enhanced_description: In 400 BC, Xenophon's "Ten Thousand" returned to Greece after their campaign in the Persian Empire, with many men enlisting with the Spartans. Their successful march inspired Sparta to initiate conflicts against Persian forces in Asia Minor.
events.name: Xenophon's Return to Greece

events.enhanced_description: In 400 BC, with the outbreak of war between Sparta and Persia, Athenian admiral Conon was appointed to joint command of a Persian fleet alongside Pharnabazus. This alliance marked a significant shift in naval power dynamics during the conflict.
events.name: Conon's Command of Persian Fleet

events.enhanced_description: The conflict between Sparta and Elis marks a significant moment in ancient Greek history, reflecting the ongoing power struggles among city-states during this period. The war is part of the larger context of the Peloponnesian War, where alliances and rivalries shaped the political landscape of Greece.
events.name: War breaks out between Sparta and Elis

events.enhanced_description: The early settlement of London, known as Londinium, began on a rise above marshy waters where the Walbrook River meets the River Thames. Under the leadership of the Celtic king Belin, an earth wall was constructed to protect the settlement, marking the beginning of what would become one of the world's great cities.
events.name: Origins of London

events.enhanced_description: Amyrtaeus of Sais led a successful revolt against Persian rule, reclaiming control over Upper Egypt. This revolt marked a significant moment in Egyptian history, as it represented a brief period of independence from foreign domination during the tumultuous times of the Persian Empire.
events.name: Amyrtaeus of Sais Revolt

events.enhanced_description: The abandonment of La Venta signifies the decline of the Olmec civilization, one of the earliest complex societies in Mesoamerica. This event marks a transition in cultural practices and societal structures in the region, paving the way for the rise of later Mesoamerican cultures.
events.name: End of the Olmec Culture

events.enhanced_description: The abandonment of San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán marks a pivotal moment in the history of the Olmec civilization, indicating a significant shift in population and cultural practices. This event reflects broader changes in Mesoamerican societies during this period.
events.name: Abandonment of San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán

events.enhanced_description: The casting of the Bianzhong, a set of bronze bells, by the Marquis Yi of Zheng represents a significant achievement in ancient Chinese metallurgy and music. These bells are renowned for their musical quality and artistic craftsmanship, reflecting the cultural sophistication of the time.
events.name: Casting of the Bianzhong of the Marquis Yi of Zheng

events.enhanced_description: The Mahabharata, one of the longest epic poems in history, encapsulates the rich cultural and philosophical heritage of ancient India. This epic not only tells the story of the Kurukshetra War but also explores profound themes of duty, righteousness, and the nature of reality.
events.name: The Mahabharata

events.enhanced_description: The invention of the catapult by Greek engineers revolutionized warfare, allowing for the effective siege of fortifications. This technological advancement played a crucial role in military strategies and conflicts throughout the ancient world.
events.name: Invention of the Catapult

events.enhanced_description: The conclusion of the Mature Classical period of sculpture in Ancient Greece marks a transition to the Late Classical period, characterized by new artistic styles and techniques. This shift reflects broader changes in Greek society and culture during the 4th century BCE.
events.name: End of the Mature Classical Period of Sculpture

events.enhanced_description: The creation of a model of the Acropolis of Athens represents a significant artistic endeavor, showcasing the architectural grandeur of this ancient site. The model serves as a testament to the cultural and historical importance of the Acropolis in ancient Greek civilization.
events.name: Model of the Acropolis of Athens

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Tholos of Delphi, a circular temple dedicated to Athena Pronaia, exemplifies the architectural innovation of the time. Designed by Theodorus from Phokaia, this structure reflects the religious significance of Delphi as a major center of worship in ancient Greece.

events.name: Construction of the Tholos of Delphi

events.enhanced_description: Dionysius I of Syracuse implemented a significant economic policy by confiscating and re-minting coins, effectively devaluing the currency. This move, considered the first known official devaluation, led to widespread inflation and discontent among the populace, highlighting the complexities of governance in ancient city-states.
events.name: Dionysius I's Currency Devaluation

events.enhanced_description: Zoroastrianism emerged as a dominant faith among Persians, emphasizing the cosmic struggle between good and evil. The teachings of the prophet Zarathustra laid the foundation for this ancient religion, which would influence various philosophical and religious traditions in the region.
events.name: Rise of Zoroastrianism

events.enhanced_description: The evolution of Brahmanism into Hinduism marks a significant transformation in religious practices and beliefs in ancient India. This gradual process, which unfolded over several centuries, reflects the dynamic nature of spiritual thought and cultural identity in the region.
events.name: Evolution of Brahmanism into Hinduism

events.enhanced_description: In 401 AD, Emperor Arcadius sent numerous gifts to Uldin, the Hunnic chieftain, in recognition of his victory over the Goths and Gainas. This act of diplomacy aimed to solidify alliances with the Huns amid the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Emperor Arcadius sends gifts to Uldin

events.enhanced_description: In 401 AD, slave-traders from Galatia engaged in piracy along the coasts of Africa, reflecting the turbulent socio-economic conditions of the time. This activity not only contributed to the slave trade but also highlighted the maritime conflicts of the era.
events.name: Piracy by slave-traders from Galatia

events.enhanced_description: The Legio II Adiutrix, a Roman legion historically stationed at Aquincum, was divided into two units and dispatched to Britannia. This strategic move was part of the Roman military's ongoing adjustments to address threats in the provinces.
events.name: Division of Legio II Adiutrix

events.enhanced_description: Stilicho, the magister militum of the Roman Empire, led a significant military campaign against the Vandals in Rhaetia. This campaign was part of the broader conflict between the Roman Empire and various barbarian groups threatening its borders.
events.name: Stilicho's Campaign Against the Vandals

events.enhanced_description: The Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was dismantled during this period. Its destruction marked a significant decline in the worship of Artemis and reflected the changing religious landscape of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Dismantling of the Temple of Artemis

events.enhanced_description: Led by King Alaric I, the Visigoths crossed the Alps and invaded northern Italy, marking a critical moment in the decline of Roman authority in the region. This invasion was part of a series of conflicts that would eventually lead to the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Visigothic Invasion of Northern Italy

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Honorius began using Ravenna as a temporary center for administrative and military functions, chosen for its strategic location and defensibility. This decision foreshadowed Ravenna's later status as the capital of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Emperor Honorius Establishes Ravenna as Administrative Center

events.enhanced_description: The Chronicon Pachale reported that the Black Sea was completely frozen, an unusual climatic event that would have had significant implications for trade and navigation in the region. Such occurrences were rare and noted by historians for their impact on society.
events.name: Black Sea Freezing Reported

events.enhanced_description: Kumarajiva, a prominent Kuchean Buddhist monk, arrived in Chang'an where he began translating important Buddhist texts into Chinese. His efforts significantly contributed to the spread of Buddhism in China and the cultural exchange between India and China.
events.name: Kumarajiva Arrives in Chang'an

events.enhanced_description: Pope Anastasius I died after a brief two-year reign, leading to the election of Innocent I as his successor. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the papacy, as Innocent I would go on to assert the pope's authority over Christendom.
events.name: Death of Pope Anastasius I

events.enhanced_description: The Mahabharata, one of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India, was finalized during this period. This epic not only serves as a literary masterpiece but also reflects the philosophical and cultural values of ancient Indian society.
events.name: Finalization of the Mahabharata

events.enhanced_description: Cyrus the Younger, seeking to challenge the Persian king Artaxerxes II, uses a dispute over the Ionian cities as a pretext to gather a significant force, including many Greek mercenaries. His campaign culminates in the Battle of Cunaxa, where he is ultimately defeated and killed, marking a pivotal moment in the struggle for power within the Persian Empire.
events.name: Cyrus the Younger gathers an army against Artaxerxes II

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Cyrus the Younger at the Battle of Cunaxa, the Greek mercenaries find themselves stranded in hostile territory. Under the leadership of Xenophon, they embark on a perilous journey northward through enemy lands to reach safety at Trapezus on the Black Sea coast.
events.name: Greek mercenaries stranded after Cyrus' defeat

events.enhanced_description: Agesilaus II ascends to the throne of Sparta following the death of his stepbrother Agis II, marking the beginning of his influential reign during a tumultuous period in Spartan history.
events.name: Agesilaus II becomes king of Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Zhou an wang ascends to the throne of the Zhou dynasty, a significant event in ancient Chinese history that reflects the ongoing power dynamics and governance of the period.
events.name: Zhou an wang becomes king of the Zhou dynasty

events.enhanced_description: Sophocles' tragic play 'Oedipus at Colonus' is performed posthumously at the Festival of Dionysus in Athens, showcasing the enduring legacy of his work in Greek theater and its cultural significance.
events.name: Performance of Oedipus at Colonus

events.enhanced_description: The Visigoths, under King Alaric I, advanced on Mediolanum (modern Milan) and besieged Asti in Liguria. Their military actions were part of a larger campaign against the Roman Empire, showcasing the growing power of the Visigoths.
events.name: Visigoths Advance on Mediolanum

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Pollentia marked a crucial confrontation between Roman forces led by Stilicho and the Visigoths under Alaric I. This battle was notable for Stilicho's strategic recall of troops from various fronts to defend Italy, resulting in a significant Roman victory.
events.name: Battle of Pollentia

events.enhanced_description: Emperors Arcadius and Honorius were appointed as Roman consuls, a title that symbolized their authority and governance within the empire. This event highlighted the political dynamics of the late Roman Empire during a time of increasing instability.
events.name: Arcadius and Honorius Become Consuls

events.enhanced_description: King Gwanggaeto the Great of Goguryeo achieved a significant military victory over the forces of Later Yan, capturing several border fortresses. This victory expanded Goguryeo's influence and solidified Gwanggaeto's reputation as a formidable ruler.
events.name: Gwanggaeto's Victory Over Later Yan

events.enhanced_description: The Avars, led by Shelun, established a vast nomadic empire following their victory over the Gaoju Dingling near Kobbo. This empire extended from Mongolia to the Irtysh River, significantly impacting the geopolitical landscape of the region.
events.name: Avars Establish Nomadic Empire

events.enhanced_description: Fa-Hien, a Chinese Buddhist monk, embarked on a pilgrimage to India, where he visited significant sites related to the life of Siddhartha Gautama. His journey initiated important Sino-Indian relations and contributed to the spread of Buddhism.
events.name: Fa-Hien's Pilgrimage to India

events.enhanced_description: Silseong ascended to the throne of the Silla kingdom, marking a significant moment in Korean history as Silla would later become one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His reign is noted for the consolidation of power and the cultural development that would characterize Silla's golden age.
events.name: Silseong becomes king of the Korean kingdom of Silla

events.enhanced_description: In this year, Jerome, a prominent Christian scholar and translator, completed two significant works defending his views against Rufinus, a fellow theologian. These writings reflect the theological disputes of the early Christian church and Jerome's role in shaping Christian doctrine during this period.
events.name: Jerome writes "Apologiae contra Rufinum" and "Liber tertius seu ultima responsio adversus scripta Rufini"

events.enhanced_description: The founding of a monastery by the Pure Land school of Buddhism on Mount Lushan signifies the establishment of a key center for Buddhist practice and scholarship in China. This event is closely associated with Hui Yuan, who advocated for the Pure Land teachings and sought to create a space for meditation and study.
events.name: The Pure Land school of Buddhism founds a monastery upon the top of Mount Lushan

events.enhanced_description: Cynegius, acting on behalf of Emperor Arcadius and under the influence of Bishop Porphyry, ordered the destruction of pagan temples in Gaza, reflecting the growing dominance of Christianity in the Roman Empire. This event illustrates the conflict between paganism and the rising Christian faith during this period.
events.name: Destruction of pagan temples in Gaza ordered by Cynegius

events.enhanced_description: Archelaus I, the King of Macedonia, plays a crucial role in establishing a pro-Macedonian oligarchy in Larissa, Thessaly, which reflects the expanding influence of Macedon in Greek affairs during this period.
events.name: Archelaus I establishes pro-Macedonian oligarchy in Larissa

events.enhanced_description: In June, the Battle of Verona saw the Visigoths, led by King Alaric I, invade Italy, where they faced the Roman general Stilicho. The battle was a pivotal moment in the conflict between the Roman Empire and the barbarian tribes, culminating in a Roman victory that temporarily halted the Gothic advance.
events.name: Battle of Verona

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Honorius and his general Stilicho were honored with a grand triumphal march in Rome, celebrating their victories against the Goths and Vandals. This event marked a significant moment in Roman history, showcasing the military successes that were becoming increasingly rare during the decline of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Triumphal march for Emperor Honorius and Stilicho

events.enhanced_description: At the age of two, Theodosius II was appointed consul of the Eastern Roman Empire, a ceremonial title that would later lead to his eventual reign. His early ascension reflects the political dynamics of the empire, where power often shifted due to familial ties and political maneuvering.
events.name: Theodosius II becomes consul of the Eastern Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: Hui Yuan, a prominent figure in Chinese Buddhism, argued that Buddhist monks should be exempt from the practice of bowing to the emperor, emphasizing the independence of the monastic community from state authority. This argument highlights the tensions between religious practices and imperial expectations in ancient China.
events.name: Hui Yuan argues for Buddhist monks' exemption from bowing to the emperor

events.enhanced_description: Asin, the king of Baekje, formed an alliance with Silla to counter the military threat posed by Gwanggaeto the Great of Goguryeo. This alliance was significant in the context of the Three Kingdoms period in Korea, influencing the power dynamics among the rival kingdoms.
events.name: Asin of Baekje allies with Silla

events.enhanced_description: The Synod of the Oak resulted in the deposition and banishment of John Chrysostom, the bishop of Constantinople, reflecting the intense political and theological conflicts within the early church. His subsequent recall and re-banishment highlight the turbulent nature of ecclesiastical politics during this era.
events.name: Synod of the Oak deposes John Chrysostom

events.enhanced_description: Thrasybulus emerges as a key leader of the democratic resistance against the oligarchic regime of the Thirty Tyrants imposed by the Spartans in Athens. His military successes culminate in the Battle of Munychia, where he defeats the forces of the oligarchs, including their leader Critias.
events.name: Thrasybulus leads resistance against the Thirty Tyrants

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Piraeus sees Athenian exiles, who have recently overthrown the Thirty Tyrants, clash with a Spartan force. Despite heavy casualties on both sides, the battle leads to a settlement that reunifies Athens and Piraeus and restores democratic governance.
events.name: Battle of Piraeus

events.enhanced_description: After defeating the oligarchs, Thrasybulus takes decisive action to restore democratic institutions in Athens, offering amnesty to all but the most extreme oligarchs, thus paving the way for a more inclusive governance.
events.name: Thrasybulus restores democracy in Athens

events.enhanced_description: Andocides, an Athenian orator and politician, returns from exile following a general amnesty, marking a significant moment in the political landscape of Athens as it transitions back to democratic rule.
events.name: Andocides returns from exile

events.enhanced_description: The states of Han, Zhao, and Wei receive official recognition as Marquesses from the Eastern Zhou dynasty, a critical event that confirms the Partition of Jin and marks the beginning of the Warring States period in Chinese history.
events.name: Recognition of Han, Zhao, and Wei as Marquesses

events.enhanced_description: Marquis Wen of Wei ascends to power, promoting Confucianism and surrounding himself with capable advisors, which sets the stage for significant political developments in the state of Wei during the Warring States period.
events.name: Marquis Wen of Wei ascends to power

events.enhanced_description: Marquis Lie of Zhao ascends to rulership in Zhao, a significant event in the power dynamics of the Warring States period, as Zhao becomes one of the prominent states in ancient China.
events.name: Marquis Lie of Zhao becomes ruler

events.enhanced_description: Marquis Jing of Han ascends to power in Han, contributing to the state's prominence during the Warring States period and influencing the political landscape of ancient China.
events.name: Marquis Jing of Han ascends to power

events.enhanced_description: Rome elects eight military tribunes with consular power, including notable figures such as Manlius Aemilius Mamercus and Appius Claudius Crassus, reflecting the political structure and military organization of the Roman Republic during this era.
events.name: Election of military tribunes in Rome

events.enhanced_description: Under the leadership of Archon Eucleides, the Athenians adopted a significant spelling reform, transitioning to the Ionian alphabet, which introduced new letters such as eta and omega. This reform marked a pivotal moment in the evolution of the Greek writing system, leading to what became known as the Euclidean alphabet.
events.name: Adoption of the Ionian Alphabet by Athens

events.enhanced_description: The last known gladiator fight in Rome is often associated with the martyrdom of Saint Telemachus, who was stoned to death by the crowd for attempting to stop the brutal spectacle. This event symbolizes the decline of gladiatorial games and the rise of Christian values in Roman society.
events.name: Last known gladiator fight in Rome

events.enhanced_description: Empress Eudoxia experienced her seventh pregnancy, which tragically ended in miscarriage, leading to her subsequent death from infection. Her death marked a significant loss in the imperial court, reflecting the personal tragedies that often accompanied political power.
events.name: Empress Eudoxia's seventh pregnancy ends in miscarriage

events.enhanced_description: Fravitta, a high-ranking Gothic general serving the Eastern Roman Empire, was executed due to political intrigue involving Ioannes, a powerful official. His execution not only removed a competent military leader but also highlighted the precarious nature of loyalty and power within the imperial court.
events.name: Fravitta executed on the behest of Ioannes

events.enhanced_description: Gwanggaeto the Great of Goguryeo launched a military campaign against the Liaodong Peninsula, successfully capturing the territory. This expansion marked a significant achievement in his reign, contributing to Goguryeo's prominence in Northeast Asia during this period.
events.name: Gwanggaeto the Great attacks Liaodong Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: Hui Yuan, a key figure in the Pure Land school of Buddhism, authored the treatise On Why Monks Do Not Bow Down Before Kings, arguing for the independence of Buddhist clergy from secular authority. This work reflects the philosophical and political challenges faced by Buddhist practitioners in a Confucian-dominated society.
events.name: Huiyuan writes On Why Monks Do Not Bow Down Before Kings

events.enhanced_description: In 404 AD, Eudoxia, the wife of Emperor Arcadius, exiled John Chrysostom, the Bishop of Constantinople, due to his outspoken criticism of her lavish lifestyle. Despite efforts by Pope Innocent I to reinstate him, Chrysostom's envoys were imprisoned, leading to a significant conflict between church and state.
events.name: Eudoxia exiles John Chrysostom

events.enhanced_description: Cleophon, a prominent Athenian leader, faced dire circumstances as he continued to advocate for resistance against the Peloponnesian forces. Ultimately, his fate turned tragic when he was arrested, condemned to death, and executed, reflecting the desperate political climate of Athens during the war.
events.name: Execution of Cleophon

events.enhanced_description: In a state of desperation marked by plague and famine, Athens capitulated, signaling the conclusion of the Peloponnesian War. This surrender not only ended years of conflict but also marked a significant shift in power dynamics in ancient Greece.
events.name: Capitulation of Athens and End of the Peloponnesian War

events.enhanced_description: Theramenes played a crucial role in negotiating terms that spared Athens from total destruction after its defeat. While Athens retained its independence, it suffered significant losses, including the dismantling of its Long Walls and the loss of its fleet, while becoming an ally of Sparta.
events.name: Theramenes Secures Terms for Athens

events.enhanced_description: Following Sparta's victory, General Lysander established a puppet government in Athens known as the oligarchy of the 'Thirty Tyrants,' led by Critias and including Theramenes. This regime was notorious for its brutal repression of dissent and the execution of numerous citizens.
events.name: Establishment of the Thirty Tyrants in Athens

events.enhanced_description: Following the defeat of Athens, many of its former allies were subjected to governance by boards of ten, known as decarchies, often supported by Spartan garrisons. This marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the region, reinforcing Spartan control.
events.name: Decarchy Rule of Former Athenian Allies

events.enhanced_description: The Athenian general Thrasybulus was exiled by the oligarchic government of the Thirty Tyrants, leading him to seek refuge in Thebes. His exile exemplified the political purges occurring during this tumultuous period in Athenian history.
events.name: Exile of Thrasybulus

events.enhanced_description: A rift developed between Theramenes and Critias, culminating in Theramenes' execution on charges of treason, as ordered by Critias. This event underscores the internal conflicts and power struggles within the oligarchic regime of Athens.
events.name: Conflict Between Theramenes and Critias

events.enhanced_description: After the Spartan victory at Aegospotami, Alcibiades sought refuge with the Persian satrap Pharnabazus in Phrygia. His attempts to garner support for Athens were thwarted when the Spartans discovered his plans, leading to his assassination.
events.name: Alcibiades Seeks Refuge in Phrygia

events.enhanced_description: Spartan general Lysander successfully conquered the island of Samos, further extending Spartan control in the Aegean. This conquest was part of the broader conflict during the Peloponnesian War, showcasing Sparta's naval prowess.
events.name: Lysander Conquers Samos for Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Amyrtaeus of Sais successfully led a revolt against Persian control in the Egyptian delta, becoming the first and only pharaoh of the Twenty-eighth Dynasty. His leadership marked a significant moment in Egypt's struggle for independence from Persian rule.
events.name: Amyrtaeus Leads Revolt Against Persia

events.enhanced_description: Darius II, the King of Persia, died of an illness in Babylon, marking the end of his reign. He was succeeded by his son Artaxerxes II, who would face numerous challenges during his rule.
events.name: Death of Darius II of Persia

events.enhanced_description: Cyrus, the younger son of Darius II, was accused by Tissaphernes of plotting against his brother Artaxerxes II. However, through the intervention of Artaxerxes and their mother, Cyrus was pardoned and returned to his satrapy, avoiding a potentially fatal outcome.
events.name: Cyrus Accused of Plotting Against Artaxerxes II

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, Emperor Honorius ordered the closure of the Flavian Amphitheatre, commonly known as the Colosseum, as part of a broader austerity measure aimed at abolishing public amusements. This marked a significant shift in the cultural landscape of Rome, reflecting the declining influence of traditional entertainment.
