events.name: Emperor Honorius closes the Flavian Amphitheatre

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, Stilicho, the Roman general and magister militum, ordered the destruction of the Sibylline Books, a collection of prophetic texts that were considered vital to the Roman state. This act, noted by the poet Rutilius Claudius Namatianus, signified a critical moment in the intersection of politics and religion in late antiquity.
events.name: Stilicho orders the Sibylline Books to be burned

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, Stilicho successfully defeated a coalition of Germanic tribes, including the Asding Vandals, Ostrogoths, and Quadi, using forces raised from the Rhine frontier. This victory, however, left the region dangerously vulnerable, highlighting the precarious state of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Stilicho defeats a coalition of Germanic tribes

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, King Radagaisus led a massive invasion of Italy with an army estimated at 20,000 men, crossing the Alps and settling in the Po Valley for the winter. This invasion posed a significant threat to the Roman Empire, as Stilicho observed the growing numbers of Germanic tribes migrating into Roman territory.
events.name: War of Radagaisus begins

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, Flavius Aetius, a prominent Roman general, was sent as a child hostage to the court of Alaric I, the king of the Visigoths. This event was significant as it established Aetius's future role as a key military leader in the defense of the Roman Empire against barbarian invasions.
events.name: Flavius Aetius sent as hostage

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, the Khitan people were first documented in Chinese chronicles, indicating their presence along the borders of Kara-muren. They were part of the Donghu confederation, marking an important moment in the history of East Asian nomadic tribes.
events.name: First mention of the Khitan

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, Jeonji ascended to the throne of Baekje, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His reign marked a significant period in the kingdom's history, characterized by cultural development and political consolidation.
events.name: Jeonji becomes king of Baekje

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, Mesrop Mashtots, an Armenian linguist and theologian, devised the Armenian alphabet, which played a crucial role in the development of Armenian literature and culture. This innovation allowed for the preservation and dissemination of Armenian heritage.

image.caption: The Armenian alphabet at the Melkonian Educational Institute in Nicosia, Cyprus.
image.credit: Alexander-Michael Hadjilyra — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2008-05-24; this is not a contemporary image of the alphabet’s development around 405 AD.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Mesrop Mashtots devises the Armenian alphabet

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, the Japanese court officially adopted the Chinese writing system, marking a pivotal moment in the cultural exchange between China and Japan. This adoption significantly influenced the development of the Japanese language and literature.
events.name: Japanese court adopts Chinese writing system

events.enhanced_description: Around 405 AD, Theon of Alexandria, a Greek mathematician, passed away at the approximate age of 70. He was known for his contributions to mathematics and astronomy, and his daughter, Hypatia, became one of the most famous female scholars of the ancient world.
events.name: Death of Theon of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, Jerome completed his Vulgate translation of the Bible into Latin, which included translations of the Tanakh from Hebrew. This work became the standard Latin version of the Bible and had a profound impact on Christianity in the West.
events.name: Completion of Jerome's Vulgate

events.enhanced_description: In 405 AD, Augustine of Hippo publicly opposed Donatism, a Christian sect he deemed heretical, in the Roman province of Africa. His theological arguments against Donatism were pivotal in shaping early Christian doctrine and ecclesiastical authority.
events.name: Augustine opposes Donatism

events.enhanced_description: After a victorious campaign at the Battle of Arginusae, the Athenian fleet, under Admiral Conon, pursued the Spartan admiral Lysander to the Hellespont. However, they faced a devastating defeat at Aegospotami, which effectively ended Athenian naval power.
events.name: Athenian Fleet's Defeat at Aegospotami

events.enhanced_description: Spartan King Pausanias laid siege to Athens while Lysander's fleet blockaded the port of Piraeus, effectively cutting off vital supplies and starving the city. This siege was a critical moment in the final stages of the Peloponnesian War.
events.name: Siege of Athens by Spartan King Pausanias

events.enhanced_description: During the protracted siege of Athens by the Peloponnesians, Theramenes undertakes a critical diplomatic mission to negotiate terms with the Spartan commander Lysander. His efforts come at a time when Athens is facing severe starvation, and he ultimately leads the embassy that negotiates the terms of capitulation to the Spartans, marking a significant moment in the Peloponnesian War.
events.name: While the Peloponnesians besiege Athens, Theramenes tries to negotiate with Lysander

events.enhanced_description: Dionysius the Elder seizes control of Syracuse and establishes himself as a tyrant, consolidating power through military and political maneuvers. He forms a strategic alliance with the Carthaginian general Himilco, whose forces are weakened by plague, and fortifies Syracuse, ensuring Carthage's dominance over much of Sicily.
events.name: Dionysius the Elder rises to power as the tyrant of Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: After rising to power, Dionysius the Elder embarks on a campaign of ruthless consolidation, fortifying Syracuse and expelling Greek citizens from their cities. His actions set the stage for conflict with Carthage, as he prepares his forces to reclaim lost territories in Sicily.
events.name: Dionysius the Elder ruthlessly consolidates and expands his power

events.enhanced_description: In January, Aristophanes' comedic play 'The Frogs' is performed in Athens, showcasing the playwright's sharp wit and critique of contemporary Athenian society. The play is notable for its satirical take on the state of Athenian drama and politics during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Aristophanes' play The Frogs is performed

events.enhanced_description: The Erechtheum, an iconic temple on the Acropolis of Athens, is completed after 16 years of construction. Renowned for its unique architectural design and the Caryatid Porch, it symbolizes the artistic achievements of classical Athens and its religious devotion.
events.name: The Erechtheum is completed on the Acropolis in Athens

events.enhanced_description: In March/April, Euripides' works 'The Bacchae' and 'Iphigeneia at Aulis' are performed posthumously at the City Dionysia festival in Athens, where they win first prize. These plays reflect Euripides' innovative approach to tragedy and his exploration of complex themes such as fate and divine influence.
events.name: Euripides' The Bacchae and Iphigeneia at Aulis are performed posthumously

events.enhanced_description: In 406 AD, after facing defeat, Radagaisus retreated into the hills of Fiesole, where he attempted to escape capture but was ultimately apprehended by Roman forces. This event marked a significant turning point in the War of Radagaisus against the Roman Empire.
events.name: Radagaisus retreats into the hills of Fiesole

events.enhanced_description: In 406 AD, Radagaisus was executed after his defeat by the Romans, leading to the incorporation of 12,000 of his followers into the Roman army or their sale as slaves. This event underscored the Roman Empire's ongoing struggles with barbarian invasions and its efforts to bolster its military ranks.
events.name: Execution of Radagaisus

events.enhanced_description: In 406, the Vandals, led by their king Godigisel, were intercepted by the Franks under King Marcomir. The battle resulted in a decisive defeat for the Vandals, leading to Godigisel's death and the ascension of his son Gunderic as the new leader.
events.name: Vandals Defeated by Franks

events.enhanced_description: In 406, the Vandals, Alans, and Suebians crossed the Rhine at Mogontiacum, marking the beginning of their invasion of Gaul. This event signified a significant shift in the power dynamics of the region as these groups sought to establish their presence in Roman territories.
events.name: Invasion of Gaul Begins

events.enhanced_description: In 406, the Chinese traveler Faxian arrived in India, where he visited major centers of Buddhist learning, including Udyana, Peshawar, and Taxila. His journey was significant for the exchange of cultural and religious ideas between China and India.
events.name: Faxian Arrives in India

events.enhanced_description: In 406, Hanzei succeeded his brother Richu to become the 18th emperor of Japan in the traditional order of succession. His reign marked a continuation of the Yamato dynasty's influence over the Japanese archipelago.
events.name: Hanzei Becomes Emperor of Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 406, the Vandals, Alans, and Sciri introduced the cultivation of rye, oats, hops, and spelt in Europe, along with a heavy wheeled plow. This agricultural innovation had a lasting impact on European farming practices.
events.name: Introduction of New Crops in Europe

events.enhanced_description: In 406, stained glass was used for the first time in churches in Rome, marking a significant development in ecclesiastical art. This innovation would influence church architecture and aesthetics for centuries to come.
events.name: First Use of Stained Glass in Rome

events.enhanced_description: Callicratidas is appointed as the navarch of the Spartan fleet, taking over from Lysander. He swiftly assembles a fleet and sails to Methymna, laying siege to the city, which poses a significant threat to the Athenian grain supply during the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Callicratidas is appointed as the navarch of the Spartan fleet

events.enhanced_description: Alcibiades is replaced by a board of generals, leading to Admiral Conon being dispatched to relieve the siege of Mytilene. Conon faces challenges as he maneuvers his smaller fleet against the Spartan forces led by Callicratidas, highlighting the intense naval struggles of the time.
events.name: Alcibiades is replaced by a board of generals

events.enhanced_description: In a pivotal naval engagement, Athens secures victory at the Battle of Arginusae, breaking the blockade of Conon. The Athenians, despite their inexperienced fleet, employ innovative tactics that lead to a decisive defeat of the Spartan forces, marking a turning point in the naval conflict.
events.name: Athens wins the Battle of Arginusae

events.enhanced_description: Following the Battle of Arginusae, Theramenes spearheads a movement against the eight Athenian generals who commanded during the engagement. The six generals who return to Athens are condemned for their failure to rescue survivors, leading to their execution and highlighting the political tensions in Athens post-battle.
events.name: Theramenes leads agitation against Athenian generals after the Battle of Arginusae

events.enhanced_description: In a significant diplomatic move, Sparta seeks peace with Athens, but the Athenian leader Cleophon rejects their overtures. This decision reflects the ongoing hostilities and the influence of external pressures, particularly from the Persian satrap Cyrus, on Spartan military strategy.
events.name: Sparta sues for peace, rejected by Cleophon

events.enhanced_description: The Roman forces initiate a prolonged siege against the Etruscan city of Veii, marking the beginning of a decade-long conflict that will culminate in the city's eventual fall. This siege is pivotal in the expansion of Roman territory and influence in the region.
events.name: The Roman forces begin a decade-long siege against Veii

events.enhanced_description: The Carthaginian forces launch another invasion of Sicily, targeting Agrigentum. The campaign is marred by a plague that decimates their ranks, leading to the death of Hannibal Mago and the subsequent capture of Agrigentum by Himilco, who also devastates Gela and Camarina.
events.name: The Carthaginians invade Sicily and attack Agrigentum

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 406, the remaining Roman legions stationed in Britain, disillusioned by the lack of support from Rome and the increasing threats from barbarian tribes, decided to mutiny. They proclaimed Marcus as their emperor in a desperate bid for autonomy during a time of chaos in the Roman Empire.
events.name: Roman Legions Mutiny in Britain

events.enhanced_description: In 407, Gratian was installed as emperor following the death of Marcus, marking a turbulent period in the Roman Empire's history. His rule was characterized by the challenges of maintaining control over the empire's far-flung territories.
events.name: Gratian Installed as Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 407, after the assassination of Gratian, Constantine III, a general, declared himself Roman emperor. He took significant military actions to extend his control over Gaul and Spain, marking the beginning of Rome's withdrawal from Britain.
events.name: Constantine III Declares Himself Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 407, after 360 years of Roman occupation, local British-Roman leaders began raising their own levies to defend against Saxon sea raiders, signaling the end of Roman rule in Britain. This marked a significant turning point in British history.
events.name: End of Roman Rule in Britain

events.enhanced_description: In 407, Liu Bobo, known as Xia Wuliedi, founded the state of Xia and claimed the title of 'Heavenly Prince'. This event was pivotal in the establishment of regional powers during a time of fragmentation in China.
events.name: Liu Bobo Founds State of Xia

events.enhanced_description: Athenian general Thrasybulus successfully recaptures the strategically important locations of Abdera and Thasos, strengthening Athenian control in the region. This military success is part of the broader conflict between Athens and its adversaries in the Aegean.
events.name: The Athenian general Thrasybulus recaptures Abdera and Thasos

events.enhanced_description: Spartan admiral Lysander strategically avoids confrontation with Athenian commander Alcibiades while stationed at Ephesus. However, when Alcibiades is away, a subordinate leads the Athenian fleet into battle, resulting in a significant defeat at the Battle of Notium.
events.name: The Spartan admiral Lysander refuses to engage with Alcibiades

events.enhanced_description: Following a significant defeat, Alcibiades is stripped of his command, marking a pivotal moment in his military career during the Peloponnesian War. He subsequently sails to his estate in the Thracian Chersonese, never to return to Athens, effectively ending his involvement in the conflict aside from a brief appearance at Aegospotami.
events.name: The defeat gives the enemies of Alcibiades an excuse to strip him of his command

events.enhanced_description: Hermocrates, the exiled leader of the moderate democrats in Syracuse, is killed in a failed attempt to reclaim power in his city. His death signifies the ongoing political turmoil and conflict within Syracuse during this tumultuous period of the Peloponnesian War.
events.name: The death of Hermocrates while attempting to return to Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: A relief decoration depicting Nike adjusting her sandal was constructed for the Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis in Athens, showcasing the artistic achievements of the period. This work, now housed in the Acropolis Museum, reflects the cultural and religious significance of victory in Athenian society.
events.name: Nike Relief Decoration

events.enhanced_description: In 408, Emperor Arcadius died in his palace in Constantinople after a weak reign of 13 years. He was succeeded by his young son, Theodosius II, who ruled under the influence of his sister Pulcheria and the regent Anthemius.
events.name: Death of Emperor Arcadius

events.enhanced_description: In 408, Stilicho was accused of treason against Emperor Honorius and was executed in Ravenna. His death led to violent reprisals against his supporters and marked a significant shift in the power dynamics within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Stilicho Executed

events.enhanced_description: The Hexamilion wall was a significant fortification built across the Isthmus of Corinth to protect the Peloponnese from invasions. This massive structure served as a strategic barrier, reflecting the military engineering capabilities of the time and the need for defense against various threats during the late Roman Empire.
events.name: The Hexamilion wall is constructed

events.enhanced_description: During his siege of Rome, Alaric I successfully negotiated the freedom of 30,000 enslaved individuals, showcasing his power and the desperation of the Roman Senate. This act not only highlights the social dynamics of the time but also Alaric's role as a significant player in the political landscape of the crumbling Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Alaric demands freedom for enslaved people

events.enhanced_description: In 408, Uldin and his Huns crossed the lower Danube, launching a devastating attack on the Eastern Roman Empire. They set fire to frontier forts and captured key locations, forcing the Romans to negotiate for peace under unfavorable terms, highlighting the volatility of the region during this period.
events.name: Huns attack the Eastern Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move, the Romans sent Flavius Aetius to the Huns in exchange for the young Attila, who was sent as a hostage to Rome at the age of two. This exchange reflected the complex diplomatic relationships between the Roman Empire and the Huns, foreshadowing Attila's future role as a formidable leader.
events.name: Attila sent as hostage to Rome

events.enhanced_description: King Yazdegerd I of Persia played a crucial role in maintaining cordial relations with the Roman Empire during a turbulent period. His stewardship included overseeing the upbringing of the young Theodosius II, showcasing the interconnectedness of political powers in the region.
events.name: Yazdegerd I maintains relations with Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 408, Alaric I demanded a substantial tribute from Rome, including 3,000 pounds of pepper, which was highly valued for its culinary and medicinal properties. This demand underscored the desperation of the Roman Senate and the shifting balance of power as barbarian leaders began to dictate terms to the once-mighty empire.
events.name: Alaric I exacts tribute from Rome

events.enhanced_description: Darius II of Persia decides to continue the war against Athens, bolstering Spartan forces with Persian support. His decision is influenced by his wife, Parysatis, who persuades him to appoint their son Cyrus as satrap of key regions, thereby strengthening Persian military presence in the conflict.
events.name: King Darius II of Persia supports Sparta against Athens

events.enhanced_description: The influence of Tissaphernes, a Persian satrap, is curtailed as Darius II reallocates military responsibilities to Cyrus the Younger. This change allows Cyrus to gather resources and support for the Spartan fleet, marking a strategic shift in the ongoing conflict against Athens.
events.name: Tissaphernes' influence is limited to Caria

events.enhanced_description: After a seven-year absence, Alcibiades returns to Athens in a grand procession, leading a religious ceremony to atone for his past actions. His return is marked by his appointment as commander-in-chief, reflecting the city's shifting political landscape during the Peloponnesian War.
events.name: Alcibiades enters Athens in triumph

events.enhanced_description: At the Panhellenic gathering in Olympia, the philosopher Gorgias publicly criticizes the alliance between Sparta and Persia, highlighting the philosophical and ethical implications of such political maneuvers during the Peloponnesian War. His speech reflects the growing dissent among Greek intellectuals regarding foreign intervention in Greek affairs.
events.name: Gorgias speaks against Spartan-Persian alliance at Olympia

events.enhanced_description: The three city-states of Rhodes—Ialysos, Kamiros, and Lindos—unite to form a single city, marking a significant political and cultural development on the island. This unification strengthens their collective identity and influence in the region during the ongoing conflicts of the era.
events.name: The unification of the city-states of Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: Euripides presents his plays 'Orestes' and 'The Phoenician Women' in Athens, showcasing his contributions to Greek drama. Following the performances, he departs Athens for the court of Archelaus I of Macedon, reflecting his dissatisfaction with the Athenian cultural scene.
events.name: Euripides' plays are performed

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 408, Emperor Honorius married Thermantia, the daughter of his general Stilicho. This marriage was politically significant, aiming to strengthen ties between the imperial family and the military leadership.
events.name: Emperor Honorius Marries Thermantia

events.enhanced_description: In September 408, King Alaric I of the Visigoths led a formidable army across the Julian Alps, marking a critical moment in the decline of Roman power in the West. His march into the heart of the Roman Empire culminated in a siege of Rome, demonstrating the growing strength of the barbarian tribes and their impact on Roman territories.
events.name: Alaric I crosses the Julian Alps

events.enhanced_description: Spartan admiral Lysander arrives in Ephesus during the autumn, where he begins to construct a formidable fleet with the backing of Cyrus the Younger, the new Persian satrap. This development plays a crucial role in the naval power dynamics of the ongoing conflict with Athens.
events.name: Lysander builds a fleet at Ephesus with Persian support

events.enhanced_description: In 409, the Vandals, led by King Gunderic, crossed the Pyrenees into the Iberian Peninsula, establishing themselves as foederati by receiving land from the Romans. This migration marked a significant shift in the power dynamics of the region, as various barbarian groups began to carve out territories within the former Roman domains.
events.name: Vandals cross into Iberian Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: In 409, Alaric I laid siege to Rome for the second time, pushing the city to the brink of starvation. Despite repeated offers for peace, Emperor Honorius, who was safely ensconced in Ravenna, refused to negotiate, leading to a critical moment in the history of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Alaric I lays siege to Rome a second time

events.enhanced_description: In 409, Emperor Honorius agreed to send the sons of prominent families as hostages to the Huns, a desperate measure to secure peace. This decision reflected the precarious position of the Roman Empire as it struggled to maintain control over its territories amidst increasing barbarian pressures.
events.name: Honorius sends hostages to the Huns

events.enhanced_description: In 409, a severe famine struck Hispania, Gaul, and the Italian Peninsula, exacerbating the already dire conditions faced by the populations in these regions. This widespread food shortage highlighted the vulnerabilities of the Roman Empire and its provinces during a time of political instability and external threats.
events.name: Famine strikes Hispania, Gaul, and Italy

events.enhanced_description: The Bacaudic Rebellion began in 409 when peasants in Armorica revolted against the oppressive conditions imposed by the Roman authorities. This uprising reflected the growing discontent among the rural population and continued until 417, showcasing the social unrest prevalent in the waning days of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Bacaudic Rebellion in Armorica

events.enhanced_description: In 409, at the young age of 17, Mingyuan ascended to the throne as the emperor of the Northern Wei dynasty. His reign marked a significant period in Chinese history as the Northern Wei played a pivotal role in the unification and consolidation of northern China during the era of the Northern Dynasties.
events.name: Mingyuan succeeds Daowu as emperor

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Linqu in 409 saw the Southern Yan defeated by the Eastern Jin, illustrating the ongoing conflicts between various Chinese states during the period of disunity. This battle was part of the larger struggle for power among the fragmented kingdoms of the time.
events.name: Battle of Linqu

events.enhanced_description: Alcibiades successfully recaptures Byzantium, effectively quelling the city's rebellion against Athenian control. This victory is crucial for securing Athenian access to vital grain supplies from the Black Sea, reinforcing Athens' strategic position in the ongoing war.
events.name: Alcibiades recaptures Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: Athenian general Thrasyllus leads a campaign into Ionia, managing to capture Colophon and raid the surrounding countryside. However, his forces face defeat outside Ephesus against a coalition of Ephesian, Persian, and Syracusan troops, underscoring the challenges faced by Athens in the war.
events.name: Thrasyllus campaigns in Ionia

events.enhanced_description: Pausanias ascends to the throne as the Agiad king of Sparta, succeeding his father Pleistoanax. His reign marks a continuation of Spartan leadership during a critical phase of the Peloponnesian War.
events.name: Pausanias becomes king of Sparta

events.enhanced_description: The city of Rhodes is founded, establishing a significant urban center in the Aegean. This development plays a vital role in the political and commercial landscape of the region during the classical period.
events.name: The founding of the city of Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: Carthage, taking advantage of the discord among Greek city-states in Sicily, launches an invasion led by Hannibal Mago. His forces achieve significant victories over the Sicilian Greeks, capturing and destroying cities, thereby reasserting Carthaginian dominance in the region.
events.name: Carthaginian invasion of Sicily

events.enhanced_description: The play 'Philoctetes' by Sophocles is performed in Athens, exploring themes related to the Trojan War. This performance highlights the cultural significance of theater in Athenian society during the Peloponnesian War.
events.name: Sophocles' play Philoctetes is performed

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 409, Gerontius, a Roman general, revolted in Hispania, elevating his domesticus, Maximus, as emperor. This revolt was part of the larger chaos engulfing the Western Roman Empire, as various factions vied for power amid its decline.
events.name: Gerontius revolts in Hispania

events.enhanced_description: In 410, raiders from Ireland, including the Uí Liatháin and Laigin, harried the coasts of Wales, particularly in Gwynedd. They plundered towns and captured slaves, leading to significant territorial changes as they began to colonize parts of Wales, including Llŷn and the Isle of Mona.
events.name: Irish Raiders Attack Wales

events.enhanced_description: In 410, Flavius Constantius was promoted to the rank of magister militum, becoming a key military leader and advisor to Emperor Honorius in the Western Roman Empire. His rise to power marked a significant shift in military leadership during a time of crisis for the Empire.
events.name: Flavius Constantius Promoted to Magister Militum

events.enhanced_description: In 410, the Visigoths under Alaric I sacked Rome after a prolonged siege, marking the first time the city had fallen to an enemy since 390 BC. The sack resulted in significant looting, although many inhabitants were spared, and it symbolized the decline of the Western Roman Empire.

image.caption: Joseph-Noël Sylvestre’s painting *The Plunder of Rome* depicts the sack of Rome.
image.credit: Joseph-Noël Sylvestre — Das Königreich der Vandalen , ed. Klaus Hattler (Mainz: Philipp von Zabern, 2009), p. 418. scan and upload: James Steakley
image.date_qualification: Retrospective painting dated 1890, depicting the sack of Rome in 410; it is not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Visigoths Sack Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 410, Galla Placidia, the daughter of Theodosius I, was captured by the Visigoths during their invasion of the Italian Peninsula. Her capture marked a significant political event, as she became a hostage during the Visigoths' subsequent movements into Gaul.
events.name: Galla Placidia Captured by Visigoths

events.enhanced_description: In 410, Alaric I planned an invasion of Africa after marching south into Calabria. However, his plans were thwarted when a storm destroyed his fleet, leading to his death in Cosenza shortly thereafter, marking a pivotal moment in Visigothic history as he was succeeded by Ataulf.
events.name: Alaric I Plans Invasion of Africa

events.enhanced_description: In 410, Emperor Honorius reportedly sent a rescript to the magistrates of Roman Britain, signaling the end of Roman rule in the region. This event is often debated among historians, with some suggesting it may refer to a different Roman province due to potential scribal errors in historical accounts.
events.name: Honorius Sends Rescript Ending Roman Rule in Britain

events.enhanced_description: Around 410, one of the first Anglo-Saxon settlements in Britain was established at Mucking, located by the mouth of the Thames River. This settlement marked the beginning of significant cultural and demographic changes in post-Roman Britain.
events.name: Establishment of Anglo-Saxon Settlement at Mucking

events.enhanced_description: In 410, the city of Aléria on the island of Corsica was devastated by a massive fire that destroyed its port and a significant portion of its population. This disaster had lasting effects on the city's economic and social structure.
events.name: Devastation of Aléria by Fire

events.enhanced_description: In 410, Prithivisena ascended to the throne as king of the Vakataka dynasty in the Deccan region of India. His rule contributed to the cultural and political landscape of the region during this period.
events.name: Prithivisena Becomes King of the Vakataka

events.enhanced_description: In 410, the Council of Seleucia was convened, where Persian Christians established a national church and adopted the Nicene Creed. This event was significant in the development of Christianity in Persia, setting the foundation for the Church of the East.
events.name: Council of Seleucia Establishes National Church

events.enhanced_description: In 410, Honoratus founded the Monastery of Lérins on the Île Saint-Honorat in France, establishing a monastic community that would become influential in the development of Christian monasticism in the region.
events.name: Honoratus Founds Monastery of Lérins

events.enhanced_description: Alcibiades established a garrison at Chrysopolis, placing Theramenes in command to levy a tithe on shipping from the Black Sea. This strategic move not only generated revenue for Athens but also facilitated the restoration of democracy in the city, ending the oligarchic regime of the Five Thousand.
events.name: Garrison at Chrysopolis

events.enhanced_description: An attempted oligarchic revolt in Corcyra failed to gain traction, reflecting the turbulent political climate in the Greek city-states during this period. The unsuccessful uprising underscored the ongoing struggles between democratic and oligarchic factions across the region.
events.name: Oligarchic Revolt in Corcyra

events.enhanced_description: Evagoras successfully reasserted his family's claim to the kingship of Salamis, a city that had been under Phoenician control for several years. His actions marked a significant moment in the struggle for power in Cyprus, as he sought to restore Hellenic influence in the region.
events.name: Evagoras' Claim to Kingship

events.enhanced_description: The Grave Stele of Hegeso, an important example of classical Greek funerary art, was created and completed approximately ten years later. This piece is notable for its intricate details and is currently preserved in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, reflecting the cultural values of the time.
events.name: Grave Stele of Hegeso

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 410, Constantine III attempted to assert his authority by crossing the Alps into Liguria, Italy. However, he was forced to retreat back to Gaul due to a revolt led by Gerontius in Spain against his son, Constans II, highlighting the instability of his rule during this tumultuous period of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Constantine III crosses the Alps into Liguria

events.enhanced_description: In 411, Emperor Honorius dispatched two Roman generals to confront the usurper Constantine III in Gaul. They successfully defeated Gerontius, a general loyal to Constantine, leading to the siege of Arles and the eventual capture and execution of Constantine III.
events.name: Emperor Honorius Sends Generals Against Constantine III

events.enhanced_description: Following the defeat of Constantine III in 411, the Burgundians and the Gallic nobility proclaimed Jovinus, a Gallo-Roman senator, as emperor of the Western Roman Empire at Mogontiacum, modern-day Mainz. This event underscored the fragmentation of imperial authority during this chaotic period.
events.name: Proclamation of Jovinus as Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 411 AD, King Ataulf of the Visigoths, motivated by a promise from Emperor Honorius to recognize a Visigothic Kingdom, led his people into Gaul to confront various usurpers threatening the Roman Empire. This marked a significant moment in the decline of Roman authority in the West and the rise of barbarian kingdoms.
events.name: King Ataulf leads the Goths into Gaul

events.enhanced_description: In 411 AD, the Alans, a group of nomadic warriors, established their dominance in the Roman province of Lusitania, which corresponds to modern-day Portugal. This event is part of the larger fragmentation of Roman control in the Iberian Peninsula during the early 5th century.
events.name: The Alans establish their rule in Lusitania

events.enhanced_description: In 411 AD, various Teutonic tribes entered into an alliance with the Roman Empire, becoming foederati, which meant they would provide military support in exchange for land and autonomy. This alliance was part of the broader strategy of the Roman Empire to secure its borders during a time of increasing instability.
events.name: Teutonic tribes join the Roman Empire as foederati

events.enhanced_description: In 411 AD, Ingyo ascended to the throne as the 19th emperor of Japan, following the death of his brother Hanzei. His reign is noted for its continuation of the Yamato dynasty and the consolidation of power in early Japanese history.
events.name: Ingyo becomes the 19th emperor of Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 411 AD, Rabbula was appointed as the bishop of Edessa, a significant center of early Christianity. His leadership would influence the theological debates of the time, particularly concerning the nature of Christ and the role of the church.
events.name: Rabbula becomes bishop of Edessa

events.enhanced_description: In 411 AD, the Councils of Carthage were convened to address the controversy surrounding Donatism, a schismatic Christian sect. These councils played a crucial role in shaping the early Christian church's response to internal divisions and heresies.
events.name: The Councils of Carthage on Donatism

events.enhanced_description: The Athenian democracy was overthrown by oligarchic extremists, including Antiphon and Theramenes, who established a 'Council of Four Hundred' to exert greater control over the war with Sparta. This regime was short-lived, lasting only four months due to internal strife and public discontent.
events.name: Overthrow of Athenian Democracy

events.enhanced_description: A mutiny erupted among the troops fortifying Piraeus, prompting the Council to send Theramenes to restore order. Instead, he allied with the mutineers, leading to the deposition of the oligarchic Council and the restoration of the traditional democratic constitution in Athens, albeit with limited citizenship rights.
events.name: Mutiny at Piraeus

events.enhanced_description: The Athenian navy, under the command of Thrasybulus, recalled Alcibiades from Sardis, confirming his election at Theramenes' request. This led to a significant naval victory against a Spartan fleet in the Hellespont, marking a turning point in the ongoing conflict between Athens and Sparta.
events.name: Recall of Alcibiades

events.enhanced_description: Antiphon delivered a remarkable defense speech, described by Thucydides as one of the greatest ever made in a trial for life. Despite his eloquence, he failed to convince the jury and was executed for treason, marking a significant moment in the political turmoil of Athens.
events.name: Antiphon's Defense Speech

events.enhanced_description: Euripides' play 'Iphigenia in Tauris' was performed, contributing to the rich tradition of Greek theater. This work reflects the themes of fate and identity that were prevalent in Euripides' writings, showcasing the cultural vibrancy of Athens during this period.
events.name: Performance of Iphigenia in Tauris

events.enhanced_description: The plays 'Lysistrata' and 'Women Celebrating the Thesmophoria' by Aristophanes were performed, highlighting the playwright's sharp wit and social commentary. These performances are emblematic of the comedic tradition in ancient Greece, reflecting societal issues through humor.
events.name: Performance of Lysistrata and Women Celebrating the Thesmophoria

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, King Ataulf led the Visigoths into southern Gaul, establishing his residence in Narbonne. This movement was part of his alliance with Emperor Honorius against the usurper Jovinus, highlighting the shifting power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Visigoths move into southern Gaul

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, Emperor Jovinus proclaimed his brother Sebastianus as co-emperor, solidifying his control over Gaul. This act was part of a broader struggle for power within the fragmented remnants of the Western Roman Empire.
events.name: Jovinus elevates Sebastianus as co-emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, Heraclianus, the governor of Africa, revolted against Emperor Honorius and declared himself Augustus, disrupting the grain supply to Rome. This rebellion exemplified the internal strife and power struggles that characterized the late Roman Empire.
events.name: Heraclianus revolts against Honorius

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, the construction of the Theodosian Walls began in Constantinople under the reign of Emperor Theodosius II, supervised by the praetorian prefect Anthemius. These fortifications would become crucial for the city's defense against invasions.
events.name: Construction of the Theodosian Walls

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, the historian Olympiodorus was dispatched on an embassy by Emperor Honorius to meet with the Huns, navigating stormy seas around Greece and up the Black Sea. This mission highlighted the complex diplomatic relations between the Roman Empire and barbarian tribes.
events.name: Olympiodorus sent on an embassy to the Huns

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, the Roman Empire undertook the rebuilding of forts along the Danube River, which had been destroyed by the Huns. This effort was part of a broader strategy to secure the empire's borders against increasing barbarian incursions.
events.name: Rebuilding of forts on the Danube

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, Emperor Honorius issued an edict outlawing Donatism, a Christian sect that had gained a following in North Africa. This decision was part of the broader efforts of the Roman state to unify religious practices within its territories.
events.name: Honorius outlaws Donatism

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, Cyril was appointed as the Patriarch of Alexandria, a pivotal role in the early Christian church. His tenure would be marked by significant theological disputes and his strong opposition to heretical movements.
events.name: Cyril of Alexandria becomes Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: In 412 AD, Bishops Lazarus of Aix-en-Provence and Herod of Arles were expelled from their sees due to accusations of Manichaeism, reflecting the ongoing struggles within the early Christian church regarding orthodoxy and heresy.
events.name: Expulsion of bishops on charges of Manichaeism

events.enhanced_description: Fa-Hien, a Chinese Buddhist monk, embarked on a significant journey to Ceylon (modern-day Sri Lanka) where he spent two years studying Buddhism. His voyage was marked by perilous sea travel, lasting over 200 days due to storms, but he successfully returned to China with sacred Buddhist texts that would influence Chinese Buddhism.
events.name: Fa-Hien's Journey to Ceylon

events.enhanced_description: Under Darius II, the Persians sought to exploit divisions among the Greek city-states to regain control of the Aegean region. The satraps Tissaphernes and Pharnabazus were tasked with collecting overdue tributes from the Greek cities, indicating a strategic shift in Persian policy towards Greece.
events.name: Persian Strategy under Darius II

events.enhanced_description: The Spartans signed the Treaty of Miletus with the Persian satrap Tissaphernes, which granted Persia significant influence in western Asia Minor in exchange for financial support for the Spartan navy. This treaty marked a pivotal moment in the Peloponnesian War, aligning Persian interests with Spartan military efforts.
events.name: Treaty of Miletus

events.enhanced_description: Alcibiades instigated revolts among Athens' allies in Ionia, aiming to weaken Spartan control in the region. However, his actions led to a loss of trust among the Spartans, prompting him to seek refuge with the Persian satrap Tissaphernes, where he continued to plot against Sparta.
events.name: Alcibiades' Revolts in Ionia

events.enhanced_description: In a critical moment during the Peloponnesian War, the Athenian assembly decided to allocate their dwindling resources towards constructing a new fleet. This decision was pivotal as it aimed to strengthen Athenian naval power in the face of increasing Spartan threats.
events.name: The Athenians vote to use their last reserves to build a new fleet

events.enhanced_description: Clazomenae, a city in Ionia, revolted against Athenian control but after a brief resistance, it was compelled to acknowledge Athenian supremacy once again. This event highlighted the ongoing struggles of Athenian dominance in the region during the Peloponnesian War.
events.name: Clazomenae revolts against Athens

events.enhanced_description: An epidemic of an unidentified disease struck Northern Greece, causing widespread fear and disruption. The impact of this epidemic on the population and the ongoing war efforts was significant, as it compounded the challenges faced by the city-states involved in the conflict.
events.name: An epidemic of an unknown disease hits Northern Greece

events.enhanced_description: The same epidemic that affected Northern Greece also spread to the Roman Republic, leading to severe food shortages. The dual crises of disease and famine posed significant challenges to the stability of the Republic during this tumultuous period.
events.name: The epidemic hits the Roman Republic and causes a food shortage

events.enhanced_description: Heraclianus, a Roman usurper, landed in Italy with a formidable army aiming to dethrone Emperor Honorius. His campaign ended in defeat in Umbria, leading to his retreat to Carthage where he faced execution by Honorius's envoys.
events.name: Heraclianus's Invasion of Italy

events.enhanced_description: In response to the devastation caused by the Visigoths, Emperor Honorius issued an edict providing tax relief to several Italian provinces, including Tuscia, Campania, and others, aiming to alleviate the burdens on the affected populations.
events.name: Honorius's Tax Relief Edict

events.enhanced_description: Under the leadership of King Ataulf, the Visigoths successfully conquered the towns of Toulouse and Bordeaux, marking a significant expansion of their territory. After a siege of Valence, they captured and executed the usurper Jovinus and his brother, sending their heads to Emperor Honorius in Ravenna.
events.name: Visigothic Conquest of Toulouse and Bordeaux

events.enhanced_description: Kumaragupta I ascended to the throne of the Gupta Empire, succeeding his father Chandragupta II. His reign marked a period of prosperity and cultural development in ancient India.
events.name: Kumaragupta I Becomes Emperor

events.enhanced_description: Jangsu ascended to the throne of the Goguryeo kingdom, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, continuing the legacy of his predecessors in consolidating power and expanding the kingdom's influence.
events.name: Jangsu Becomes Ruler of Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 59, Augustine of Hippo began writing his influential work, 'De Civitate Dei' (City of God), as a response to criticisms that Christianity was responsible for the decline of the Roman Empire. This work would become a cornerstone of Christian philosophy and theology.
events.name: Augustine Begins Writing De Civitate Dei

events.enhanced_description: Following a devastating defeat at the Battle of Syracuse, Athenian commander Lamachus was killed, and Demosthenes urged a retreat to defend Athens against an impending Spartan invasion. The Athenians faced heavy losses, leading to a significant shift in the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: Tissaphernes, the Persian satrap, forged a crucial alliance with Sparta, significantly altering the dynamics of the Peloponnesian War. With strategic guidance from Alcibiades, the Spartans advanced towards Athens, threatening Athenian control in the region.
events.name: Tissaphernes forms an alliance with Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Archelaus I ascended to the throne of Macedonia after a violent power struggle that included the murder of his family members. His reign marked a significant period of consolidation and expansion for Macedonia during its formative years.
events.name: Archelaus I becomes King of Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: The play 'Electra' by Euripides was performed, showcasing the playwright's exploration of themes such as revenge, justice, and the complexities of familial relationships. This work contributed to the rich tradition of Greek tragedy and reflected the societal issues of the time.
events.name: Euripides' play Electra is performed

events.enhanced_description: Galla Placidia, the half-sister of Emperor Honorius, married King Ataulf of the Visigoths in a politically strategic union celebrated in Narbonne. The marriage was marked by Roman festivities, symbolizing a temporary alliance between the Romans and the Visigoths.
events.name: Galla Placidia's Marriage to Ataulf

events.enhanced_description: At just 13 years old, Emperor Theodosius II ceded power to his older sister Aelia Pulcheria, who became the regent and proclaimed herself empress of the Eastern Roman Empire. This transition marked a significant shift in power dynamics within the imperial court.
events.name: Theodosius II Yields Power to Aelia Pulcheria

events.enhanced_description: Constantius III, a Roman general, initiated a military campaign against the Visigoths in Gaul, laying siege to Marseille and blockading Gallic ports. His actions were part of the broader conflict between the Roman Empire and the invading barbarian tribes.
events.name: Constantius III's Campaign Against the Visigoths

events.enhanced_description: Priscus Attalus was proclaimed as a rival emperor by the Visigoths for a second time in Bordeaux, a strategic move to exert pressure on Emperor Honorius and impose the Visigoths' terms. This event underscored the political instability of the Roman Empire during this period.
events.name: Priscus Attalus Proclaimed Rival Emperor

events.enhanced_description: The Southern Liang, one of the states during the Sixteen Kingdoms period of the Jin Dynasty, came to an end, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of ancient China. This event contributed to the fragmentation and eventual reunification of China in later periods.
events.name: End of the Southern Liang State

events.enhanced_description: After his extensive travels, Fa-Hien returned to China and began the important work of translating Buddhist texts into Chinese. His efforts were crucial in the dissemination of Buddhist teachings in China, influencing the development of Buddhism in East Asia.
events.name: Fa-Hien Returns and Translates Buddhist Texts

events.enhanced_description: Abdas, the bishop of Susa, instigated a significant religious conflict by burning a Zoroastrian temple, which provoked King Yazdegerd I of Persia to retaliate by ordering the destruction of Christian churches. This event highlights the tensions between Christianity and Zoroastrianism during this period.
events.name: Abdas Burns Zoroastrian Temple

events.enhanced_description: In response to pleas from General Nicias, Athens dispatched a fleet of 73 vessels under Demosthenes to aid in the siege of Syracuse. This military action was part of Athens' broader strategy to expand its influence in Sicily during the ongoing Peloponnesian War.
events.name: Athenian fleet sent to assist in the siege of Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: The Athenian army advanced to capture Syracuse while their fleet blocked maritime access. Despite initial successes, the Athenian forces were ultimately routed by the Spartan commander Gylippus, leading to significant losses and the death of commander Lamachus.
events.name: Athenian army moves to capture Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: The comedic play 'The Birds' by Aristophanes was performed, satirizing contemporary Athenian society and politics. This work is notable for its imaginative plot and sharp social commentary, reflecting the cultural vibrancy of Athens during this period.
events.name: Aristophanes' play The Birds is performed

events.enhanced_description: Constantius, a Roman general, successfully drove the Visigoths out of Gaul, capturing the usurper Priscus Attalus in the process. This military action was part of the ongoing struggle between the Roman Empire and barbarian invasions during the late antiquity period.
events.name: Constantius Drives the Visigoths Out of Gaul

events.enhanced_description: In 415 AD, the Visigoths, led by King Ataulf, invaded the Iberian Peninsula, seizing territories previously occupied by the Vandals. This period marked significant turmoil as Ataulf's reign was short-lived, culminating in his assassination, which further destabilized the region.
events.name: Visigoth Invasion of the Iberian Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 415 AD, Wallia ascended to the throne of the Visigoths, succeeding his brother Ataulf. He negotiated a peace treaty with Emperor Honorius, securing vital grain supplies for his people, and sent Galla Placidia to Rome as part of the agreement.
events.name: Wallia Becomes King of the Visigoths

events.enhanced_description: In 415 AD, the Daysan River experienced significant flooding, impacting the city of Edessa, a notable center of early Christian thought and culture. This natural disaster would have had profound effects on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: Flooding of the Daysan River in Edessa

events.enhanced_description: In 415 AD, Hypatia, a renowned Neoplatonist philosopher, was brutally murdered by a Christian mob incited by the patriarch Cyril of Alexandria. Her death symbolized the decline of classical philosophy and the rise of religious intolerance in the late Roman Empire.
events.name: Murder of Hypatia of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: Around 415 AD, Cyril of Alexandria, newly appointed patriarch, instigated violence against the philosopher Hypatia, reflecting the growing tensions between pagan philosophy and emerging Christian doctrine. His actions contributed to the sociopolitical upheaval in Alexandria.
events.name: Cyril's Influence in Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: In 415 AD, John Cassian settled in Marseille, France, where he founded monastic communities modeled after Eastern monasticism. His work significantly influenced the development of Western monastic practices and spirituality.
events.name: John Cassian Establishes Monastic Communities

events.enhanced_description: In 415 AD, the Eustathian schism in Antioch, which had caused significant division within the Christian community, was resolved. This event marked a crucial step towards unity in the early Church during a time of theological conflict.
events.name: Healing of the Eustathian Schism in Antioch

events.enhanced_description: Andocides, an Athenian orator, was imprisoned on suspicion of involvement in the desecration of the Hermae. This incident caused widespread panic in Athens, leading to political upheaval and the execution of several prominent figures, including Alcibiades.
events.name: Andocides imprisoned over Hermae mutilation

events.enhanced_description: The Athenian expedition to Sicily, led by generals Nicias, Lamachus, and Alcibiades, commenced its journey. However, Alcibiades faced accusations of impropriety and was recalled to Athens, highlighting the political tensions that accompanied military campaigns.
events.name: The Athenian expedition to Sicily sets sail

events.enhanced_description: After learning of his death sentence in absentia, Alcibiades defected to Sparta, shifting allegiances in the ongoing conflict. His defection had significant implications for the Athenian campaign in Sicily, as he influenced Spartan strategy against Athens.
events.name: Alcibiades defects to Sparta

events.enhanced_description: Alcibiades, now allied with Sparta, played a crucial role in persuading the Spartan leadership to send reinforcements to Syracuse. This strategic move intensified the conflict and contributed to the stalemate between Athenian and Spartan forces in Sicily.
events.name: Alcibiades persuades Sparta to assist Syracuse

events.enhanced_description: The Temple of Hephaestus, dedicated to the god of craftsmanship, was completed in 415 BC and is one of the best-preserved ancient temples in Greece. Its construction reflects the architectural advancements of the time and the importance of religion in Athenian society.
events.name: Construction of the Temple of Hephaestus in Athens is completed

events.enhanced_description: Euripides' tragedy 'The Trojan Women' was performed in Athens shortly after the brutal Athenian conquest of Melos, which saw the massacre of its male population. The play serves as a poignant commentary on the consequences of war and the suffering of women in the aftermath of conflict.
events.name: Euripides' play The Trojan Women is performed shortly after the massacre by Athenians of the male population of Melos

events.enhanced_description: In 416 AD, Priscus Attalus, a Roman usurper, was forced to participate in a triumph in Rome, celebrated by Emperor Honorius. This public humiliation marked the end of Attalus' claim to power, leading to his exile.
events.name: Priscus Attalus' Triumph in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 416 AD, the Visigoths, under King Wallia, continued their invasion of Hispania, successfully capturing Tarraconensis. This conquest included the strategic gold mines at Las Médulas, further solidifying their power in the region.
events.name: Visigoth Control of Tarraconensis

events.enhanced_description: In 416 AD, the eruption of Krakatoa was recorded in the Javanese historical chronicle known as the Book of Kings. This early documentation highlights the significant geological activity in the region and its impact on local societies.
events.name: Eruption of Krakatoa Documented

events.enhanced_description: In 416 AD, Rutilius Claudius Namatianus began his journey from Rome back to Gaul, an experience that he later immortalized in his unfinished poem, De Reditu Suo. His work reflects the cultural and political climate of the time.
events.name: Rutilius Claudius Namatianus' Journey to Gaul

events.enhanced_description: In 416 BC, under the influence of Alcibiades, the Athenians launched a military campaign against the neutral island of Melos during the Peloponnesian War. The brutal conquest resulted in the execution of all male inhabitants capable of bearing arms and the enslavement of women and children, marking a significant and tragic episode in Athenian imperialism.

image.caption: Map showing the Spartan and Athenian alliances, with Melos marked in red.
